Optimization and Control.title: Incentive-Based Regulatory Mechanism for Tariff Design in District Heating and Cooling Networks
Optimization and Control.summary: Low-temperature district heating and cooling networks exchange heat bidirectionally at near-ambient temperatures. When one supplier owns the shared loop, it controls both the tariff and the network temperature that sets every user's conversion efficiency. Existing price-cap and cost-based rules leave this non-price instrument unregulated and reach neither the first-best dispatch nor an explicit division of gains. This paper proposes a two-part, incentive-based tariff that anchors the supplier's lump-sum fee, per building and hour, to an audited outside alternative and divides the participation gains through one regulated share. We model a mixed-integer bilevel Stackelberg game in which the supplier sets hourly tariffs and the temperature regime, anticipating the buildings' co-optimization of electricity and thermal exchange. We prove that the mechanism attains the first-best welfare, posts the shadow price of the efficient dispatch as its tariff, keeps every building at or above its outside option every hour, and keeps the supplier solvent whenever operation adds surplus. A Belgian case study confirms these properties. The mechanism reproduces the centralized welfare whenever operation is worthwhile, declines to operate otherwise, holds the loop at its first-best temperature, and outperforms cap-based regulation and Ramsey pricing in welfare, user protection, and cost recovery.

Optimization and Control.title: Approximating technique for the solution to the ${H}^{\infty}$ -optimal control problem
Optimization and Control.summary: This paper continues the results published in [G. Marinoschi, Appl. Math. Optimiz. 94:44, 1-29, 2026], by presenting an approximating method of calculating the solution to the $H^{\infty }$-optimal control problem, which solves the robust stabilization of a system by a feedback controller, and to the associated Riccati equation. This method generates a sequence of infinite dimensional systems approximating the original system and the solution to the approximating $H^{\infty }$-optimal control problem is proved to converge to the solution of the original $H^{\infty }$-optimal control problem. An example for calculating the solution to the Riccati equation and the feedback controller is provided at the end.

Optimization and Control.title: Constraint-Aware Anticlustering Decomposition for Certifying Pairwise-Constrained Clustering
Optimization and Control.summary: Certifying the quality of feasible solutions to large-scale minimum sum-of-squares clustering with pairwise must-link and cannot-link constraints remains challenging, as it requires strong lower bounds on the optimal objective value. We propose a decomposition framework that partitions the data points into smaller subsets, called anticlusters, and solves the induced clustering subproblems to obtain a certified optimality gap for the original problem. To preserve pairwise information, we introduce the Constrained Anticlustering Problem (CAP), which assigns each connected component of the constraint graph to a single anticluster while seeking geometrically representative subsets. We formulate CAP as a mixed-integer second-order cone program and develop a variable neighborhood search heuristic to construct high-quality decompositions. The resulting lower bound remains valid even when the induced subproblems are not solved to global optimality. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets with up to approximately 4,000 observations show that our approach can achieve mean optimality gaps below 1% at a modest computational cost.

Optimization and Control.title: Boundary gradient asymptotics for superquadratic viscous Hamilton--Jacobi equations via optimal control
Optimization and Control.summary:
We study the boundary behavior of the maximal solution of \[
  -Δu + |\nabla u|^{p} + λu = f \] on arbitrary bounded $C^{2}$ domains, where $p > 2$ and $λ> 0$. For bounded state-dependent terms $f$, we resolve a conjecture of Lasry and Lions by establishing sharp boundary gradient asymptotics without geometric restrictions on the domain. Previously, such asymptotics were established only for certain classes of domains with additional restrictions on $p$ and $f$. We also extend the analysis to state-dependent terms that may be singular near the boundary and obtain sharp boundary profiles and gradient asymptotics.
  Our approach relies on stochastic optimal control and boundary blow-up analysis. Dynamic programming estimates and comparisons of near-optimal trajectories establish tangential invariance of boundary blow-up limits, leading to the identification of one-dimensional profiles and the asymptotic formulas. For the associated state-constrained control problem, we establish sharp asymptotics for the minimizing feedback and deduce its admissibility and optimality, with corresponding results for the ergodic problem.

Optimization and Control.title: Orlicz space relaxation of total variation denoising
Optimization and Control.summary: We consider variational image denoising with spatially dependent Orlicz regularization and introduce an Orlicz--Sobolev approximation of the ROF model based on a scaled $L\log L$-type density. For a general class of uniformly superlinear integrands satisfying a $Δ_2$-condition, we establish existence and uniqueness of minimizers and derive a Fenchel dual problem with dual attainment and pointwise optimality conditions. We then specialize the framework to a logarithmic density whose correction is activated above a prescribed local gradient scale. For this model, we obtain explicit expressions of the Fenchel dual and optimality conditions as well as a pointwise radial formula for the dual proximal map involving the Lambert $W$-function. As the logarithmic parameter tends to zero, we prove equicoercivity and $Γ$-convergence to the ROF functional, together with convergence of the corresponding minimizers. Numerical illustrations indicate that the logarithmic correction can reduce staircasing for diffuse transitions, while retaining behavior comparable to ROF for sharp interfaces and a natural image.

Optimization and Control.title: Readiness Barrier Functions: Forward-Invariant Control Authority for Overactuated Multirotor Allocation
Optimization and Control.summary: Allocators that greedily maximize a readiness metric over the actuator fiber bundle of an overactuated multirotor jump between disconnected optimal strata, demanding actuator rates no motor can deliver; effort-minimizing allocators are continuous but cannot keep wrench-rate authority above any certified level. We reconcile the two by treating authority as a forward-invariant quantity: a control barrier function on the log-determinant of the drag-aware authority co-metric, enforced at torque level by a quadratic program in the allocation null space. A single design inequality makes the certified set compact and strictly interior to the actuator box; the readiness cost of a rotor deactivation is $\ln(n/(n{-}m))$ for symmetric designs. An alignment ratio states when tracking stays exact, otherwise the wrench error is $\mathcal{O}(ρ^{-1/2})$, and a robust variant handles motor-parameter uncertainty with a closed-form floor shift independent of the airframe matrix. On a hexarotor and a fully-actuated octorotor the closed-form gap matches simulation to machine precision. Over $300$ randomized missions, greedy maximization violates the certified floor in up to $51\%$ of authority-scarce missions, while the proposed filter never leaves the certified set and, in the hardest moment reversal, commits a $79\times$ smaller wrench error. The robust variant holds the floor on all $150$ perturbed plants. A high-fidelity simulation with measured propeller and motor data shows where the floor holds under unmodeled aerodynamics, electrical limits, and delay, and where it stops applying.
Optimization and Control.comment: Accepted for publication in IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters

Optimization and Control.title: Consensus of Consensus: Decentralized Consensus-Based Optimization
Optimization and Control.summary: We propose and analyze a decentralized variant of Consensus-Based Optimization (CBO) for the global minimization of continuous, possibly non-convex functions accessible only through a stochastic, possibly biased, zeroth-order oracle with bounded mean-squared error. The agents are split among $N$ units of an undirected communication network. Each unit evolves its swarm of $M$ agents towards a local tracking variable, which follows the network average of the local consensus points through one round of neighbour-to-neighbour communication via a doubly stochastic mixing matrix, without any central coordinator. We show that, under an explicit condition linking the drift and diffusion parameters to $M$, all agents reach consensus almost surely, at an exponential mean-square rate governed by the spectrum of the mixing matrix. Using a finite-agent quantitative Laplace principle, we prove that, for large $α$ and provided some agent visits a neighbourhood of the global minimizer with sufficient probability, the expected mean-squared distance of the swarm from the minimizer falls below any tolerance within an explicit number of iterations, at a rate that deteriorates for poorly connected networks. We verify this hitting assumption for a simplified dynamics. Experiments on benchmarks up to dimension $d=1000$, with stochastic objectives, and on a federated learning task demonstrate the method's effectiveness.

Optimization and Control.title: Accelerated Bregman Proximal Gradient Methods from Dual Geometric Perspectives
Optimization and Control.summary: We study Bregman proximal gradient (BPG) algorithms under relative smoothness for convex, relatively strongly convex, and nonconvex objectives. Existing accelerated BPG algorithms for convex objectives typically require additional assumptions on Bregman divergences, most notably triangle-scaling conditions, which can lead to slower convergence rates. We propose a family of geometry-accelerated BPG algorithms that exploit Bregman geometry in both proximal-gradient and mirror-space updates, without imposing a triangle-scaling condition. Our methods adapt the stepsizes and mirror-space updates through local backtracking and computable acceptance criteria, without a global relative-smoothness constant as input. We derive convergence bounds in terms of the parameters accepted during the iterations. These bounds yield an $\mathcal O(k^{-2})$ rate for convex objectives and a linear rate for relatively strongly convex objectives when the geometry-acceleration parameters remain uniformly bounded. For nonconvex objectives, we establish an $\mathcal O(k^{-1})$ rate for a stationarity measure without requiring a lower Bregman bound or a full-domain Bregman divergence. Numerical experiments on inverse problems, entropy-regularized least squares, D-optimal design, and nonnegative matrix factorization demonstrate faster practical convergence than established Bregman baselines.

Optimization and Control.title: Out-of-the-Box Global Optimization for Packing Problems: New Models and Improved Solutions
Optimization and Control.summary:
Recent LLM-driven discoveries have renewed interest in geometric packing problems. In this paper, we study several classes of such packing problems through the lens of modern global nonlinear optimization. Starting from comparatively direct nonlinear formulations, we consider packing circles in squares and fixed-perimeter rectangles, packing circles into minimum-area ellipses, packing regular polygons into regular polygons, and packing Platonic solids into Platonic solids. For ellipse packing, we derive a novel containment formulation based on the S-lemma. For polygon and Platonic solid packing, we develop compact non-overlap formulations based on the Farkas lemma and study several natural modeling variants computationally.
  Using off-the-shelf global optimization solvers, namely FICO Xpress and SCIP, we obtain numerous new incumbent solutions as well as first solutions for previously unstudied variants without any problem-specific solver modifications beyond writing down the models. Our computational results analyze the impact of various formulation choices.
  Beyond the individual packing results, the paper illustrates a broader point. It provides further evidence that global nonlinear optimization has matured into an increasingly practical model-and-solve technology for highly nonconvex problems.

Optimization and Control.title: Recovery guarantees for compressed sensing photoacoustic tomography
Optimization and Control.summary: Photoacoustic tomography is an emerging medical imaging technology whose primary aim is to map the high-contrast optical properties of biological tissues by leveraging high-resolution ultrasound measurements. Mathematically, this can be framed as an inverse source problem for the wave equation over a specific domain. In this work, for the first time, it is shown how, by assuming signal sparsity, it is possible to establish rigorous stable recovery guarantees when the data collection is given by spatial averages restricted to a sparse, randomly sampled portion of the boundary. Our framework encompasses many approaches that have been considered in the literature. The result is a consequence of a general framework for subsampled inverse problems developed in previous works and refined stability estimates for an inverse problem for the wave equation with surface measurements.

Optimization and Control.title: "It Was a Magical Box": Understanding Practitioner Workflows and Needs in Optimization
Optimization and Control.summary: Optimization underpins decision-making in domains from healthcare to logistics, yet for many practitioners it remains a "magical box": powerful but opaque, difficult to use, and reliant on specialized expertise. While prior work has extensively studied machine learning workflows, the everyday practices of optimization model developers (OMDs) have received little attention. We conducted semi-structured interviews with 15 OMDs across diverse domains to examine how optimization is done in practice. Our findings reveal a highly iterative workflow spanning six stages: problem elicitation, data processing, model development, implementation, validation, and deployment. Importantly, we find that optimization practice is not only about algorithms that deliver better decisions, but is equally shaped by data and dialogue---the ongoing communication with stakeholders that enables problem framing, calibrated trust, and adoption. We discuss opportunities for future tooling that foregrounds data and dialogue alongside decision-making, opening new directions for human-centered optimization.
Optimization and Control.comment: Proc. ACM Hum.-Comput. Interact., Vol. 11, No. 2, Article CSCW010

Optimization and Control.title: Critical-Point Characterization of Rank-Constrained Optimization and Global Convergence of Projected Gradient Descent
Optimization and Control.summary: We study the rank-constrained problem $\min_{\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{X})\leq r} f(\mathbf{X})$ when the unconstrained minimizer $\mathbf{X}_*$ has rank $r_*\leq r$. We apply a sharp matrix inequality to characterize critical points and establish deterministic global linear convergence of projected gradient descent (ProjGD). First, assuming that $f$ satisfies rank-$(r+r_*)$ restricted smoothness and strong convexity with constants $L$ and $μ$, respectively, where $0<μ<L$, we show that every nonoptimal rank-$r$ critical point satisfies the inequality $\|P_{T(\mathbf{X})^\perp}\nabla f(\mathbf{X})\|/σ_r(\mathbf{X}) \geq (2Lμ/(L-μ))\sqrt{r/r_*}$. Here $P_{T(\mathbf{X})^\perp}\nabla f(\mathbf{X})$ is the component of the gradient normal to the tangent space $T(\mathbf{X})$ and $σ_r(\mathbf{X})$ is the $r$-th singular value of $\mathbf{X}$. Second, this inequality implies that $\mathbf{X}_*$ is the unique fixed point of ProjGD whenever the step size $η$ satisfies $η>\sqrt{r_*/r}(L-μ)/(2Lμ)$. Finally, under an additional rank-$2r$ restricted smoothness assumption, we apply the argument to the actual ProjGD iterates, establish a uniform improvement estimate for every iteration, and prove deterministic global linear convergence from every initialization of rank at most $r$ for $\sqrt{r_*/r}(L-μ)/(2Lμ)<η<1/L$. The result allows arbitrary rank overparameterization $r\geq r_*$, and its convergence rate is independent of the singular-value condition number of $\mathbf{X}_*$. As a consequence, a rank-preserving curve argument proves the no-spurious-local-minima property whenever $(L-μ)/(L+μ)<(1+\sqrt{r_*/r})^{-1}$. This matches the sharp threshold established by McRae et al. (2026). A quadratic example shows that the lower bound on the step size $\sqrt{r_*/r}(L-μ)/(2Lμ)$ is also sharp.

Optimization and Control.title: A Structured Levenberg--Marquardt Method for Binary Tensor Completion
Optimization and Control.summary: We develop a structured Levenberg--Marquardt (LM) method with trust-region globalization for binary tensor completion, using triple decomposition and a logistic loss. Under a local component-residual error bound and positive outer curvature, we prove quadratic convergence of the exact iteration for damping exponents $1\leδ\le2$, without requiring full row rank. A constant-rank criterion and an explicit rank-one certificate provide sufficient conditions for the residual error bound. The analysis decomposes the local error into outer-loss linearization, factor linearization, and regularization contributions. For a symmetric nonquadratic logistic--LSE family with $δ=2$, cancellation improves the objective-model error to fourth order and the decrease-ratio error to second order. A synthetic experiment illustrates the local quadratic convergence rate. On the HCP and Enron datasets, the proposed method improves binary tensor completion accuracy while requiring fewer outer iterations than the first-order methods.

Optimization and Control.title: Linear Convergence of Adaptive Accelerated Gradient Methods: A Unified Framework
Optimization and Control.summary: We establish a unified Lyapunov framework for adaptive accelerated gradient methods on smooth, strongly convex objectives. Conditions on local curvature, stepsize ratios, and coefficient variation ensure eventual linear convergence without assuming stepsize convergence. We verify these conditions for specified AdaNAG-G, smooth unconstrained AC-FGM, and AdaAGM policies and use them to design VC-FG and CC-FG. The verified adaptive main iterations require neither global smoothness nor strong-convexity parameters and avoid restart and backtracking. The framework also sharpens a fixed-step FISTA/NAG-type bound. Experiments on four smooth, strongly convex problem families illustrate complementary performance of the new methods.

Optimization and Control.title: Gradient-based optimization of buoyancy distributions for lazy-wave risers
Optimization and Control.summary: This paper presents a novel gradient-based approach for optimizing the buoyancy distribution of lazy-wave offshore risers. The static response is modeled with a total potential energy formulation for a geometrically nonlinear, inextensible beam on an elastic seabed. The total potential energy is discretized by finite differences and the resulting nonlinear equilibrium system is solved by a two stage continuation procedure, in which the line length and then the buoyancy load are increased incrementally, with Newton--Raphson iterations and an Armijo line search. The design variables are the uplift ratios at the nodes where buoyancy modules may be installed. The optimization minimizes a quadratic measure of buoyancy demand subject to constraints on the maximum curvature and effective tension. The gradients of the constraints are computed by means of a discrete adjoint sensitivity analysis. Three design parametrizations are compared: a continuous formulation with independent nodal uplift ratios, a grouped formulation with fixed module assignments, and a formulation inspired by discrete material optimization that simultaneously selects the uplift ratios of a small catalog of module types and their placement along the riser. The latter yields practical designs with a limited number of module sizes. The framework provides a flexible and computationally efficient tool for preliminary design of lazy-wave configurations.

Optimization and Control.title: Halpern Iteration Accelerates Solving High-Order Monotone Variational Inequalities
Optimization and Control.summary: In this short note, we revisit the classical Halpern iteration in 1967 and show its new applications in designing second- and higher-order methods for solving smooth monotone variational inequalities (MVI). By using a large-step inexact Halpern iteration, we propose a novel $p$th-order method Halpern-ATM, that achieves a fast convergence rate of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{-p})$. This improves the best-known results for $p \ge 2$ since 2012.
Optimization and Control.comment: A short note interpreting a new result by GPT-5.6 Sol

Optimization and Control.title: A Validation-Driven Bilevel Optimization Method for Mesh-Free PDE Solvers and Its Error Analysis
Optimization and Control.summary: Mesh-free partial differential equation (PDE) solvers construct discrete systems from residuals at sampled points. These solvers fit coefficients in a parameterized trial representation and select solver-design parameters governing the representation, training-residual weighting, and regularization. These parameters strongly affect solution accuracy, yet existing selection strategies are largely tailored to particular solver classes. To address this limitation, we formulate a unified validation-driven bilevel optimization framework applicable across different solver classes, in which the lower level fits coefficients using training collocation residuals, while the upper level selects solver-design parameters using held-out validation residuals. For nonlinear PDEs, however, solving the nonlinear lower-level problem to high accuracy is costly, while the adjoint system is typically ill-conditioned and indefinite. To address this issue, we propose an efficient implicit hypergradient method that approximates the lower-level response using finite, warm-started damped Gauss-Newton (GN) updates. For the adjoint solve, we use the damped GN matrix to compute an initial adjoint and to precondition a finite number of minimum residual iterations. To quantify the errors introduced by these approximations, we derive local hypergradient error bounds that separate the contributions of the finite lower-level solve, adjoint damping, and the final adjoint residual. Combining this analysis with validation sampling bounds and residual stability, we relate validation residuals to PDE solution accuracy and establish error bounds for the computed PDE solution. Numerical experiments on several nonlinear PDEs, including a high-dimensional problem, demonstrate the accuracy and efficiency of the proposed method across Kansa, random feature and extreme learning machine, and physics-informed neural network solvers.

Optimization and Control.title: When and Why SignSGD Outperforms SGD: A Theoretical Study Based on $\ell_1$-norm Lower Bounds
Optimization and Control.summary: Sign-based optimization algorithms, such as SignSGD and Muon, have garnered significant attention for their remarkable performance in training large foundation models. Despite this empirical success, we still lack a theoretical understanding of when and why these sign-based methods outperform vanilla SGD. The core obstacle is that under standard smoothness and finite variance conditions, SGD is known to be minimax optimal for finding stationary points measured by $\ell_2$-norms, thereby fundamentally precluding any complexity gains for sign-based methods in standard settings. To overcome this barrier, we analyze sign-based optimizers leveraging $\ell_1$-norm stationarity, $\ell_\infty$-smoothness, and a separable noise model, which can better capture the coordinate-wise nature of signed updates. Under this distinct problem geometry, we derive matched upper and lower bounds for SignSGD and explicitly characterize the problem class in which SignSGD provably dominates SGD. Specifically, we compare the upper bound of SignSGD with the lower bound of SGD, illustrating that SignSGD effectively reduces the complexity by a factor of $d$ under sparse noise, where $d$ is the problem dimension. Furthermore, we elevate this framework to the matrix domain, providing an equivalent optimal lower bound for the Muon optimizer, proving that extending the sign operator to matrices preserves this optimal scaling with dimensionality. Finally, we bridge our theoretical bounds to practice, demonstrating that the theoretical superiority of SignSGD accurately predicts its faster convergence during the pretraining of nanoGPT and LLaMA, with Muon also outperforming SGD in these experiments. Code is available at https://github.com/Dingzhen230/SignSGD_Outperforms_SGD.

Optimization and Control.title: On the Existence of Koopman Linear Embeddings for Controlled Nonlinear Systems
Optimization and Control.summary: Koopman linear representations have become a popular tool for control design of nonlinear systems, yet it remains unclear when such representations are exact. In this paper, we establish sufficient and necessary conditions under which a controlled nonlinear system admits an exact Koopman linear representation in both infinite-dimensional and finite-dimensional settings. We show that such a system must be transformable into a special control-affine preserved (CAP) structure, which enforces affine dependence of the state on the control input and isolates all nonlinearities into an autonomous subsystem. We further prove that a finite-dimensional representation additionally requires this autonomous subsystem must itself admit a finite-dimensional Koopman linear model with a sufficiently-rich Koopman invariant subspace. Finally, we introduce a symbolic procedure to determine whether a given controlled nonlinear system admits the CAP structure, thereby elucidating whether Koopman approximation errors arise from intrinsic system dynamics or from the choice of lifting functions.

Optimization and Control.title: Data Informativity for Robust Feedback Rectification of Switched Linear Systems
Optimization and Control.summary: Feedback rectification is a method for switched linear systems that constructs a mode-dependent state feedback such that the closed-loop subsystems share a common eigenvector basis. If the assigned eigenvalues lie inside the unit disk, this yields a common quadratic Lyapunov function and guarantees exponential stability under arbitrary switching. In this paper, we study robust feedback rectification from input-state data affected by bounded disturbances. Using the concept of data informativity, we derive necessary and sufficient conditions for approximate feedback rectification without requiring full row-rank of the collected input-state data. If the rectification error is smaller than the stability margin of the prescribed eigenvalues, we obtain global exponential stability under arbitrary switching in the disturbance-free case, and practical global asymptotic stability under bounded disturbances. The approach is illustrated by a mass-spring-damper chain with varying stiffness, where prescribed poles are assigned in every mode from data that do not determine the system matrices uniquely.

Optimization and Control.title: From data pencils to image representations of continuous-time LTI systems
Optimization and Control.summary: The continuous-time fundamental lemma describes the set of all trajectories of a linear time-invariant system by a Gramian matrix built from measured input--output data and their derivatives. The jet of a trajectory is represented as the Gramian applied to a nonunique parameter satisfying a differential-algebraic equation. We determine the complete Kronecker structure of the associated data pencil for multiple-input multiple-output systems. This enables the construction of a polynomial image representation of the input--output behavior directly from the data. The resulting image matrix has column degrees equal to the controllability indices, and its latent variable is free and serves as a flat output of the system. The computation relies on an orthogonal staircase reduction followed by basis reconstruction using polynomial kernels. We also propose a structure-preserving preconditioning of the Gramian to improve its condition number and facilitate rank decisions in the reduction. We illustrate our approach on a chain of mass-spring-damper systems.

Optimization and Control.title: Error-Corrected Physics-Informed Neural Operator for Optimal Control of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles under Uncertainty
Optimization and Control.summary: We solve open-loop optimal control problems under parametric uncertainty using a physics-informed DeepONet that returns trajectories for all sampled scenarios in one evaluation. Trained only on the residual at generic controls, the operator is reused across targets and horizons. Because a gradient-based optimizer exploits surrogate errors, we correct the prediction by one Newton step on the dynamics, computed for all scenarios and times by one parallel scan. The corrected state has a second-order error bounded by the residual alone, and the corrected cost is honest for every control up to the sampling error. On a fixed-wing UAV benchmark, the corrected operator matches the accuracy of a batched Adam solver and an Ipopt solver at equal sample size and is 8 times faster than the Adam solver on the same GPU at a few hundred scenarios and 15 times faster than Ipopt on a CPU.

Optimization and Control.title: Stinespring's Dilation, Universal-NOT, and Limitations of Quantum Uncoupled Learning
Optimization and Control.summary: Uncoupled learning, in which players know only their own payoff, are a standard model of decentralized learning toward Nash equilibrium. We study their quantum counterpart, where strategies are quantum states and, in each round, a player receives a physical copy of their opponent's current strategy and updates their own state by a quantum channel. This adds to uncoupledness a constraint with no classical analogue: every update must be physically realizable. In fact, this constraint is decisive in conjugation games, in which Bob has a strictly dominant pure strategy and Alice's unique best response is its transpose. In this work, we show some limitations of uncoupled (learning) dynamics in finding the Nash equilibrium for conjugation games. First, we prove that no autonomous, memoryless, uncoupled dynamics converge to Nash equilibrium in a family of four single-qubit conjugation games. Specifically, any memoryless channel that keeps all four equilibria fixed will leave Alice's strategy frozen. This result also extends to $4^n$ games on $n$-qubit registers. Second, we show that this barrier disappears with a small classical memory: for any finite family of $L$ pure targets, a guess-and-test rule with $O(\log L)$ classical bits converges to equilibrium, with an explicit bound on its convergence rate. Finally, we prove that no finite memory, classical or quantum, suffices for the continuum of all pure-qubit targets. Our proof of the impossibility for memoryless channels relies on Stinespring's dilation theorem, while the impossibility for finite-memory channels relies on the optimal universal-NOT (in)fidelity bound by Bužek, Hillery, and Werner.

Optimization and Control.title: When Speed Changes Where to Build: Optimal Placement of an Optional Fast Connection
Optimization and Control.summary: Express roads, limited-stop transit, and air taxis speed up only the trips that choose them, while others stay on the ground network. Where should such a connection's terminals go? Because its users change with the design, expected travel time is nonconvex and nonsmooth in the terminal locations. Previous models have therefore been solved numerically or in restricted settings. We solve a canonical case exactly: uniform trips in a square with grid streets and a straight link. We find that every optimal design is centered and diagonal or axis aligned, and the alignment switches once, near 2.18 times ground speed. The two designs tied there differ sharply in coverage and ridership. A planner also choosing speed, at a smooth cost of speed, never selects the switching speed. If the cost is proportional to speed, above a threshold unit cost the planner builds a slower diagonal link, below it a faster axis-aligned one, and the optimal speed skips a band around the switch. On a rectangle, every optimum is again centered, centered designs have a closed-form travel time, and only two families of links can be optimal, those along the long axis and those tilted toward the long side.

Optimization and Control.title: Performance guarantees for optimization-based state estimation using turnpike properties
Optimization and Control.summary: In this paper, we develop novel accuracy and performance guarantees for optimal state estimation of general nonlinear systems (in particular, moving horizon estimation, MHE). Our results rely on a turnpike property of the optimal state estimation problem, which essentially states that the omniscient infinite-horizon solution involving all past and future data serves as turnpike for the solutions of finite-horizon estimation problems involving a subset of the data. This leads to the surprising observation that MHE problems naturally exhibit a leaving arc, which may have a strong negative impact on the estimation accuracy. To address this, we propose a delayed MHE scheme, and we show that the resulting performance (both averaged and non-averaged) is approximately optimal and achieves bounded regret with respect to the infinite-horizon solution, with error terms that can be made arbitrarily small by an appropriate choice of the delay. In various simulation examples, we observe that already a very small delay in the MHE scheme is sufficient to significantly improve the overall estimation error by 20-25% compared to standard MHE (without delay). This finding is of great importance for practical applications (especially for monitoring, fault detection, and parameter estimation) where a small delay in the estimation is rather irrelevant but may significantly improve the estimation results.

Optimization and Control.title: Geometry-Preserving Neural Architectures on Manifolds with Boundary
Optimization and Control.summary: A growing number of neural architectures have been developed to enforce geometric constraints, including projection-based networks, exponential-map updates, and manifold neural ODEs. In this paper, we study several such architectures, with the goal of understanding their approximation-theoretic properties and trade-offs. We distinguish between architectures that enforce constraints at intermediate layers and those that enforce constraints only at the output. For projected neural ODEs on uniformly prox-regular sets, we establish stability estimates and derive universal approximation results on compact smooth manifolds, including manifolds with boundary. In particular, we establish universal approximation of measurable manifold-valued maps in the $L^2$ topology. In contrast, architectures that enforce constraints only at the output can admit uniform approximation guarantees for continuous target maps under suitable geometric assumptions. We further investigate how the choice of constraint-enforcing map, namely metric projection or the Riemannian exponential map, affects these guarantees. While both constructions can be used to preserve constraints at intermediate layers, their use at the output leads to different approximation properties. In particular, exponential-map output architectures can encounter topological obstructions to uniform approximation, motivating approximation guarantees in $L^2$. On the other hand, metric projection-based output architectures can retain uniform approximation guarantees when the constraint set has positive reach. Our study raises the broader question of when the additional complexity of enforcing constraints at intermediate layers, as motivated by neural ODE approaches, and different choices of constraint-enforcing map are justified by the resulting benefits in approximation and learning performance.

Optimization and Control.title: Intercity EV Charging Readiness in Türkiye: A Countrywide Scheduling and Economic Assessment
Optimization and Control.summary: This paper assesses whether Türkiye's 9,641 public charging stations licensed by the Energy Market Regulatory Authority (EPDK) can support intercity electric vehicle (EV) travel, and at what cost relative to internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles. A charging scheduling framework based on a directed acyclic graph plans the charging stops of 3 million synthetic intercity trips on a 55,236-link highway network built from OpenStreetMap. Virtually all trips can be completed with the existing stations under both 10--100% and 20--80% state-of-charge windows; the 0.3% feasibility that a 20--80% window can produce arises only when trips must also start within the window, not from gaps in the network. Capacity, not coverage, is the binding constraint: with plug counts calibrated to EPDK socket statistics, uncoordinated charging builds long queues at the stations where trips converge, whereas coordinating charging times with reservations nearly eliminates waiting at today's adoption level of about 3%. In the 350 kW scenario at 3% adoption, the EV is 49.8% cheaper than the ICE vehicle in operating costs (energy, refueling, detour, and charging time) and 7.4% cheaper in total cost of ownership, an advantage that holds as long as the EV costs at most about 9% more than a comparable ICE vehicle. Adding the cost of charging infrastructure makes the EV more expensive at low adoption with high-power chargers and cheaper as adoption grows.

Optimization and Control.title: Carleman estimates and $φ$-null controllability for a fully discrete fourth-order parabolic equation
Optimization and Control.summary: We consider a fully discrete approximation of a one-dimensional fourth-order parabolic equation with clamped boundary conditions, obtained by centered finite differences in space and the implicit Euler method in time, and controlled by two boundary controls acting at the left endpoint. We prove a Carleman estimate for the corresponding discrete adjoint operator, in which the large Carleman parameter is connected to the space and time discretization parameters $h$ and $Δt$. As a consequence, we obtain a relaxed observability inequality and a $φ(h)$-null controllability result, in which the controls are bounded uniformly with respect to $h$ and $Δt$, and the norm of the solution at the final time is of order $\sqrt{φ(h)}$, with $φ(h)$ exponentially small, provided $Δt\le h^μ$ for some $μ\ge1$.

Optimization and Control.title: Fair Property Tax: Reducing Regressivity in Machine-Learning Valuation
Optimization and Control.summary: Advanced machine-learning models are increasingly used for property valuation in tax assessment. Although these models can achieve high predictive accuracy, they may systematically assign higher valuation-to-sale ratios to lower-priced properties, a pattern known as regressivity. In collaboration with the Cook County Assessor's Office (CCAO), we develop and evaluate two training methods that substantially reduce this regressive pattern while maintaining price-scale predictive accuracy. The Direct method has been incorporated into CCAO's public residential valuation software. Retaining the LightGBM model class used at CCAO, we propose a Direct penalty on squared covariance between log valuation errors and log sale prices, and an observation-additive Surrogate that yields a weighted squared-error loss. We evaluate both methods in our implementation of the CCAO workflow, using seven chronological validation folds, a held-out test set, and a 2025-forward test set. Measured by the magnitude of price-related bias (PRB), regressivity falls by approximately 49% on held-out sales and 39% on 2025 sales at a Surrogate setting selected by cross-validation, relative to the same LightGBM model fitted without the penalty. Price-scale $R^2$ is essentially unchanged. Its small rise, from 0.893 to 0.897 on held-out sales and from 0.904 to 0.908 on 2025 sales, reflects overall valuation level. Log-price RMSE rises by 3.1% and 1.7%, respectively. Paired sale-bootstrap 90% intervals for the PRB reductions lie within about two percentage points of these estimates. In an additional eight-county benchmark, both methods reduce regressivity in every county, with higher log-price prediction error as the expected tradeoff. These findings demonstrate a practical way to reduce measured regressivity within an existing assessor workflow while preserving price-scale predictive performance.

Optimization and Control.title: Error analysis and optimal sample allocation for randomized unbiased estimation: the single term estimator
Optimization and Control.summary: Randomized unbiased estimation can be highly efficient for approximating expectations of functionals of stochastic differential equations. However, in practice, the optimal computational efficiency is rarely attained due to errors arising from parameter estimation and truncation. The effects of these errors on computational efficiency have not been investigated. In this article, we study the error analysis and optimal sample allocation for the single term estimator. Specifically, under mild assumptions on the estimated parameters, we develop a unified error analysis that incorporates both sources of error, and establish the relevant convergence rates for the computational efficiency loss. Based on this analysis, we further investigate the optimal allocation of the computational budget for parameter estimation, and propose several efficient sample allocation strategies. Numerical experiments support the theoretical convergence rates and demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed methods.

Optimization and Control.title: Uncovering Multimorbidity Patterns Through a Novel Randomized Clustering Algorithm
Optimization and Control.summary: Patients with several chronic conditions rarely share the same combination: in four years of the nationally representative Medical Expenditure Panel Survey (MEPS), we find 32,789 distinct combinations of two to seven conditions, and over 90% of those involving four or more occur in a single patient. Methods that search for common combinations discard most of this heterogeneity. We present the Randomized Length Sequential Clustering Algorithm (RLSCA), which links diseases by lift, a pairwise association measure counted only above a user-set support threshold. A mixed-integer program repeatedly selects and removes the group of conditions with the greatest internal lift, up to a random size; 100 iterations yield a database of clusters scored by size, rediscovery frequency, and body systems spanned. In MEPS 2019, stratified by age and sex, RLSCA recovers known groupings at a high threshold, such as diabetes with lipid disorders and hypertension, and at a lower threshold returns clusters of up to eight conditions spanning five body systems. Frequent itemset mining, at its lowest feasible support, finds no set above five conditions; hierarchical clustering cannot control cluster size. With a clinical large language model, the database could suggest which further conditions a patient is at risk of.

Optimization and Control.title: A Lower Bound on the Sliced Wasserstein Comparison Constant for Translated Measures
Optimization and Control.summary: We provide closed-form expressions for standard 1-Wasserstein distance ($W_1$) and Sliced 1-Wasserstein distance ($SW_1$) for translated probability measures on $\mathbb{R}^d$. Furthermore, we construct an explicit lower bound for the constant $c_d$ established by Carlier, Figalli, Mérigot, and Wang between $W_1$ and $SW_1$ [1] for translated probability measures on $\mathbb{R}^d$. Sliced Wasserstein distances are computationally efficient and used in image generation and other applications, which raises natural questions in computational efficiency versus theoretical correctness. A lower bound on the constant $c_d$ gives information about the cost of that efficiency.
Optimization and Control.comment: 2nd version: extended Propositions 1 & 2 to finite-dimensional real Hilbert spaces, fixed typos and added acknowledgments

Optimization and Control.title: Pooled Inverse Optimization: Learning the Unique Optimal Decision from Repeated Observations
Optimization and Control.summary: Inverse optimization infers a decision-maker's objective from observed decisions. We study repeated noisy observations of one decision. Classical formulations impute a separate optimum for each observation, so their size grows with the sample, and may return one of many equally compatible objectives. With a bounded polyhedral feasible set and a cost vector drawn from a distribution with a density, the optimum is almost surely a unique vertex. Its compatible costs form a full-dimensional cone that repeated observations of the same decision cannot shrink. Pooled inverse optimization fits one optimum to all observations and reports its compatible cost cone. Under squared loss, the optimization model has fixed size after aggregation, the decision estimate has a finite-sample error bound, and guarded rounding recovers the true vertex and its full cone with probability tending to one. A single convex program sufficed in every linear scaling run. With 50 variables and 10,000 observations, median runtimes were 8 milliseconds under squared loss and 8 seconds under absolute loss. The standard mixed-integer formulation reached its time limit at 100 observations. At 10,000 observations, the remaining two exact formulations under absolute loss and two convex baselines reached their 10- to 60-minute limits. Using national survey data on women with hypertension and diabetes or prediabetes, the method finds in milliseconds the diet closest to each woman's mean reported intake subject to DASH-based nutrient bounds in a food-group model and identifies which bounds bind.

Previous title: "From Non-Identifiability to Goal-Integrated Decision-Making in Parametric Inverse Optimization". This version treats the pooled model and its computational study; the goal-integrated models of version 1 are not included

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: No Polynomial-Time Algorithm For Tarski Fixed Points Unless Cryptographic Assumptions Fail
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study the time complexity of finding a Tarski fixed point. We provide a subexponential-time reduction from the Unique End of Potential Line (UEOPL) problem to the problem of finding a Tarski fixed point. Using a range of known cryptographic lower bounds for UEOPL, our reduction implies a range of conditional lower bounds on the running time of any algorithm that finds a Tarski fixed point. The strongest of these give quasi-polynomial-time lower bounds for the problem. We also obtain a similar quasi-polynomial-time lower bound for Tarski based instead on a weak exponential-time type hypothesis for UEOPL. These running time lower bounds match the recently discovered quasi-polynomial query lower bounds for the problem.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Recognizing $k$-inducible Digraphs is NP-complete
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: A digraph is k-inducible if its arcs correspond to the pairwise majority relation of a preference profile with k voters. By McGarvey's theorem, every asymmetric digraph is k-inducible for some k, but for every fixed k there are digraphs that are not k-inducible. Whether a digraph is 1-inducible or 2-inducible can easily be decided in polynomial time. The complexity of deciding whether a digraph is k-inducible for every fixed $k\geq 3$ has been a long-standing open problem. We prove that deciding whether a tournament is 3-inducible is NP-complete and then leverage this result to show that deciding whether a digraph is k-inducible is NP-complete for every fixed $k\geq 3$. Our results imply that, unless P=NP, k-inducible digraphs cannot be characterized by finitely many forbidden induced subdigraphs.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: 22 pages

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: No, Cake Cutting Really is a Piece of Cake
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We design and analyze a deterministic cake cutting algorithm that achieves proportional fairness using a linear number of cuts. The best previous upper bound on the number of cuts for a deterministic algorithm was $O(n \log n)$, which was obtained by a natural divide-and-conquer algorithm due to Even and Paz. It has long been conjectured that $O(n \log n)$ cuts was optimal for a deterministic algorithm.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Kidney Exchange in Deterministic $O^*(4^{t+o(t)})$ Time
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Kidney exchange admits a randomized $O^*(4^t)$ algorithm parameterized by the target number $t$ of transplants, but the best previous deterministic algorithm requires $O^*(6.855^t)$ time. We nearly close this gap by developing a deterministic $O^*(4^{t+o(t)})$ algorithm. Our approach uses Dynamic Representative Sets to execute the semi-feasible packing recurrence under a global cardinality budget of $2t$, exploiting a residual extension-budget invariant to avoid repeated static representative-family compression. To handle admissible cycles containing at least $t$ vertices, we establish a deterministic $O^*(4^{k+o(k)})$ algorithm for finding a shortest simple directed cycle of length at least $k$. Beyond feasibility, our framework supports additive optimization, yielding the same running-time bound for maximizing arc utility among packings with exactly $t$ transplants. Consequently, a packing that lexicographically maximizes the number of transplants and then additive utility can be computed deterministically in $O^*(4^{τ+o(τ)})$ time, where $τ$ is the maximum achievable number of transplants.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: 24 pages; submitted

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Learning to Allocate Resources with Censored Feedback
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study the online resource allocation problem in which at each round, a budget $B$ must be allocated across $K$ arms under censored feedback. An arm yields a reward if and only if two conditions are satisfied: (i) the arm is activated according to an arm-specific Bernoulli random variable with unknown parameter, and (ii) the allocated budget exceeds a random threshold drawn from a parametric distribution with unknown parameter. Over $T$ rounds, the learner must jointly estimate the unknown parameters and allocate the budget so as to maximize cumulative reward facing the exploration-exploitation trade-off. We prove a worst-case regret lower bound $Ω(\sqrt{T})$ for the general model, even with known uniform threshold distributions. We then propose RA-UCB, an optimistic algorithm that leverages non-trivial parameter estimation and confidence bounds. When the budget $B$ is known at the beginning of each round and every arm receives a positive allocation at the optimum (interior optimum, with a known lower bound), RA-UCB achieves a regret bound of order $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$, and even $O(\mathrm{poly}\log T)$ under stronger assumptions. For unknown, round-dependent budgets, we introduce MG-UCB, which allows within-round switching and infinitesimal allocations, and matches the regret guarantees of RA-UCB; we also discuss an implementable discretization. We then validate our theoretical results through experiments on real-world datasets.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Nashtopes and their A-discriminants
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
An $n$-player game in normal form is said to be of format $\boldsymbol{d} = (d_1, \dots, d_n)$ if the $i$-th player has $d_i$ options for $1 \le i \le n$, and is said to be balanced if $d_n - 1 \le \sum_{i=1}^{n-1}(d_i - 1)$. The Nash equilibria of the game correspond to solutions of the system of indifference equations for the game, with payoff differences as coefficients and strategy probabilities as variables. As such, the mixed discriminant of this system gives some information about which games could have an unusual number of totally mixed Nash equilibria. This mixed discriminant can be regarded as an $\mathcal{A}$-discriminant for some matrix $\mathcal{A}$ in the sense of [Gelfand--Kapranov--Zelevinsky 1994], and the convex hull of the columns of $\mathcal{A}$ is a polytope, which we call the Nashtope.
  We study this $\mathcal{A}$-discriminant for each balanced game format with at least three players. This discriminant is a subset of the Nash discriminant variety introduced in [Abo--Portakal--Sodomaco 2026]. We compute the codimension and degree of this discriminant for all balanced game formats, including on-boundary formats, using the Euler obstruction formula in [Matsui--Takeuchi 2011]. Our $\mathcal{A}$-discriminant locus corresponds to a special multigraded Hurwitz locus studied in [Pratt--Sodomaco--Sturmfels 2026]. As a consequence of [Pokidkin 2026], we obtain the codimensions and degrees of the irreducible components of the Nash discriminant variety for each balanced game format with at least three players, fully resolving Problem 3.8 of [Abo--Portakal--Sodomaco 2026].
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: 36 pages, 4 tables. Supplementary software documentation is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23190651

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Epistemic Social Learning: Latent Behavioral Structure under Endogenous Multi-Agent Interaction
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: In multi-agent interaction, a learner's actions shape the observations from which it infers other agents' behavior. A behavioral model may predict these observations well yet support poor adaptation when opponents change. We introduce Epistemic Social Learning (ESL), which couples fast, interaction-specific Bayesian beliefs with slower online learning of population-shared behavioral prototypes. Belief-conditioned decisions influence subsequent observations and, in turn, the representations learned from them. Under explicit regularity and averaging assumptions, we provide a conditional stochastic-approximation characterization of these coupled dynamics. Across twelve synthetic $3\times3$ cooperative, coordination, and adversarial games, ESL achieves the lowest aggregate post-switch regret among the evaluated online latent-adaptation methods, including a switch-aware Bayesian filter. Additional experiments examine observation loss, noise, and asymmetric incentives. These findings illustrate how predictive fit can differ from decision-relevant adaptation under policy-dependent interaction.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: The Complexity of Fair and Stable Data Exchange
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Data exchange is a fundamental challenge for Web applications such as recommender systems, personalized search, and fraud detection, where combining data across participants can improve predictions. Sustaining such collaboration requires fair returns for contributions and protection against groups leaving for a more beneficial exchange. These requirements are captured by reciprocity, which equates each participant's received utility with its credited contribution to others, and core stability, which rules out any coalition exchanging its own data to make every member strictly better off. Akrami et al. prove that such exchanges exist under broad assumptions, but leave efficient computation open. Two fundamental cases are submodular utilities, capturing diminishing returns from overlapping datasets, and supermodular utilities, capturing complementarities. We settle the approximate computation of reciprocal and core-stable exchanges in both cases, establishing a computational separation under Shapley sharing. For cross-monotone shares, which include Shapley shares under monotone submodular utilities, we give a circulation algorithm that computes an exactly core-stable, $ε$-reciprocal exchange in time poly$(n,1/ε,L)$ given efficient access to approximate shares, where $n$ is the number of participants and $L$ bounds how fast each donor's credit changes with its own contribution. This yields an FPTAS when $L$ is polynomially bounded. In contrast, finding an $ε$-reciprocal, $ε$-core-stable exchange is PPAD-hard for monotone lattice-supermodular utilities, even at inverse-polynomial accuracy, with constant $L$ and exact polynomial-time evaluation of Shapley shares. Thus overlapping information permits efficient fair and stable exchange, while complementarities create a computational barrier even when contribution credits are easy to evaluate.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: A Sequence-Form Path-Following Method for Selecting Normal-Form Perfect Equilibria via a Logistic QRE Variant
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Logistic quantal response equilibrium (QRE) provides a systematic mechanism for equilibrium selection in extensive-form games through their reduced normal-form representations. To ensure normal-form perfection of the limiting equilibria, a perturbed logistic-QRE variant has been developed, but its direct computation is hindered by the exponential growth of the reduced normal-form strategy space. To address this difficulty, we construct an entropy-regularized artificial game in sequence form and establish that its Nash equilibria characterize the perturbed logistic-QRE variant in the reduced normal form. Based on this characterization, we develop a differentiable path-following method starting from a prescribed interior realization plan. We prove the existence of a smooth solution path and show that the mixed-strategy profiles corresponding to its limiting realization plans are normal-form perfect. Furthermore, by reformulating the dilated-entropy terms as weighted standard entropy terms, we derive an equivalent smooth system that generates the same theoretical realization-plan path. Numerical experiments illustrate the equilibrium-selection behavior of the proposed methods and demonstrate their computational advantages over the original normal-form method.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Equilibrium Numbers in Non-Square Bimatrix Games
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Bimatrix games may have an exponential number of mixed Nash equilibria if both dimensions of the game are allowed to grow. Bounds on their maximal number give structural insights that have been used to construct hard-to-solve games. We show new sharp or asymptotically sharp bounds on the (polynomial) number of equilibria for generic games where one dimension of the game is fixed and the number of strategies of the other player grows. These results go beyond the hitherto studied square games. Our methods employ combinatorial properties of polytopes, and recent obstructions that relate to the graph of those polytopes. For $n\ge5$, we construct $3\times n$ games that have all $2n+1$ vertices of the best-response polytope as equilibrium strategies, proved using a simple case of the 4-color theorem for planar graphs. Generic $4\times 5$ games are shown to have at most 17 equilibria, using computer calculations with existing datasets for all combinatorial types of the relevant polytopes. For $d\times n$ games, we construct games where all but a fraction of $O(1/n)$ of the maximum number of vertices are equilibrium strategies.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Stinespring's Dilation, Universal-NOT, and Limitations of Quantum Uncoupled Learning
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Uncoupled learning, in which players know only their own payoff, are a standard model of decentralized learning toward Nash equilibrium. We study their quantum counterpart, where strategies are quantum states and, in each round, a player receives a physical copy of their opponent's current strategy and updates their own state by a quantum channel. This adds to uncoupledness a constraint with no classical analogue: every update must be physically realizable. In fact, this constraint is decisive in conjugation games, in which Bob has a strictly dominant pure strategy and Alice's unique best response is its transpose. In this work, we show some limitations of uncoupled (learning) dynamics in finding the Nash equilibrium for conjugation games. First, we prove that no autonomous, memoryless, uncoupled dynamics converge to Nash equilibrium in a family of four single-qubit conjugation games. Specifically, any memoryless channel that keeps all four equilibria fixed will leave Alice's strategy frozen. This result also extends to $4^n$ games on $n$-qubit registers. Second, we show that this barrier disappears with a small classical memory: for any finite family of $L$ pure targets, a guess-and-test rule with $O(\log L)$ classical bits converges to equilibrium, with an explicit bound on its convergence rate. Finally, we prove that no finite memory, classical or quantum, suffices for the continuum of all pure-qubit targets. Our proof of the impossibility for memoryless channels relies on Stinespring's dilation theorem, while the impossibility for finite-memory channels relies on the optimal universal-NOT (in)fidelity bound by Bužek, Hillery, and Werner.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: GENSTRAT: Toward a Science of Strategic Reasoning in Large Language Models
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Fixed game suites for evaluating strategic reasoning in large language models (LLMs) saturate and are hard to keep free of contamination. We introduce GENSTRAT, a system for evaluating the strategic capabilities of LLMs driven by procedural generation of two-player zero-sum imperfect-information betting games, allowing an evaluator to draw novel, fresh games on demand. Each game is characterized on a scale of five complexity axes (state space, temporal contingency, opponent dependence, private information, precision) and measured by Monte Carlo simulation. Using this generator, we construct a 50-game benchmark and hold a tournament of twelve frontier and open-weight models, gathering data from over 40,000 LLM vs. LLM matches. We further construct a composite complexity axis, and find that, on the eight hardest games, the gap between the best and worst model is 1.7x its value across the whole set of games (1.6x with held-out weights or with hard games chosen by the outcome-free temporal axis alone, and 1.35x with payoffs scaled by their random-play standard deviation). Ablations show that a higher thinking budget, disclosing the opponent's strategy, and higher reasoning matched to a game's specific demands (for private information and planning depth) were associated with higher margins for the LLM player. On 27 solved games, frontier models play at the value of the equilibrium while weaker models lose to it, and the leaderboard predicts strength on fresh games and on six new games, even after controlling for a general-capability leaderboard.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: 42 pages, 17 figures, 21 tables (4 figures, 2 tables in main paper)

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Beyond Arrow: From Impossibility to Possibility in Multi-Criteria Benchmarking
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Modern benchmarks such as HELM MMLU account for multiple metrics like accuracy, robustness and efficiency. When trying to turn these metrics into a single ranking, natural aggregation procedures can produce cyclic pairwise comparisons or rankings that are unstable to changes in the model set. We formalize this aggregation as a social choice problem where each metric induces a preference ranking over models on each dataset, and a benchmark operator aggregates these votes across metrics. While prior work has focused on Arrow's impossibility result, we identify sufficient conditions under which the impossibility disappears and meaningful multi-criteria benchmarking becomes possible. In particular, we deal with three restrictions on the combinations of rankings and show that on single-peaked, group-separable and distance-restricted preferences, the benchmark operator allows for the construction of well-behaved rankings of the involved models. Empirically, we investigate several modern benchmark suites like HELM MMLU and verify which structural conditions are fulfilled on which benchmark problems.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Bottlenecked: The Capital Cost of Protected DeFi Lending
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Securing hundreds of billions of dollars in decentralized finance (DeFi) requires both cryptographically secured collateral and economic capital to absorb losses that collateral alone cannot cover. Composability makes both the amount and location of this protection matter: Kelp's nearly \$300 million April 2026 bridge exploit showed how an attacker could borrow against stolen assets across lending markets. We study how to allocate junior capital that absorbs losses before users incur losses in lending protocols. The main object we study is a tripartite graph that records user assets, their covered liabilities, and the junior capital permitted to pay them. Cuts in this graph determine what protection is missing, while a static security game on the graph defines how much such protection should cost. We call this cost the adversarial default premium (ADP), which can be viewed as the excess cost of insurance in composable financial systems. We then study the joint cost of funding loans and protecting their creditors via this insurance. In a tripartite graph with $N$ borrowers and $M$ lenders, we show that existing systems such as Aave and Morpho have an insurance cost that is $Θ(N)$. Under mild assumptions, we show that the optimal graph has an insurance cost that is $Θ(\sqrt{N})$ with small constants. We apply our model to numerous 2026 DeFi cyber attacks and estimate ADP and the performance of optimized graphs. We find practical capital cost savings of up to 34.5% for our optimized design versus designs that resemble Aave and Morpho. Our results suggest that new lending protocols can improve capital efficiency by treating junior capital as a first-class constraint in protocol design.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: A Characterized Softmax for Distributing Standing Across Multiple Affiliations
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Cooperative game theory answers canonical questions on payoff allocation (Shapley, Owen), interaction attribution (Grabisch-Roubens, Faith-Shap), and coalition formation and stability. None answers a fourth question that arises whenever players carry known, overlapping group tags fixed independently of the game: how should a player's standing be distributed across the groups it already belongs to? We call this membership attribution, formalize it, and give a complete characterization of its solution. The direct, ratio-based answer is provably invalid whenever a player's group-level signals have mixed sign --- a common, structurally unavoidable case. We propose a restricted-domain softmax construction instead, and prove that, for any player satisfying a precisely defined richness condition on the group structure, it is the unique such map, up to a temperature parameter, satisfying five requirements. A sixth requirement fixes the sign of this temperature; a seventh, shown independent of the rest via an explicit counterexample, forces one shared temperature across all eligible players. A worked example on an exact cooperative game confirms the applicable requirements numerically and shows the construction degrades gracefully, valid but uninformative, when a player's evidence fails to distinguish between its groups.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Functional Flexibility in Generative AI Interfaces: Text Editing with LLMs through Conversations, Toolbars, and Prompts
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Many recent user interfaces (UIs) promise great flexibility via access to Large Language Models (LLMs) through prompting. This shifts efforts in accessing functionality from developers to users. However, is a maximum of functional flexibility always beneficial? We find: no -- and develop Functional Flexibility as a concept by reflecting on our long-term exploration of integrating LLMs into a text editor: In a prompt-elicitation survey, people (N=121) envisioned elaborate prompts for delegating flexible tasks to AI. In contrast, when interacting with a prototype (N=10), users preferred short command-like prompts, as prompting repeated functionality is tedious. Another prototype offered such commands in a toolbar, in addition to flexible prompting, leading users (N=12) to dynamically work with both. We contribute Functional Flexibility as a theoretical construct with analytical, critical, and constructive value. Overall, we encourage designing UIs for generative AI that go beyond free text prompting by explicitly considering functional flexibility in design.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Just submitted. This is the author's version of the work

Human-Computer Interaction.title: TopoPilot: Reliable Conversational Workflow Automation for Topological Data Analysis and Visualization
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Recent agentic systems demonstrate that large language models can generate complex codebases from natural language prompts. Despite this progress, they present reliability concerns for scientific visualization due to invalid operations, subtle errors, and failure to resolve underspecified inputs. In this work, we introduce TopoPilot, a reliable and extensible agentic framework for automating complex scientific visualization workflows. We focus on topological data analysis and visualization as a primary use case, while designing the framework to generalize to broader visualization domains. TopoPilot employs a two-agent architecture: an orchestrator translates user prompts into workflows composed of atomic backend actions, while a verifier evaluates workflows prior to execution. Its modular design isolates components and supports new topological descriptors and domain-specific workflows without modifying the core system. It also employs numerous deterministic guardrails to ensure semantic consistency and accurate execution. To systematically improve reliability, we develop a taxonomy of failure modes and employ targeted safeguards for each class of error. Across 2,000 simulated multi-turn conversations spanning 100 prompts, including adversarial and infeasible requests, TopoPilot achieves a success rate exceeding 95%, compared with under 50% for a baseline without comprehensive guardrails and verification. We also show that TopoPilot outperforms Claude Code and Codex on similar prompts in terms of accuracy, completion time, and token usage.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Shared Understanding in Human-AI Teams: Coordination Continuity in Evolving Work
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: People are increasingly working with AI agents as part of extended, asynchronous workflows. In these settings, shared access to information does not guarantee a shared basis for action: goals, plans, and roles may persist while their current significance changes. We introduce coordination continuity, the extent to which collaborators sustain a workable basis for interdependent action as work progresses. Drawing on research on collaborative work, along with two qualitative team studies and a reflexive case from our own repository-based environment, we present a framework of three elements: durable representations of collaborative work; relative coordination properties that support interpretation of representations in the moment; and interaction mechanisms through which the status of representations can be understood and altered. We use a build-act-drift-rebuild heuristic and the notion of consequential moments to characterise when rebuilding may be needed. We draw eight design implications for collaborative AI infrastructure.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: GAZEAIDE: Recording Gaze Context for Research on AI-Assisted Development
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Developers increasingly review code they did not write, much of it generated by AI. Where they look while reading may indicate what is relevant to them, but tools rarely have access to this information. We demonstrate GAZEAIDE, an open-source research prototype for collecting it. Using a webcam, GAZEAIDE estimates which parts of the code a developer looks at and for how long, and records this viewing history together with the text shown on screen. Such context can serve different purposes: providing visual feedback on what has been viewed, guiding code review, and preparing context for a question, which a developer can choose to send to an AI assistant. An IntelliJ plugin records work in the editor; a browser companion records assistant conversations. Attendees can record a short session, replay their viewing history, and try these scenarios.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Submitted to ACM IUI 2027 Demos track

Human-Computer Interaction.title: The Times They Are A-Changin': Tracking Global Trends through the Lens of Web Search
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Human societies have always left traces of their collective priorities, from cave drawings and stone carvings to chronicles on papyrus and printed books. In the digital era, these traces increasingly emerge through social media footprints and web search behavior at a global scale. We construct the first large-scale longitudinal dataset of Google Year in Search trends, spanning 15 years, to characterize how collective public attention evolves across countries and time. Because search engines like Google and Bing do not publicly release raw search logs, Year in Search provides a rare cross-national archive of annually salient search interests. The dataset is supplemented with a manually curated, unified ten-category semantic taxonomy with strong inter-annotator agreement. We focus on four categories (Information Seeking, Personality, Entertainment, and Sports) to investigate how collective attention varies across geographic and socio-cultural contexts. Our analyses reveal a consistently glocalized structure of collective attention: countries converge strongly in profession-level personality attention while remaining differentiated in the specific individuals they search for, yet profession-level similarity is only weakly associated with geographic region and income group. Information seeking is globally dominated by politics and health, while regional distributions show varying degrees of divergence. Crisis periods are associated with both shared and regionally differentiated shifts. Entertainment and sports attention likewise combine globally prominent interests with regional differentiation. Overall, our findings suggest that web search data provide a valuable computational lens for observing collective attention at scale, acting as a living archive of how societal priorities vary across countries and change over time.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: This paper has been accepted at the 21st International AAAI Conference on Web and Social Media (ICWSM 2027)

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Standard-Anchored Delegation in Teachers' Use of Generative AI
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Teachers who use generative AI must decide which parts of their work to hand over, while they remain accountable for what reaches students. We studied these decisions in Punjab, Pakistan, through a qualitatively driven mixed-methods study. We interviewed 13 teachers from government, private, NGO and vocational institutions, four administrators and one student, and coded each teacher's position on twelve educational tasks. Nine teachers accepted AI drafts or substantial assistance with lesson planning, but none accepted AI-drafted learning objectives, and eleven did not use AI to encourage or emotionally support students. Teachers who would accept AI marking required that the model be given a rubric or marking criteria. Building on assessment research and HCI work on verifiability, we call this pattern standard-anchored delegation: teachers handed a component of a task to AI when a standard outside the model, such as a textbook or rubric, defined a correct output and the teacher could apply that standard to the result. Having a standard was not always enough. Several government-school teachers did not use AI to mark quizzes even though the quizzes had answer keys, because they expected students to look for evidence of the teacher's effort. Checking AI output required subject knowledge and time, and private schools gave teachers more support for this than government schools did. Participants also read disclosure of AI use as a statement about whether the teacher had reviewed the work. We propose that teacher-facing AI tools ask for the relevant standard before generating and show each output beside it, and that schools account for the time that checking takes.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: On the Challenges of Using LLMs in High-Risk AI Recruitment: Guiding Questions for Legal Conformity with the AI Act
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: The EU Artificial Intelligence Act (AI Act) imposes detailed obligations on providers of high-risk AI systems but offers limited operational guidance, particularly when these systems integrate third-party General-Purpose AI (GPAI) models. This paper introduces a toolkit that fosters the development of legal-by-design AI-assisted recruitment systems by translating the core legal obligations of the AI Act's conformity assessment---specifically Articles 9--15 and Annex IV---into techno-normative requirements and corresponding guiding questions. While recruitment pipelines may involve components with varying technical complexity and differing levels of algorithmic transparency, this paper focuses on the most challenging case: the integration of third-party GPAI models into critical stages of the selection process, including resume and job description parsing, applicant scoring, and shortlist generation. This scenario presents significant challenges for downstream providers of high-risk AI systems, as it underscores the difficulties in obtaining the technical information needed to demonstrate compliance with the AI Act's techno-normative requirements, both prior to and during market deployment. After introducing the toolkit and illustrating its application through a simplified example, the paper explores informational dependencies between upstream and downstream GPAI model providers. These dependencies may produce informational gaps across the AI supply chain, potentially hindering the collection of evidence necessary for the AI system provider to ensure legal compliance. The resulting lack of technical transparency negatively affects the deployer, who may struggle to maintain meaningful oversight of the system, and ultimately impacts the persons subject to the AI output.
