Standard debiasing procedures for high-dimensional inference commonly rely on design-covariance information or additional structural assumptions on precision-matrix directions. In mediation models, however, the full outcome-design covariance depends on unknown mediator-model coefficients, creating an addi- tional challenge when such information or structure is unavailable. To address this challenge, we introduce an approximate debiasing procedure based on partial ridge regression and show that the resulting estimator is asymptotically bias-corrected and Gaussian. We also develop a cross-fitted estimator with a smaller asymptotic variance than its sample-split counterpart. In addition, we construct consistent estimators of the limiting variances of both the sample-split and cross-fitted estimators. Together, these results provide feasible inferential procedures for global and pathwise mediation effects.

Methodology.title: Augmented Inverse Hybrid Weighting: Robust Inference under Deterministic and Random Distribution Shifts
Methodology.summary: Reweighting source samples to match a target covariate distribution is a standard response to distribution shift when generalizing evidence across populations. It is well suited to deterministic, learnable covariate discrepancies, but can fail when source--target differences extend beyond covariate shift or when estimation of the density-ratio weights is unstable. We introduce a new model where the discrepancy between two population laws comprises a deterministic covariate shift and a non-systematic component, modeled as random perturbation of the probability space. This separates systematic shifts, treated as bias and corrected by reweighting, from random perturbations, treated as distributional uncertainty and reduced by dataset pooling. Under pure random perturbations, this principle yields Augmented Inverse Distance Weighting, which combines regression augmentation with variance-optimal dataset-level pooling and attains asymptotic variance no larger than exact covariate balancing. When both components are present, we develop Augmented Inverse Hybrid Weighting, which interpolates between AIDW and standard augmented importance weighting. Both estimators tradeoff sampling and distributional uncertainty via a distributional distance quantifying the strength of random perturbations. We establish asymptotic normality of both estimators and provide tuning and diagnostic tools. On three real-world multi-site datasets exhibiting diverse distribution shifts, the proposed methods consistently reduce mean-squared error compared with weighting baselines, and improve empirical coverage when covariate-shift adjustment alone undercovers.

Methodology.title: Subspace Inference for Multilayer Latent Space Networks: Intrinsic Geometry and One-Step Estimator
Methodology.summary: Multilayer networks on a common node set, such as brain connectomes of several animals with one layer per animal, often share a low-dimensional geometry but differ in how strongly each layer expresses it and in node activity. We study a multilayer latent space network model that combines an invariant subspace common to all layers with layer-specific interaction matrices and node-by-layer degree effects. By introducing the generalized Cayley transform of the invariant subspace, we characterize the intrinsic geometry of the model and obtain sharp convergence rates for the maximum likelihood estimator, asymptotic normality and Neyman orthogonality for vertex-level parameters, and asymptotic normality for the interaction matrices with a non-negligible bias. Plug-in estimates of the bias and covariance give debiased confidence regions and tests of equality between layers. We also propose an easy-to-implement one-step estimator that attains the same vertex-level limits. In a real-world mouse connectome dataset, the inbred strain that lacks a corpus callosum shows about twice the hemispheric segregation of the other three strains.

Methodology.title: Average Causal Effect Estimation in DAGs with Hidden Variables: Beyond Back-Door and Front-Door Criteria
Methodology.summary: The identification theory for causal effects in directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) with hidden variables is well established, but methods for estimation and inference beyond the g-formula remain less developed. Previous studies have introduced influence-function-based estimators for broad classes of identifiable effects. When implemented through the observed-data density factorization, these estimators can require conditional density estimation and numerical integration, which can be statistically challenging and computationally demanding for continuous or multivariate variables. Prior work on related causal functionals has used sequential regressions and Bayes-rule representations of density ratios to avoid these requirements. Building on established identification and influence-function results, we make these reparameterizations explicit for effects identified under treatment primal fixability, Tian and Pearl's necessary and sufficient condition for identification of post-intervention law, encompassing settings beyond classical back-door and front-door identification. We construct one-step estimators under alternative nuisance parameterizations and characterize how these choices affect robustness properties and nuisance-specific L2(P) product-rate conditions for asymptotic linearity and root-n consistency. The estimators accommodate data-adaptive machine learning for nuisance estimation. To address potential violations of the target parameter bounds by one-step estimators, we also develop targeted minimum loss-based estimators (TMLEs) that respect these bounds. Our robustness characterizations and sufficient rate conditions apply to both the one-step estimators and TMLEs. Building on prior efficiency theory for hidden-variable DAGs, we further develop modifications of our estimators that exploit ordinary independence restrictions. Implementations are provided in the R flexCausal package.

Methodology.title: Randomization Tests in Randomized Saturation Designs
Methodology.summary: Randomized saturation designs are widely used to study spillover effects in clustered populations. In these designs, clusters are first assigned to treatment saturation levels, and units are then randomized within clusters according to the assigned saturation. This paper develops randomization tests for such experiments under several null hypotheses that arise naturally in spillover analysis. We first compare each unit's untreated potential outcomes at two saturation levels: the partially sharp null requires zero spillover for every unit, while the bounded null imposes a prespecified upper bound on each unit's spillover effect. Both hypotheses can be tested using a common conditional randomization framework that provides finite-sample validity. We next develop a finite-sample valid unconditional randomization test of whether each unit's untreated potential outcome is nondecreasing across saturation levels. Finally, we study weak average-spillover nulls and show that our conditional randomization framework delivers asymptotically valid inference using studentized statistics. Simulations and an application to the Zomba Cash Transfer experiment illustrate the finite-sample behavior and practical implementation of the methods.

Methodology.title: A generalized Bayesian method for identifying local and global changepoints in dynamic network data
Methodology.summary: We introduce a generalized Bayesian approach to multiple changepoint analysis in dynamic network data based on a multinomial log loss function and a prior distribution that imposes low-rank structure and sparsity on the model parameters. The method can detect local and global changes in network structure by incorporating information from both the full adjacency matrices and network summary statistics. Moreover, the proposed method is agnostic to the true data-generating process. From the generalized posterior distribution, we can make simultaneous inferences with meaningful uncertainty quantification about the locations of changepoints as well as deduce the network attributes and summary statistics that characterize them. For posterior simulation, we develop an efficient Gibbs sampler based on Pólya-Gamma data augmentation with a computational cost that grows linearly with the number of observed edges in the dynamic network. Simulations across several benchmark network models show that the proposed method is often more accurate and flexible than competitors. We demonstrate the practical value of the method through applications to an email communication network and an international conflict network.

Methodology.title: MG-EDA: Maturity-Gated Skew-Normal Estimation of Distribution Algorithms
Methodology.summary: Gaussian estimation of distribution algorithms shrink their variance on slopes and stall far from the optimum. This paper equips the corrections that act along the direction of movement -- a mean shift, an elongation of the covariance along the path and a skewness -- with the rule they lack: a calibrated gate, driven by a maturity statistic of the population, decides whether, how strongly and for how long each correction acts, and when the gate is closed the algorithm is exactly the estimation of multivariate normal algorithm (EMNA). The statistic is a cumulative path of whitened mean shifts with an inverse-Wishart correction, whose expectation is one under a null model without systematic movement and whose quantiles give thresholds with known false-alarm rate. It gates the three corrections as three rank-one terms of one matrix sampling equation, the skewness being carried by a skew-normal sampler that preserves the estimated mean and covariance; all vanish at maturity. We call the resulting algorithm the maturity-gated EDA (MG-EDA). A full factorial study on a training set of black-box optimization benchmarking (BBOB) functions separates the parameters: variance scaling is the prerequisite, the mean shift needs a feedback correction removing the injected shift from the statistic, the elongation turns the variance loss on a slope into a gain, and the skewness substitutes for the mean shift rather than complementing it. On held-out instances MG-EDA with the first- and second-order corrections is significantly better than the skewness-only predecessor and than EMNA with variance scaling, ties with EMNA with anticipated mean shift, and trails the adapted maximum-likelihood Gaussian model (AMaLGaM) in 20 dimensions.
Methodology.comment: 20 pages (13 pages main text and a 7-page supplement), 8 figures, 19 tables. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Evolutionary Computation

Methodology.title: Uncovering Multimorbidity Patterns Through a Novel Randomized Clustering Algorithm
Methodology.summary: Patients with several chronic conditions rarely share the same combination: in four years of the nationally representative Medical Expenditure Panel Survey (MEPS), we find 32,789 distinct combinations of two to seven conditions, and over 90% of those involving four or more occur in a single patient. Methods that search for common combinations discard most of this heterogeneity. We present the Randomized Length Sequential Clustering Algorithm (RLSCA), which links diseases by lift, a pairwise association measure counted only above a user-set support threshold. A mixed-integer program repeatedly selects and removes the group of conditions with the greatest internal lift, up to a random size; 100 iterations yield a database of clusters scored by size, rediscovery frequency, and body systems spanned. In MEPS 2019, stratified by age and sex, RLSCA recovers known groupings at a high threshold, such as diabetes with lipid disorders and hypertension, and at a lower threshold returns clusters of up to eight conditions spanning five body systems. Frequent itemset mining, at its lowest feasible support, finds no set above five conditions; hierarchical clustering cannot control cluster size. With a clinical large language model, the database could suggest which further conditions a patient is at risk of.

Methodology.title: Random weighting inference for linear regression under serial dependence of unknown form
Methodology.summary: We construct confidence regions for a linear regression's coefficients, with regressors and errors forming a stationary ergodic sequence of serial dependence not necessarily known. We weight the observations by random variables from an independent auxiliary sample and estimate the coefficients by weighted least squares. We prove the estimator to be asymptotically normal with the sandwich covariance if and only if the bandwidth shrinks fast enough for the weights' randomness to dominate the score's serial dependence. Wald regions have the nominal level, under short memory with the dependence left unspecified and under long memory with a non-normal least-squares limit. We derive a condition specific to the slopes and a bandwidth from consistent memory-order estimates, and identify the estimator asymptotically with least squares perturbed by independent noise. In simulations, we compare our regions with self-normalized, fixed-bandwidth, and resampled intervals under short and long memory, and we apply the method to daily wind speeds at Irish stations, a long-memory series.

Methodology.title: Targeted Learning for Externally Controlled Trials and Beyond
Methodology.summary: This paper focuses on externally controlled trials (ECTs), which consist of a single-arm clinical trial supplemented by an external control arm (ECA). Potential data sources for the ECA can be broadly classified into three categories: (i) the control arm of a historical clinical trial, (ii) a concurrent cohort study, and (iii) external real-world data (RWD). In this paper, we consider a broad class of estimands defined through balancing weights. For a given estimand in the class, we discuss the efficient influence function (EIF) and the targeted maximum likelihood estimator (TMLE), together with practical implementation algorithms. Within the targeted learning framework, TMLE is a substitution estimator that enjoys several desirable theoretical properties and favorable finite-sample performance. Finally, the proposed framework is extended to two additional settings: (1) randomized controlled trials (RCTs) augmented with external covariate information to define a target population, and (2) indirect treatment comparisons (ITCs) that combine individual patient data (IPD) from an internal RCT with aggregate data (AgD) from an external RCT.

Methodology.title: Neural-network-powered new-physics searches by predictive goodness of fit
Methodology.summary: Model-independent searches for new physics test whether data agree with a Reference model with unknown nuisance parameters. Because the shape and location of a signal are not specified, these tests call for flexible learners (fitting procedures such as neural networks), and a likelihood ratio maximized over a neural network falls outside the standard asymptotic theory, making the calibration a major challenge. We propose a predictive alternative: the departure from the Reference is fitted on part of the data and its likelihood gain over the fitted Reference is evaluated on the rest, cross-fitted over several folds to preserve sample efficiency. The nuisance estimation error is propagated into the variance of the test statistic to first order, in the spirit of Neyman's C(alpha) test, so that the test need not be recalibrated at each nuisance value. The randomness in the fitted departure is treated by a central limit theorem for cross-validated statistics under algorithmic stability, plus a variance correction when stability is not achieved. The calibration is analytic, and no pseudo-experiments are needed. On established one-dimensional and five-dimensional (dilepton) benchmarks, the false-positive rate always stays within Monte Carlo error of nominal across different nuisances and the learners' tuning. The test's power relative to existing learned tests is mixed: higher for some signals and lower for others, depending on how well the fitted departure captures the signal.

Methodology.title: Geometric ergodicity of Gibbs samplers for linear mixed models with several heavy-tailed random-effect components and unknown tail parameters
Methodology.summary: Linear mixed models with heavy-tailed random effects are widely used for robust Bayesian analysis of longitudinal data. We study the three-block Gibbs sampler for such models when the random effects are split into several components, such as random intercepts and slopes, each with its own scale and its own scale mixture of normals, when the tail parameters have priors on finite grids and are drawn jointly with the latent weights, and when the random-effects design is rank deficient, as when some subjects contribute a single observation. We give sufficient conditions for geometric ergodicity that attribute the rank deficiency to the components that cause it, and show that, under conditions on the gamma priors on the precision parameters, they hold for Student-t and slash random effects with individual weights, any grid of tail parameters and any design. The result extends to random-effect vectors whose coordinates share a weight, for subject-specific designs with known shape matrices. It justifies Monte Carlo standard errors for regression coefficients, log-scales and posterior probabilities of the tail parameters. Simulations show that the scale and the tail parameter can mix much more slowly than the regression coefficients, and an analysis of beta-HCG data illustrates the methods.

Methodology.title: Amortized Inference for Correlated Discrete Choice Models via Equivariant Neural Networks
Methodology.summary: Discrete choice models are fundamental tools in management science, economics, and marketing. Logit models dominate applied work because they yield closed-form choice probabilities, but IID Gumbel errors impose restrictive substitution patterns. We propose an amortized inference approach based on a neural network emulator that approximates choice probabilities under general, potentially correlated, error distributions. We develop a specialized neural network architecture respecting the invariance properties of discrete choice models and provide group-theoretic foundations for universal approximation from a minimal set of invariant features. Using Sobolev training, the emulator learns choice probabilities and their derivatives, enabling rapid likelihood and gradient evaluation. We show that emulator-based maximum likelihood estimators are consistent and asymptotically normal under mild approximation conditions. Simulations show substantial gains over the GHK simulator in accuracy and speed. Using NielsenIQ data on household laundry-detergent purchases, we estimate correlated-probit and correlated-Gumbel models with rich household-level random effects. The IID period-error restriction---and hence the conditional-IIA restriction underlying conventional mixed logit---is strongly rejected. The Bayesian information criterion (BIC) selects a correlated-Gumbel model with a three-factor period-error covariance structure. We find that allowing correlated period errors materially changes predicted product substitution patterns.

Methodology.title: Statistical inference under response-adaptive experimental designs: a systematic review
Methodology.summary: Response-adaptive designs, including bandit-based approaches, update treatment allocation using accrued outcomes. In this paper, we systematically reviewed how studies in health and biostatistics conducted and evaluated inference under these designs. We searched six databases for studies published from January 2010 through October 2025. Of 774 records identified, 36 studies met the inclusion criteria. We summarized them using study-level counts and structured narrative comparisons, with reporting guided by PRISMA 2020. Most studies focused on methods or designs. Evidence supporting inference came mainly from theory and simulation. Among studies for which each metric was relevant, 26 of 32 numerically evaluated power, 23 of 32 type I error, eight of 35 estimator bias, and five of 12 interval coverage. These findings suggest that studies more often quantified power and type I error than estimator bias or interval coverage. Evaluations of adaptive allocation should also examine estimation and interval performance when these are relevant to the study objective.

Methodology.title: Treatment Policy Design in the Presence of Measurement Error
Methodology.summary: In many applications, treatments are assigned based on unit features, leading to personalized treatment policies. This often involves optimizing objective functions with counterfactual quantities such as the conditional average treatment effect (CATE). In practice, some key features may be measured with error and ignoring such errors can introduce systematic bias. We study how to design personalized treatment policies when some features are latent and only noisy measurements are available. We ask how policies can be constructed when the CATE is not identifiable, and how uncertainty from measurement error can be incorporated into policy design. We propose two frameworks for treatment policy design based on partial identification, focusing on the measurement mechanism-the conditional distribution of observed measurements given unobserved features. The first framework builds on ideas from proximal causal inference. The second adopts a modular Bayesian approach based on a reparameterized likelihood, using Hamiltonian Monte Carlo and Bayesian regression models to separately perform posterior inference on the measurement mechanism and nuisance functions. Posterior quantiles are then used to construct credible intervals for the CATE that account for uncertainty in both components. Treatment policies are then derived by comparing the null value of the CATE to these bounds. The proposed methods provide a coherent way to account for measurement error and model uncertainty in personalized treatment policy design.

Methodology.title: Which Loans, Not How Many: Exactly Level-Invariant, Anytime-Valid Monitoring of Deployed Risk Models
Methodology.summary: A refinancing wave can change the number of mortgage prepayments without changing the relationship between scores and prepayment. In a logistic model, conditioning on the monthly count removes the intercept from the likelihood of which loans prepay. Our fixed-start slope product tests a lower bound on the calibration slope. At threshold 20 its probability of ever crossing under the null is at most 5%. The restarted level sum tracks departures from intercept tolerance. A confidence sequence estimates a constant slope, and the restart-intersection rule detects changes in that slope. A continuous mixture avoids the off-grid width floor of a discrete prior. On Freddie Mac loans, fixed-slope resampling reproduces 78% of maintained-model monthly AUC variance in development and 70% in the holdout (95% intervals 57-100% and 48-100%). From fresh holdout starts, the restarted level sum crosses on both paths, and the fixed-start slope product stays below threshold on both. The restart-intersection rule signals a downward change for the frozen model in April 2018 and an upward change for the maintained model in a supplementary run in August 2019.

Methodology.title: Skew-Symmetric Factor Models
Methodology.summary: The paper introduces and analyzes a factor model for (real) skew-symmetric data, which arise naturally in directed flows and in pairwise comparisons used for rankings. Working within a signal-plus-noise framework, we analyze spectral inference and establish a BBP-type phase transition in signal strength. Under Gaussian noise, we derive joint eigenvalue fluctuation limits. Above the separation threshold, the estimated signal strength is asymptotically normal whenever the population strength has multiplicity one. For a general multiplicity $k$, the joint limiting fluctuations of the corresponding sample eigenvalues above the threshold are given by the eigenvalues of a scaled $k\times k$ Gaussian unitary ensemble matrix. The skew-symmetric structure induces paired eigenspaces, and we characterize the canonical angles between the population and sample eigenspaces. Below the threshold, the corresponding largest sample eigenvalue converges to the edge of the semicircle law, with fluctuations governed by the Tracy--Widom $F_2$ distribution, in contrast to the $F_1$ law familiar from real symmetric models. The approach is illustrated through financial and demographic applications.

Methodology.title: A CV-TMLE global test approach to improve power in rare disease clinical studies with multiple-component endpoints
Methodology.summary: Rare disease trials face unique statistical challenges due to limited patient populations and heterogeneous clinical manifestations among patients. Multiple endpoints are often necessary to comprehensively capture treatment benefits. A global test is an approach for evaluating whether a treatment has any beneficial effect across multiple endpoints. We propose a new global test based on a weighted composite endpoint. The proposed global test employs shrinkage-based cross-validated targeted maximum likelihood estimation (CV-TMLE) to learn data-adaptive weights that maximize power while maintaining Type I error control. Shrinkage can be tailored to incorporate existing domain knowledge, such as anticipated relative effect sizes. In simulation studies designed to reflect real rare disease trial settings, the proposed procedure demonstrated improved power over standard multiplicity adjustments and classical global tests (such as the O'Brien test), while maintaining nominal Type I error, when effects are heterogeneous across endpoints. The proposed method simultaneously learns an optimal weighted composite outcome and provides an unbiased and efficient targeted maximum likelihood estimator (TMLE) for the average treatment effect (ATE) on that weighted outcome, with valid inference taking into account that the ATE is data dependent.
Methodology.comment: Added link to the R code for the simulation studies

Methodology.title: Vaccine sieve analysis on deep sequencing data using competing risks Cox regression with failure type subject to misclassification
Methodology.summary: Understanding how vaccines perform against different pathogen genotypes is crucial for developing effective prevention strategies, particularly for highly genetically diverse pathogens like HIV. Sieve analysis is a statistical framework used to determine whether a vaccine selectively prevents infection by certain genotypes while allowing breakthrough of other genotypes that evade immune responses. Traditionally, these analyses are conducted with a single sequence available per individual acquiring the pathogen. However, modern sequencing technology can provide detailed characterization of intra-individual viral diversity by capturing up to hundreds of pathogen sequences per person. In this work, we introduce methodology that extends sieve analysis to account for intra-individual viral diversity. Our approach estimates vaccine efficacy against viral populations with at least a small threshold of vaccine-mismatched mutations. To account for differential resolution of information from differing sequence counts per person, we use competing risks Cox regression with modeled causes of failure and propose an empirical Bayes approach for the classification model. Simulation studies demonstrate that our approach reduces bias, provides nominal confidence interval coverage, and improves statistical power compared to conventional methods. We apply our method to the HVTN 705 Imbokodo trial, which assessed the efficacy of a heterologous vaccine regimen in preventing HIV-1 infection.

Methodology.title: Threshold Generalized Autoregressive Moving Average Models
Methodology.summary: Non-Gaussian time series often exhibit nonlinear dynamics and changes in dependence structures that may not be adequately captured by conventional single-regime models. To address this limitation, we introduce a class of threshold generalized autoregressive moving-average (TGARMA) models that combines observation-driven GARMA dynamics with threshold-based regime switching. The proposed framework accommodates multiple regimes, determined by a lagged endogenous or exogenous threshold variable, and allows regression coefficients, autoregressive and moving-average orders and coefficients, and, where applicable, dispersion parameters to vary across regimes. Parameters are estimated by maximum partial likelihood, while model selection is conducted using information criteria. We examine model admissibility and stability, assess model adequacy through residual diagnostics, and conduct a Monte Carlo simulation study to investigate the finite-sample performance of the estimators. The proposed methodology is illustrated using monthly counts of hospitalizations due to respiratory diseases among older adults in São Paulo, Brazil. In this application, the TGARMA model outperforms its single-regime GARMA counterpart in terms of in-sample mean squared error, highlighting the potential benefits of incorporating regime-dependent dynamics into the analysis of non-Gaussian time series.

Methodology.title: Faster Estimates from Binned Test Scores---With Discussion of Normality, Bias, and Reliability
Methodology.summary:
Education agencies often summarize test score distributions by counting how many students scored in 3 to 5 bins. Means and standard deviations (SDs) can be estimated from bin counts using a HETOP model, which assumes that scores are normally distributed within each school or district. However, most HETOP software takes minutes to hours if the number of schools or districts is large.
  We present a fast HETOP algorithm that produces HETOP estimates in less than a millisecond per district. The algorithm is implemented in the fast_hetop function of the binest package for RL: https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/binest/refman/binest.html#topic+fast_hetop
  HETOP estimates of the mean are highly reliable; estimates of the SD are not as good. Maximum likelihood estimates are generally excellent but can be biased and unreliable if scores are not normal or scores are concentrated in the top or bottom bin. Empirical Bayes shrinkage improves unreliable estimates. Standard errors are smaller if the data represents the whole population of students rather than a sample.
  HETOP estimates are usable for many purposes, but it would be better if education agencies reported means and SDs directly.

Methodology.title: Conditional Independence Testing for Random Objects via Generative Models
Methodology.summary: We propose a test of conditional independence for random objects taking values in metric spaces of negative type, allowing the conditioning variable to be either a random object or a high-dimensional vector. Our method uses multidimensional scaling and Nyström extensions to obtain finite-dimensional representations of random objects from their pairwise distances, and generative neural networks to estimate conditional distributions in the embedded space. Samples from the fitted generators are then used to construct a doubly robust test statistic. Our main theoretical contribution is to quantify how errors from estimating and truncating the embeddings, together with errors in learning the conditional distributions, affect inference. We establish conditions under which these errors are asymptotically negligible, even when the embedding dimensions grow with the sample size. In particular, we derive explicit convergence rates when the conditional distributions admit generators with smooth, low-dimensional compositional structure. We establish asymptotic validity of the bootstrap test, consistency against fixed alternatives, and nontrivial power against local alternatives. Simulations with distribution-valued data demonstrate its competitive finite-sample performance.

Graphics.title: TopoPilot: Reliable Conversational Workflow Automation for Topological Data Analysis and Visualization
Graphics.summary: Recent agentic systems demonstrate that large language models can generate complex codebases from natural language prompts. Despite this progress, they present reliability concerns for scientific visualization due to invalid operations, subtle errors, and failure to resolve underspecified inputs. In this work, we introduce TopoPilot, a reliable and extensible agentic framework for automating complex scientific visualization workflows. We focus on topological data analysis and visualization as a primary use case, while designing the framework to generalize to broader visualization domains. TopoPilot employs a two-agent architecture: an orchestrator translates user prompts into workflows composed of atomic backend actions, while a verifier evaluates workflows prior to execution. Its modular design isolates components and supports new topological descriptors and domain-specific workflows without modifying the core system. It also employs numerous deterministic guardrails to ensure semantic consistency and accurate execution. To systematically improve reliability, we develop a taxonomy of failure modes and employ targeted safeguards for each class of error. Across 2,000 simulated multi-turn conversations spanning 100 prompts, including adversarial and infeasible requests, TopoPilot achieves a success rate exceeding 95%, compared with under 50% for a baseline without comprehensive guardrails and verification. We also show that TopoPilot outperforms Claude Code and Codex on similar prompts in terms of accuracy, completion time, and token usage.

Graphics.title: Same Pixels, Different Documents: Measuring Part-Level Editability in Image Vectorization
Graphics.summary: Image vectorization is often evaluated by rendering fidelity, which cannot distinguish documents that render identically but support different edits. Edit-based evaluation tests outcomes, but an oracle that gathers a part's fragments can conceal the cost of selecting them. We introduce Pass@k, which tests whether a prescribed edit can succeed using objects selectable within k clicks under a specified interaction model. Eight document diagnostics characterize properties relevant to editing beyond these tasks. We assess structural sensitivity through controlled perturbations, practical relevance through designer operations, and reference dependence through alternative drawings. We evaluate twelve open and commercial methods on 211 references, with 635 edit tasks on 93 of them. In each of four reference sets, including two drawn by designers, 64-88% of oracle-passed tasks on parts composed of multiple shapes fail at Pass@1, against 6-40% for single shapes, pooling counts over configurations. Higher fidelity does not guarantee higher Pass@1, while selected diagnostics are associated with designers' effort in our study.

Graphics.title: VeilGS: Solving Darkness as a Veil of 2D Basis Maps over Retinex 3DGS
Graphics.summary: In a dark capture, the darkness is not uniform. How much light reaches a surface depends on where it lies relative to the few light sources, and the camera compresses what remains with a tone curve. Most low-light 3D reconstruction methods either apply one curve to every pixel of a view, so a dark object beside a lamp and a bright one in an unlit corner receive the same correction, or store the darkness in the 3D representation, where it can absorb scene detail. We present VeilGS, a 3D Gaussian Splatting method for low-light novel view synthesis that treats the degradation as a veil drawn over a clear scene. Each Gaussian carries an albedo and a shading latent instead of spherical harmonics, separating surface colour from illumination. Each view is darkened by a spatially varying gain followed by a global tone curve, and rendering without this veil gives the restored scene. A small network predicts a coarse basis for the gain from the observation, and its coefficients are solved for each view rather than learned. Training through this solve discourages the Gaussians from absorbing what the veil can explain. VeilGS needs no paired normal-light supervision and stores no per-view parameters. On Gaussian-DK, its restored renders score best on no-reference NIQE and CLIP-IQA and are rated highest in a blind user study with 55 participants. On LOM, it achieves results competitive with the state of the art.

Graphics.title: GLUT: 3D Gaussian Lookup Table for Continuous Color Transformation
Graphics.summary: 3D Lookup Tables (3D LUTs) are widely used for color mapping, but their grid-based representation discretizes the RGB space, leading to a capacity-memory trade-off that becomes prohibitive when storing large numbers of LUTs. Recent approaches use implicit neural representations to improve scalability, but their black-box nature limits interpretability and localized editing. In this paper, we propose Gaussian LUT (GLUT), a continuous and explicit representation of color transformations using learnable 3D Gaussian primitives. By eliminating fixed-resolution grids, GLUT provides flexible representational capacity with a compact memory footprint. Its spatially localized primitives also facilitate interpretation and targeted editing. Building on GLUT, we introduce Conditional Gaussian LUT (CGLUT), a compact generator that predicts GLUT parameters for multiple LUTs within a shared framework, enabling smooth blending between color styles. GLUT further supports efficient local editing by allowing targeted adjustments to specific color regions without retraining the model. Experiments show that GLUT outperforms existing neural LUT representations in both accuracy and efficiency, while supporting controllable localized color editing. CGLUT further improves compact modeling and smooth blending of multiple color styles. Code is available at https://github.com/CVC-Color/glut.

Graphics.title: PennyGS: Full Resolution 3DGS Training in Minutes on Consumer GPUs
Graphics.summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting is increasingly fed by high-resolution captures from commodity devices, yet training still happens at reduced resolution with research-grade GPUs. We present PennyGS, a method to achieve full-resolution (4K) training of 3DGS on consumer GPUs by improving the efficiency of every stage of a training step. Improvements include a leaner splat with flat RGB color and a directional cone opacity, fused projection and key emission, forward rasterization optimizations with strided pixel sampling, an approximate tile SSIM loss, a warp-per-splat backward rasterization, and a fused backward projection and sparse Adam step. At the standard 30k-step budget, PennyGS is the fastest of 10 methods on Mip-NeRF 360 and Tanks&Temples 4K on all four GPUs at competitive quality, at least 3.9x faster than the quickest of the others, while peaking below 2 GB of GPU memory. On an RTX 3060, a full-resolution Mip-NeRF 360 scene trains in 6m 25s, faster than any other method trains it on an RTX 4090.

Graphics.title: ParaBMG: A Parallel Block Multigrid Framework for Large-Scale Evolving Sparse Systems on Unstructured Meshes
Graphics.summary: Solving large-scale, evolving sparse linear systems on unstructured meshes remains the primary performance bottleneck in many GPU-accelerated geometry processing pipelines. Although modern linear solvers like multigrid and multilevel additive Schwarz (MAS) methods offer fast convergence and strong parallelization potential, a unified benchmark and solver design tailored for geometry processing tasks have been lacking. Addressing this gap, we present ParaBMG, a parallel block multigrid preconditioning framework that combines fully parallel geometric hierarchy construction, fast block-Jacobi smoothing, and GPU-optimized operators. We develop CUDA implementations of four standard geometry processing pipelines to form a large-scale benchmark for GPU linear solvers, comprising more than 40K linear systems with up to 6.6M unknowns. Across comparisons in this dataset, ParaBMG achieves speedups of 3.7x-7.7x over strong general-purpose algebraic multigrid baselines, 6x-105x speedups over our custom GPU implementations of the state-of-the-art CPU multigrid solvers for Poisson problems, and 6x-96x speedups over MAS. Compared with open-sourced multigrid baselines, ParaBMG reduces repeated hierarchy construction costs through hierarchy reuse and improves convergence through MAS-inspired block-Jacobi smoothing. Compared with MAS, the complementary coarse corrections reduce iteration counts by an order of magnitude while maintaining low per-iteration costs. It enables three interactive geometry processing applications with order-of-magnitude speedups over their public implementations.

Graphics.title: KV-Control: Parameter-Efficient K/V Injection for Trajectory-Controlled Text-to-Motion
Graphics.summary: Text-conditioned 3D human motion models now synthesize plausible motions from prompts, but practical animation and embodied-agent workflows rarely stop at text: a character may need to follow a sketched root path, hit an end-effector target, or satisfy a multi-joint trajectory while still preserving the gait, style, and intent described by language. This exposes a control trade-off. A trajectory controller should be precise without overwriting the pretrained text-conditioned motion prior, yet existing solutions either duplicate large portions of the generator to regain per-layer control access or move much of the cost to test-time optimization. We introduce KV-Control, a compact attention-side control interface for frozen masked text-to-motion transformers. The key idea is to make geometric constraints available as memory inside self-attention rather than injecting them through a global pose token or enforcing them only at the output side. To support this interface, we co-design a part-tokenized motion substrate and controller: \textbf{PartVQ} learns anatomy-aligned part codebooks, T-Concat exposes each frame--part token as an attention-addressable site, and KV-Control injects control-conditioned key/value memories at every self-attention layer while preserving the pretrained query stream, text cross-attention, FFN, and all backbone weights. The resulting adapter adds only trainable injection parameters atop a shared trajectory encoder, yet tracks root and multi-joint constraints with sub-centimeter accuracy under the inherited refinement protocol while retaining text-conditioned motion quality. KV-Control reframes trajectory conditioning as lightweight memory retrieval, providing a small, precise, and transparent control interface for text-to-motion generation.

Graphics.title: Frozen Scenes, Shifting Winners: Configuration Fragility in Text-to-3D Evaluation
Graphics.summary: Can a text-to-3D leaderboard change when every generated scene stays fixed? We audit this question for rendered-image evaluation, where camera settings and caption wording become part of the measurement protocol. Across 300 frozen scenes from six generators, we vary eight render and caption factors for 19 alignment evaluators plus one perceptual-quality control, then test four targeted scene degradations. Peak configuration variance exceeds between-generator variance for 19/19 alignment evaluators, with prompt-bootstrap lower bounds above 1 for 19/19. Rankings are more stable than scores, yet 18/19 evaluators change their point-estimate winner under some configuration. Pairwise protocol margin envelopes show which comparisons keep their direction across the tested settings. Selected pairs have opposite pointwise intervals, but no reversal survives simultaneous inference over the full search. Thus the observed winner changes are descriptive, not confirmed changes in generator superiority. Sensitivity remains separate: no evaluator exceeds 71% tie-adjusted directional discrimination on layout scrambling, and a preregistered blinded human study classifies part of the configuration variance as metric artifact. The audit separates score stability, decision uncertainty, and targeted sensitivity, and recommends reporting (generator, score, card ID) with protocol-dependent comparisons and selection-aware uncertainty.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Language Models Steer on Injected Uncertainty Tokens, but Fail to Self-Monitor In Situ
Artificial Intelligence.summary:
Prompting language models to verbalize stepwise numerical confidence during generation is an increasingly popular approach for triggering backtracking and error correction in agentic reasoning. This strategy presupposes two capabilities: (1) in-situ monitoring fidelity (does confidence drop when an error occurs?) and (2) downstream steering control (does an uncertainty token causally steer the model to repair its error?). We evaluated four open-weights models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, and Phi-4, 14.7B) across 15,200 math benchmark attempts, isolating 2,017 reasoning errors within each model's capability frontier. Applying 27,568 counterfactual continuations across these failure points, we demonstrate a consistent decoupling between monitoring and control.
  On monitoring, all four models fail to detect their own errors. Verbalized confidence does not distinguish mistake steps from sound reasoning, yielding near-chance within-position AUROCs between 0.500 and 0.561. Even at a model's first reasoning error, trajectory confidence remains saturated at 95.1% to 99.9%, with noticeable drops ($\ge 10$ points) appearing on fewer than 9% of errors in Llama and under 1.6% in the other three models. In contrast, models respond readily to external uncertainty: injecting a low-confidence tag (10%) at the error step significantly increases downstream correction across all models (+3.7 to +22.5 points over format-matched 95% certainty; all $p \le 0.0022$), reaching up to 38.5% under active rethinking instructions. However, injecting doubt onto already-correct steps causes models to discard valid reasoning, reducing solve rates by up to 22.8 points. Inference-time self-correction is thus bottlenecked by in-situ error detection rather than downstream repair capacity: models readily steer toward recovery when prompted with doubt, yet fail to self-monitor during generation.

Artificial Intelligence.title: CTLink: A Text-Prompted Segmentation Model for Linking Radiology Report Findings to 3D Chest CT Scans
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Radiology reports describe findings in text only, without visually marking them on the scan, so readers cannot directly see which abnormality each reported finding refers to. We introduce CTLink, a text-prompted 3D segmentation model that segments findings described in a chest CT report. CTLink was trained on 4123 noncontrast chest CT scans with 9547 segmented report findings, including ReXGroundingCTv2, a newly annotated dataset of 1134 scans and 1895 findings with every instance of each finding segmented. On the 200 ReXGroundingCT validation scans, CTLink achieved a hit rate of 0.816, an instance F1 score of 0.456, and a mean Dice score of 0.400, compared with 0.533, 0.175, and 0.234 for VoxTell, a publicly available text-prompted segmentation model (P < .001 for all). On the test set of the MICCAI 2026 ReXGrounding challenge, an ensemble of seven CTLink models achieved the highest hit rate (0.782) and instance F1 score (0.386) of all 48 participating teams. On 50 test scans segmented twice by independent radiologists, CTLink matched or exceeded inter-rater agreement. Diffuse non-focal findings remained the main limitation, partly because their extent is outlined inconsistently even between radiologists. The CTLink model weights are available at https://huggingface.co/rajpurkarlab/CTLink, and the dataset at https://huggingface.co/datasets/rajpurkarlab/ReXGroundingCT.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Seeking in Space: Benchmarking Purposeful Active Exploration of Vision-Language Models for Spatial Reasoning
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Humans explore unfamiliar spaces with purpose, deciding where to look until they have gathered the evidence a spatial question requires. However, can vision-language models (VLMs), which reason increasingly well over curated images and videos, also seek in space when the evidence is not handed to them? We present ActSpace-Bench, a benchmark of 994 questions across 234 exploration episodes in 72 real-scanned indoor scenes, where a model starts from a single view, navigates real captured frames, and must gather evidence before answering. To assess whether such exploration is purposeful, we introduce a controlled evaluation protocol that fixes each model as the reasoner and compares its own exploration against a same-budget random walk and an oracle route, separating evidence seeking from spatial reasoning. Every question is verified to require exploration and answered from 3D annotations, masked-evidence questions test whether models know when to abstain, and over 95% of sampled questions are confirmed correct by human verification. Evaluations of 23 proprietary, open-weight, and spatially specialized VLMs reveal that the strongest models do seek evidence with purpose but lose much of it to limited memory, whereas weaker and specialized models explore no better than a random walk or fail to reason over the evidence they are given, pointing to memory and evidence-grounded reasoning as the next targets for active spatial intelligence.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Neural Field Thermal Tomography: A Differentiable Physics Framework for Non-Destructive Evaluation
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Inverse problems for stiff parabolic partial differential equations (PDEs), such as the inverse heat conduction problem (IHCP), are severely ill-posed: the forward map rapidly damps high-frequency interior structure before it reaches the boundary. Soft-constrained physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), which embed the PDE as a residual penalty, decouple the diffusivity from the surface data in their standard two-network inverse formulation, and the evaluated variants fit boundary measurements while leaving the interior field essentially untouched. We propose Neural Field Thermal Tomography (NeFTY), a hard-constrained neural field framework for label-free three-dimensional inverse heat conduction. NeFTY represents the unknown diffusivity as a continuous coordinate-based neural network, and at every optimization step passes the candidate field through a differentiable implicit-Euler heat solver with harmonic-mean interface flux, so that the simulated temperature satisfies the discretized heat equation up to the solver tolerance. Adjoint gradients propagate the surface reconstruction error back to the network weights at solver-level memory cost, making test-time inversion tractable on a single GPU. Across synthetic 3D benchmarks, NeFTY outperforms soft-constrained PINN variants, a voxel-grid baseline, and classical L-BFGS voxel inversion through the same solver on label-free volumetric recovery, and it transfers to real thermography data, surpassing classical signal-processing baselines in both defect segmentation and depth estimation. Additional details at https://cab-lab-princeton.github.io/nefty/

Artificial Intelligence.title: ToolSmith: An Automatic Tool-Generation Framework for Multimodal Search Agents
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Recent multimodal search agents use reasoning, vision, and live web search across many turns to answer questions beyond parametric knowledge by orchestrating a small library of hand-crafted search and visual tools. However, the library is laborious to create and maintain, and frozen when new query types, evidence formats, and failure modes are encountered in the wild. Human practitioners, by contrast, cope with insufficient tools by fashioning new ones from familiar parts and reusing them across tasks. Inspired by this, we propose ToolSmith, an automatic tool-generation framework that grows and reuses modules on top of a lean base tool library. We evaluate ToolSmith on three in-domain multimodal search benchmarks and ten out-of-domain benchmarks under a VLM-as-a-Judge protocol. ToolSmith consistently improves over the base library across deployed agents of varying scales, with larger backbones reaping greater gains, demonstrating the scalability of the approach. Our code and data are available at https://threesr.github.io/toolsmith/.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Learning Neurovascular Codes for EEG-to-fMRI Synthesis
Artificial Intelligence.summary: In this paper, we introduce Neurovascular Codes as shared EEG representations for fMRI generation. We first train a separate EEG encoder to predict each fMRI signal, learning target-specific temporal and spectral features from the same EEG window. After training, we freeze the encoders and project their concatenated hidden features into a shared neurovascular code. Conditioned on this code, stochastic interpolant transforms Gaussian noise into a vector of fMRI signals, allowing different responses to be sampled for the same EEG window. We evaluate our approach on eight public simultaneous EEG-fMRI datasets, including four resting-state and four task-based datasets with 61,646 volume-level pairs. Under within-subject and held-out-subject evaluation, our model improves average Pearson correlation over the strongest encoder baselines by 19.1% and 19.8%, respectively. The corresponding improvements over the strongest generator baselines are 18.8% and 47.9%. Beyond reconstruction accuracy, we also evaluate the generated signals using subject-identification classifiers trained on real fMRI. Our method achieves the highest mean accuracy among the evaluated generators. We hope that our work opens up new opportunities for cross-modal brain modeling.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Know When to Abstain: Conformal Confidence Estimation for Text-to-SQL
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Text-to-SQL systems often return queries that execute successfully but answer the wrong question. Detecting these errors at deployment is hard because execution correctness is defined against a gold query, which exists only in labeled data. We formulate confidence estimation for Text-to-SQL as probabilistic query validation under a latent correctness variable that is observable at calibration time through gold-SQL execution and latent at deployment. Our estimator separates generation from validation. A generator LLM writes and executes the query, and a different critic LLM judges the query and its execution result. The critic's validation and execution-grounded alignment scores are fused with the generator's verbalized confidence, token-level uncertainty, and SQL-structural features in a Random Forest, using two sequential LLM calls. Two calibration steps give finite-sample guarantees. A Learn-then-Test threshold ensures, with probability $1-δ$, that the error rate among accepted queries stays below a user-chosen budget. A conformal p-value bounds the false abstention rate. On Spider we use GPT-OSS-120B as generator and Gemma-4-31B as critic. The estimator obtains an AUARC of 0.899. Without abstention, 22.6% of queries are wrong. With a 15% risk budget ($δ=0.1$), a threshold is certified on all 10 resampled splits, and the system accepts 52.4% of queries on average with 9.1% observed error. Five different critic models give similar results. In a controlled comparison on Spider with Olmo-3-32B as generator, the estimator obtains an AUARC of 89.5, compared with 81.2 for the strongest logit-based baseline. Applied to BIRD without retraining, the confidence scores remain informative (AUROC 0.72, against 0.79 on Spider), but the risk guarantee does not transfer, as expected without exchangeability.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Roundtable Policy: Confidence-Weighted-Consensus Aggregation Improves Multi-Agent-System Reasoning
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Multi-agent systems have demonstrated exceptional performance in downstream tasks beyond diverse single agent baselines. A growing body of work has explored ways to improve their reasoning and collaboration, from vote, debate, to complex interaction protocols. However, it still remains opaque why specific choice would be preferred in multi-agent systems. Inspired by the decision-making mechanism of democratic committees and The Society of Mind, we introduce Roundtable Policy, an inference-time reasoning framework for multi-agent systems that performs inference through the weighted consensus of multiple LLMs. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate its that this approach significantly enhances reasoning in complex heterogeneous scientific tasks. Roundtable Policy emphasizes structured and interpretable inference rather than opaque convergence, while requires only black-box access and uniform procedures, making it broadly applicable to diverse multi-agent systems.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Fully Interpretable Minimal Transformers: From Geometry to Algorithm
Artificial Intelligence.summary: We present a framework for building and interpreting minimal transformer models. By constraining a transformer's embedding dimension and head size to 2, we enable full two-dimensional visualization of its internal representations. Embeddings, query/key/value transforms, attention outputs, residual streams, and decision boundaries can all be seen directly. Our central claim is that the learned geometry implies an algorithm. The arrangement of points and boundaries in R^2 can be read as a step-by-step procedure. We train a transformer on a simple task where it must produce the most recently observed even number whenever the '+' operator appears in a sequence of digits. Once trained, we visually walk through every step of the transformer's computation. We show how the model embeds the tokens and their respective positions in the sequence, transforms them via the Q, K, and V matrices, uses the dot product between the Q and K representations to form the attention matrix, and uses the attention matrix to select values that move the representation of each input token embedding to the region of the domain of the output layer that will correctly predict the next token. We introduce a suite of interpretability visualizations that make the algorithmic interpretation of this procedure explicit. Our framework offers a pedagogical and experimental testbed to explore how transformers use information geometry to implement next-token prediction.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 27 pages, 15 figures, 2 tables. Code and training-dynamics animations: https://github.com/Raneem-mahajne/creating_transformer

Artificial Intelligence.title: CO-GRAFT: Attributing Reinforcement Learning Gains in Search Agents via Role-Level Policy Grafting
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) improves large language model search agents by up to 32 exact-match (EM) points over their pre-RL initializations, yet overall accuracy gains do not identify which underlying functional capabilities improve or interact during training. We introduce CO-GRAFT, a reward-agnostic interventional attribution framework in which an RL-trained agent and its pre-RL initialization jointly generate a single trajectory under closed-loop execution with live retrieval. Each policy controls a mutually exclusive subset of four functional roles: intermediate reasoning, search-or-answer decision, search query generation, and final answer extraction. Evaluating all 2^4=16 role assignments without modifying weights or retraining defines a cooperative game whose Shapley values decompose the total RL gain across roles, while M"obius interaction terms distinguish standalone role improvements from multi-role coupling. Applying CO-GRAFT to Search-R1 agents across Qwen2.5 and Llama-3.2 models (spanning two sizes, base and instruction-tuned initializations, GRPO and PPO optimizers, and NQ and HotpotQA datasets), we show that query generation never exceeds 15% of the total gain; instead, gains are governed by pre-RL answer validity, search retention, model scale, and fixed task-level search budgets, shifting credit from reasoning toward answer extraction in larger or well-formatted answer response checkpoints while smaller base models rely on reasoning--decision coupling.

Artificial Intelligence.title: DeliChess: A Multi-party Dialogue Dataset for Deliberation in Chess Puzzle Solving
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Multi-party dialogue is a critical setting for studying collaborative reasoning and decision-making, yet existing datasets rarely focus on structured, reasoning-intensive tasks. We introduce DeliChess, a dataset of group deliberation dialogues in which participants collaboratively solve multiple-choice chess puzzles. Participants first answer independently, then engage in multi-party deliberation and revise their individual answers. The dataset comprises 107 sessions containing 321 puzzle discussions across 24 unique positions, with full transcripts, pre- and post-deliberation choices, and utterance-level annotations of communicative function, epistemic stance, and usefulness in supporting deliberation. Our analyses show that greater diversity in initial solution quality is associated with larger gains, while answer trajectories reveal how deliberation can recover, discover, or lose strong answers. Cases in which groups surpass every independent answer are associated with sustained reasoning and epistemic openness. We further propose a diagnostic action-selection task: the tested LLMs show limited exact agreement with human-attested helpful actions, while ranked predictions reveal partial alignment. Overall, our dataset provides a testbed for modelling group reasoning, dialogue dynamics, and conditions for effective deliberation.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Needwise: Generation-Free Conversational Recommendation from Need-Level Typed Decisions
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Conversational recommenders must rank items against needs that catalogs record only in part, while users add, withdraw and reverse needs and switch between requests. LLM rankers re-read the dialogue at every turn: they are slow, and their ordering does not show which needs an item meets. We show that a conversational recommender can be built from typed decisions instead: named questions over fixed options, answered with option probabilities rather than generated text. On each turn, one typed request maps the message onto the catalog's fields, keeps what no field expresses in the user's words, and decides how the turn changes each earlier need. Needwise then ranks candidates must-first: the needs on the kind of item, its place and its price form a tier, and within it one holistic decision and need-level verdicts (supported, contradicted or unknown) are combined with equal weight (Needwise-HF). With the graded attributes withheld from the records, so that needs must be inferred from names, descriptions and reviews, Needwise-HF ranks Google Local requests significantly better than GPT-6 Sol (0.383 against 0.343 nDCG@10) and is not significantly different from the strongest LLM ranker on Google Local and Yelp; these comparisons keep their sign under every treatment of unrecorded attributes we test. It costs a fraction of GPT-6 Sol's API price and answers in 2.5 s at the median on Google Local, against 5.6 s for GPT-6 Sol. In conversations, the typed state keeps the ranking across switches and returns, but it recognizes only 19-27% of withdrawn needs.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Reducing Order Sensitivity in Decision Models
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Decision models are emerging as fast components of larger AI systems. Yet recent decision models, such as Jev, process options sequentially, leading to different predictions based on their ordering. Across ten open- and closed-source decision models, we find that \emph{order-sensitivity} is pervasive, causing substantial accuracy degradation and unreliable decision-making. These effects become more pronounced as the number of options grows and can compound across multi-step decisions. To address this problem, we systematically compare eight methods for mitigating order sensitivity in terms of robustness, predictive accuracy, and inference efficiency. Among these methods, we find that \emph{tree attention} is a surprisingly effective and efficient method. It achieves order invariance by processing options as parallel branches of a shared context. When used during training, it matches the baseline's average accuracy. Applied to the baseline without retraining, it also eliminates order sensitivity with only a 1.1-point drop in accuracy. Our findings demonstrate that order invariance can be enforced directly in decision models with little or no loss in predictive accuracy.

Artificial Intelligence.title: When Does Overriding the Majority Vote Help?
Artificial Intelligence.summary: When should additional reasoning or verification replace a majority-vote answer? We call such a replacement an override. We examine two obstacles: the availability of correct alternatives and the reliability of methods that produce or select them. We compare additional reasoning, executed programs, and cross-model reasoning on 150 competition-mathematics questions with three open reasoning models. Starting from a majority vote over 16 responses, we measure how often overrides occur and how many errors they correct or introduce across agreement thresholds. When the vote is incorrect, the correct answer is often absent from the original responses. Additional same-model reasoning rarely overrides, while executed programs correct more errors than they introduce at every evaluated threshold. Cross-model overrides improve some weaker baselines but do not establish an advantage over the more accurate model alone, even with only eight standalone responses. Stricter agreement reduces how often overrides occur but does not consistently increase the fraction that correct errors. At the strictest thresholds, overrides occur on few distinct questions, limiting conclusions about their reliability.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Habitats: A Framework for Open-Ended Evolution of Agent Objectives
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Designing what an agent should optimize can be as difficult as optimizing the agent itself. Existing language-model-based reward-generation methods typically refine objectives for predefined tasks and couple the decision of what to explore with the synthesis of how to implement it, potentially narrowing the resulting behavioral repertoire. We introduce Habitats, a framework for open-ended evolution of executable agent objectives. Habitats maintains a population of reward-policy pairs and evaluates every policy under every population reward, producing a cross-fitness matrix that exposes self-mastery, transfer, and functional diversity. A population-level Planner uses this information to select parent rewards and issue targeted mutation directives, while a separate Mutator translates those directives into validated reward programs. We evaluate Habitats in a discrete Card Sandbox and three continuous-control environments (Cart-Pole, Hopper, and Cheetah) against Independent Generation and Direct Mutation baselines. Across four environments and three random seeds, Habitats achieves the highest macro-averaged final Specialist Quality and Behavioral Diversity, with final diversity reaching 1.8x that of Direct Mutation and 2.5x that of Independent Generation. Finally, across ten downstream objectives unseen during evolution, frozen Habitats policy libraries achieve higher paired win rates than size-matched Direct Mutation and Independent Generation libraries at 10,000 adaptation episodes, while also surpassing task-specific policies trained from scratch for 20,000 episodes. These results suggest that separating population-level planning from reward synthesis enables the discovery of diverse, learnable, and reusable behaviors.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: To be published in the Managing Agents that Manage Agents Workshop on Responsible Use of Meta-Agents at the Fortieth Annual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (2026)

Artificial Intelligence.title: Deneb-Vritra: Descriptions, Edges and Names Examined by Blocking Via Restoring Token Representations and Attention
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Laya is a 421M-parameter encoder that answers a question about a text in one pass: each answer option, written as a name plus a description, gets a marker token, and one score is read from the network at each marker. We first confirm that such models can follow an option's name when it contradicts the description; the question is where in the network this happens. We locate it. On 951 synthetic questions we move each name onto another option's description and count how often the model picks the option with the right name (the name shortcut): 53% for the released checkpoint, 59% for our fine-tune v1, 11% for a fine-tune with name randomisation. On a 320-item sample, blocking attention from each marker to its own name tokens in layers 14 to 17 of 28 cuts v1's shortcut from 67% to 16% (19% on two schemas held out from component selection) while accuracy with the original names stays at 90%; blocking marker edges to the question, other options or text has no effect. No single head matters (largest effect 9 points), and restoring clean marker states undoes the swap from layer 16. Attention mass tracks the window by layer but not by head. Repeated on 5 checkpoints (released, fine-tuned, name-randomised, and a pair trained without two schemas), the knockout finds similar layers; in the name-randomised ones, blocking the description edges instead brings the shortcut back to 56-58%, so the read persists and is outvoted. Marker states decode the name from layer 0; a one-direction probe erasure changed nothing but was weaker than a random edit. Copying layers 0-13 or 14-27 of a name-randomised sibling into a fine-tune recovers 66% and 65% (v1); 21% and 45% (pair A) of its shortcut reduction. 9 of the 12 predictions we could score, written before running, failed. Head sweeps cover 5 of 5 checkpoints; data are synthetic and LLM-labelled; one architecture.

Artificial Intelligence.title: SRCWDNet: Semantic-Relational Cross-Window Dual-Graph Network for Multi-Label Remote Sensing Scene Classification
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Multi-label remote sensing scene classification remains a challenging task due to complex spatial-spectral patterns, extreme class imbalance, and inter-label dependencies that are often insufficiently modeled. To address these challenges, we introduce a Semantic-Relational Cross-Window Dual-Graph Network (SRCWDNet), which integrates three key modules: (1) a Cross-Window Attention module that captures local and global visual context through learnable global tokens; (2) a Dual Label-Graph module that adaptively combines statistical co-occurrence graphs and learned semantic-embedding graphs to facilitate label-relational reasoning; and (3) a Neural Classifier Chain that sequentially predicts labels to exploit inter-label dependencies. Evaluated using five-fold cross-validation and trained with an Asymmetric-Graph-Consistency loss, SRCWDNet achieves accuracies of 98.93% and 96.53%, with corresponding F1-scores of 0.9365 and 0.8723 on the MLRSNet and China-MAS50k datasets, respectively, outperforming CNN, transformer, and lightweight baselines. These findings demonstrate that jointly modeling visual attention and adaptive label correlations can substantially improve multi-label remote sensing scene classification, particularly under long-tailed class distributions.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Genome-to-Image Translation: Reconstructing Escherichia coli Morphology from Genomic Sequences
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Antimicrobial resistance in Escherichia coli is established in routine practice by culture-based susceptibility testing, which is slow relative to the clinical need for an early treatment decision. Resistance status also leaves a measurable trace in cell morphology, and whole-genome sequencing of clinical isolates is increasingly available, which raises the question of whether colony appearance can be predicted directly from an isolate's genome. We formulate this as a conditional image-generation problem. The assembled contigs of each isolate are encoded into a single 768-dimensional vector by a frozen genomic language model through a segment-contig-isolate aggregation hierarchy, and a conditional Wasserstein GAN with gradient penalty synthesizes colony images from this embedding together with the applied antibiotic and the resistance label. We train on 167,356 single-cell images from 22 clinical blood isolates imaged under azithromycin, ciprofloxacin, tetracycline, and a no-drug control, compare seven pretrained convolutional backbones inside the generator, and select ConvNeXt-Tiny on distributional image-quality metrics. The synthetic images are then assessed extrinsically: added to a reduced real training set, they improve per-antibiotic resistance classification, with a significant gain in resistant-class recall.

Artificial Intelligence.title: FATCAT: Fault Injection Attacks Targeting Chip-level Alignment
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Model alignment is the primary safety and security mechanism for enforcing refusal of malicious prompts in modern foundation models; yet, existing adversarial evaluations implicitly assume underlying hardware integrity. In this paper, we present FATCAT, the first physical fault-injection attacks capable of eliminating refusal in modern large language and vision-language models. Specifically, we present a non-invasive electromagnetic (EM) fault injection attack targeting GPU-accelerated Systems-on-Chip with physical access, requiring neither software execution privileges nor model-layer access. By leveraging an autonomous Radio Frequency (RF) side-channel trigger to synchronize EM faults to the prompt prefill phase, the attack corrupts safety-critical memory transactions across off-chip LPDDR5 DRAM and on-chip LPDDR physical interfaces without crashing the system while preserving model coherence. Evaluated on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano and AGX Thor running Llama 3.2 1B and Gemma 3 1B, localized physical faults reliably force models to fulfill restricted requests, demonstrating that model-level alignment provides no robust security guarantees without hardware-level fault tolerance. Finally, we demonstrate the physical-world consequences of this vulnerability on an active 6-DoF robotic manipulator controlled by a SmolVLA vision-language-action policy. Our attack silently corrupts the model forcing the arm into abrupt, hazardous lunges; in two instances the robotic arm attempted to pinch the paper author -- proving that hardware faults can directly translate into real physical harm.

Artificial Intelligence.title: IDP AutoOpt: Agent-Driven Optimization of Document Processing Pipeline Configurations
Artificial Intelligence.summary: We present IDP AutoOpt, an autonomous LLM agent that discovers high-performing configurations for intelligent document processing (IDP) pipelines. Tuning IDP prompts, models, OCR settings, and schemas jointly currently costs domain specialists 20 to 80+ person-hours per document type and does not scale as enterprises add document classes. IDP AutoOpt runs a closed loop: it scores a configuration on a small labeled set, diagnoses field-level errors, generates targeted edits, and re-evaluates, guided by human-authored domain skills that encode production expertise. Across extraction, classification, and packet-splitting tasks deployed in healthcare, marketing-intelligence, and financial-services settings, IDP AutoOpt matches or exceeds human-expert accuracy at equal or lower cost (on an extraction benchmark, 90.2% vs 81.6% at 4.6 x lower per-page cost), cutting configuration time from weeks to under two hours. We further show that agent LLM capability has a hard threshold below which optimization fails, and that curated domain skills outperform raw source-code access, which can degrade performance when provided without structure. We also share practical lessons on context management and variance mitigation. Requiring only a configurable pipeline, a scoring function, and a small labeled set, the approach extends beyond IDP to other enterprise AI systems, such as RAG and multi-agent workflows, where configuration bottlenecks deployment.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Self-Upgrading Embodied Agents
Artificial Intelligence.summary: An embodied agent built on a language model goes to work with the weights it was given and keeps them for life. To get better, it needs more training, or reflection, memory, search or prompts that cost every step and are lost when the task changes. Editing weights by reasoning, weight-space programming, could end this, but has stayed with models that only reason or relied on a far larger commercial model. We introduce the self-upgrading embodied agent, to our knowledge the first that learns from its own experience by upgrading its own weights on the job, between its tasks, with no training, no gradient, no reward model, no second model, no test-time scaling and no harness or prompt engineering. By day a 27B agent works in a household environment. At night it reads its record, finds many of its steps wasted on replies that reach the token limit before any action, traces the habit to one direction in its hidden states, and rewrites one tensor of its weights. An agent that rewrites itself must first never break itself, so it is its own examiner: it tests every change against its unchanged self on practice tasks and keeps only what holds. When an edit holds, the next day it is a better agent, at the same cost per step: over thousands of held-out episodes, 48 fresh seeds a task, its one kept edit makes it complete significantly more tasks, in fewer steps, with fewer wasted and fewer tokens. This self-improvement is multi-round, stable and continual: through the nights that follow, the upgrade holds, without collapse. Of four sizes of its family, only the 27B agent does this. From here on, an embodied agent need not keep training and inference apart: as it works, it gathers its own experience and upgrades itself, with no separate pre-training or post-training and no human intervention. We believe this opens lifelong continual learning for robots: stable, continual, recursive self-improvement.

Artificial Intelligence.title: RUIBench: What Makes a Good Robot-Use Interface?
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Foundation models can reason about complex physical tasks, yet translating this intelligence into reliable robot execution remains challenging. We argue that a critical, often overlooked factor is the robot-use interface (RUI), which determines how agents express and execute physical actions. To systematically study its impact, we introduce RUIBench, comprising 30 manipulation tasks across five suites spanning world knowledge, in-context learning, discovery, dynamic interaction, and contact-rich manipulation. We further develop RUIKit, a unified framework that crosses six action abstractions with two interaction forms, yielding 13 interfaces under shared perception and control. In simulation, changing only the RUI shifts a frontier agent's success rate from 45% to 81%, and that of a fine-tuned 4B model from 13% to 47%.
