We further examine the relationships between bankruptcy-based and cost-gap-based allocation mechanisms and use a numerical example with simulated data to compare their implications. The proposed framework links alternative fairness principles for allocating cooperative savings to economically interpretable pricing mechanisms, providing a unified basis for analyzing how group purchasing gains are distributed among heterogeneous buyers.

Optimization and Control.title: National-scale scheduling of long-distance electric vehicle charging under plug capacity
Optimization and Control.summary: Can today's U.S. public charging network serve long-distance trips by electric vehicles (EVs), and at what cost to travelers? We plan the charging stops of 2.2 million long-distance trips that need en-route charging, from a 1% sample of a one-month simulation, through the contiguous U.S. fast-charging network. Plans value detour, charging, and waiting time. Charging to a fixed battery level makes each trip's problem a shortest path, solved exactly; common modeling shortcuts can reverse the cost comparison. For trips competing for plugs, we compare four coordination methods, from none to reservations by departure time; the best two come within 2.2% and 6.1% of the best known solutions on small cases. First, if every plug serves every EV, existing fast chargers can reach 98.5% of the trips that need to charge, excluding those with an overly long link, with under four stops and about seven minutes of detour. Second, charging speed and electricity price decide the cost comparison: at \$0.15 per kWh, the EV is cheaper only for travelers valuing their charging time below \$11 per hour with 50 kW, or \$111 per hour with 350 kW chargers; at \$0.45 per kWh, it costs more at either speed. Third, without coordination, long queues form at several hundred small stations at 50 kW while nearby larger ones are less busy. If every trip books a plug, almost all waiting disappears on all trips at 350 kW for under a minute of extra detour, and at \$0.15 per kWh the EV trip stays about 21% cheaper.
Optimization and Control.comment: 35 pages, 3 figures, 12 tables; includes supplementary material

Optimization and Control.title: Small-time global exact controllability of nonlinear Schrödinger equations on the circle with bilinear controls
Optimization and Control.summary:
We study nonlinear Schrödinger equations on the circle with nonlinearity $κ|ψ|^{2p}ψ$, a fixed smooth real potential $V$, and bilinear controls. Using only the three control potentials $\mathbf 1,\cos x,\sin x$, we prove global approximate controllability in $H^s$ on the unit sphere of $L^2$ for all integers $s,p\ge1$, every $κ\in\mathbb R$, and any prescribed positive time. The proof combines two ingredients: the approximate controllability between nowhere vanishing states from our companion paper, and a new mechanism that steers any nonzero initial state to a nowhere vanishing state in arbitrarily small time.
  When $V=0$ and the nonlinearity is defocusing or sufficiently weakly focusing, adding two explicit control potentials of finite regularity gives local exact controllability in $H^2$ near the constant state, via a moment problem and the inverse mapping theorem. Together, these results imply global exact controllability in $H^2$ on the unit sphere of $L^2$, at any prescribed positive time, with five control potentials. To~the best of our knowledge, this is the first global exact controllability result for a nonlinear Schrödinger equation with finitely many bilinear controls.

Optimization and Control.title: New Lower Bounds for Stochastic Non-Convex Optimization through Divergence Decomposition
Optimization and Control.summary: We study fundamental limits of first-order stochastic optimization in a range of nonconvex settings, including L-smooth functions satisfying Quasar-Convexity (QC), Quadratic Growth (QG), and Restricted Secant Inequalities (RSI). While the convergence properties of standard algorithms are well-understood in deterministic regimes, significantly fewer results address the stochastic case, where only unbiased and noisy gradients are available. We establish new lower bounds on the number of noisy gradient queries to minimize these classes of functions, also showing that they are tight (up to a logarithmic factor) in all the relevant quantities characterizing each class. Our approach reformulates the optimization task as a function identification problem, leveraging divergence decomposition arguments to construct a challenging subclass that leads to sharp lower bounds. Furthermore, we present a specialized algorithm in the one-dimensional setting that achieves faster rates, suggesting that certain dimensional thresholds are intrinsic to the complexity of non-convex stochastic optimization.
Optimization and Control.comment: Revised the examples arguments in the proof of Lemma 2.1. Corrected numerical constants, budget conditions, and terms involving the initial distance in the displayed SGD bounds. Clarified the role of auxiliary reference distributions in the lower-bound proofs. Refined concentration bounds and stopping arguments in the one-dimensional analysis. The main rates and algorithmic approach are unchanged

Optimization and Control.title: Near-Optimal Smooth Convex Optimization with a Comparison Oracle
Optimization and Control.summary: We study the minimization of a convex $d$-dimensional function with $L$-Lipschitz gradient when the only available information is a comparison oracle that reports which of two points has the smaller objective value. Given an initial point within distance $R$ of a minimizer, the constants $L$ and $R$, and $A = LR^2/\varepsilon$, we give a deterministic method that returns an $\varepsilon$-optimal point using $O(\sqrt{A}\,[d\log(2dA)+\log^2(2A)])$ comparisons for $A\ge1$, counting all comparisons spent in inner subroutines. The method is based on a normalized variant of Nemirovski's subspace method: each iteration performs a line search along an estimated gradient direction followed by a minimization over a two-dimensional affine subspace, and both subroutines rely on a comparison oracle and basic arithmetic operations only. With exact function values, combining finite-difference gradients with an accelerated method gives the well-known bound of $O(d\sqrt{A})$ evaluations; our bound shows that one bit per query suffices to match it up to logarithmic factors. Since two function values determine one comparison, the exact function-value lower bound of Dorn et al. implies that our bound is optimal up to logarithmic factors when $32\le A\le d^2$.

Optimization and Control.title: A Single-Loop Method with Optimal Leading-Order Oracle Complexity for Optimization and Game Stationarity in Nonconvex--Concave Minimax Optimization
Optimization and Control.summary: We develop a single-loop first-order framework for smooth nonconvex--concave minimax optimization, with matching leading-order upper and lower bounds for optimization and game stationarity in a projected zero-respecting oracle model. We propose a single-loop projected damped extragradient method coupling projected extragradient updates with dual momentum and a moving proximal center. Each iteration uses at most three gradient evaluations, without nested subproblems. For game stationarity, a deterministic best iterate has first-order residual below $\varepsilon$ with leading oracle complexity $\mathcal{O}(L^{3/2}D_Y^{1/2}Δ_φ\varepsilon^{-5/2})$, where $L$ is the gradient Lipschitz constant, $D_Y$ bounds the dual feasible-set diameter, and $Δ_φ$ is the initial-point-dependent value-function gap. For optimization stationarity, a uniformly selected iterate has expected squared Moreau-envelope gradient norm at most $\varepsilon^2$ with leading oracle complexity $\mathcal{O}(L^2D_YΔ_φ\varepsilon^{-3})$. Matching lower bounds are $Ω(L^{3/2}D_Y^{1/2}Δ_φ\varepsilon^{-5/2})$ for game stationarity and $Ω(L^2D_YΔ_φ\varepsilon^{-3})$ for optimization stationarity over projected zero-respecting first-order methods. Under dual strong concavity, the same framework achieves leading first-order oracle complexity $\mathcal{O}(\sqrtκLΔ_φ\varepsilon^{-2})$ under both criteria, where $κ$ is the dual condition number. Matching lower bounds hold for both criteria in the same oracle model. To our knowledge, this is the first work to close the oracle complexity gap for smooth nonconvex--concave minimax optimization under both stationarity criteria by simultaneously improving upper and lower bounds in the projected zero-respecting oracle model.

Optimization and Control.title: Controlled nonstationary G-diffusions: dynamic programming, weighted Harris contraction and entrance risk
Optimization and Control.summary: We study controlled nonstationary \(G\)-diffusions in a canonical-law formulation of covariance uncertainty. The principal structural result is an abstract weighted Harris--oscillation contraction theorem for translation-covariant nonlinear evolution families. A Lyapunov estimate for a dominating terminal-perturbation bound and a local space--time oscillation estimate for differences imply exponential contraction in a weighted quotient norm, without positive homogeneity, subadditivity or convexity. For elementary sample-and-hold feedback controls and a rectangular family of martingale laws, we construct a measurable controlled state map and prove deterministic- and stopped-time dynamic programming principles for the robust lower value. Under uniform ellipticity, differences of Bellman values belong to a common parabolic Pucci class; a local Harnack argument and an all-policy Lyapunov estimate verify the abstract hypotheses. For zero running cost, the contraction yields a unique tempered entrance nonlinear expectation and exponential attraction. With running cost, it yields a unique normalized nonstationary corrector and an additive cocycle, together with exponential convergence of relative values. Subtracting a scalar primitive of the cocycle gives an all-time viscosity solution of the backward Bellman--Isaacs equation. Autonomous and periodic coefficients yield additive eigenpairs, stationary and periodic ergodic equations, and convergence of long-time average costs. The results provide a long-time theory for optimally controlled dynamic risk evaluation under nonstationary covariance uncertainty.

Optimization and Control.title: Agentic Discovery of Simple Symbolic Inventory Policies
Optimization and Control.summary: Designing simple inventory policies becomes increasingly difficult as operational features and system configurations expand. We develop an Agentic Inventory-Policy Discovery System based on explicitly defined simple operational formula (SOF) policy and template classes. Large language models (LLMs) revise symbolic structures, while a numerical engine fits parameters separately for each instance and evaluates the induced policies. Multicriteria parent selection, state-specific operational diagnostics, and reusable symbolic motifs guide structural evolution. A three-stage progression develops shared templates across instances and configurations with varying state dimensions. Experiments on 15,600 instances spanning 50 demand distributions cover lead times, perishability, their combination, and lead times with limited customer patience. The discovered templates improve aggregate empirical performance over evaluated SOF benchmarks and are competitive with policies requiring more elaborate online computations. For a lost-sales system with a three-period lead time, we develop an average-cost decomposition and prove that, under specified demand and cost conditions, a capped dual-shortfall specialization of a discovered policy strictly outperforms every policy in the considered capped base-stock benchmark class. This analysis links the performance advantage to the discovered replenishment mechanism. Together, these results highlight the potential of agentic discovery to generate simple inventory policies with strong empirical performance and identify operational mechanisms amenable to rigorous theoretical analysis.

Optimization and Control.title: A proof of the Reinhardt conjecture
Optimization and Control.summary: We prove the Reinhardt conjecture: among centrally symmetric convex disks in the plane, the smoothed regular octagon has the least optimal lattice packing density, and equality holds precisely for its nonsingular affine images. Local cost inequalities reduce arbitrarily long switching cycles of a minimizer to six types. We exclude those types by geometric comparisons and rigorous finite verification, and identify the remaining short minimizer.
Optimization and Control.comment: 430 pages. The author hopes that further work will lead to a shorter and more beautiful proof

Optimization and Control.title: On Big-M Reformulations of Bilevel Linear Programs: Hardness of A Posteriori Verification
Optimization and Control.summary: A standard approach to solving optimistic bilevel linear programs (BLPs) is to replace the lower-level problem with its Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) optimality conditions and reformulate the resulting complementarity constraints using auxiliary binary variables. This yields a single-level mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model involving big-$M$ parameters. While sufficiently large big-$M$s that preserve at least one bilevel-optimal solution can be computed in polynomial time, verifying a priori that given big-$M$s do not cut off any feasible or optimal lower-level solutions is known to be computationally difficult. In this paper, we establish two complementary hardness results. First, we show that, even with a single potentially incorrect big-$M$ parameter, it is coNP-complete to verify a posteriori whether a given optimal solution of the resulting MILP model is bilevel optimal. In particular, this negative result persists for min-max problems without coupling constraints and applies to strong-duality-based reformulations of mixed-integer BLPs. Second, we show that verifying global big-$M$ correctness remains computationally difficult a posteriori, even when an optimal solution of the MILP model is available.
Optimization and Control.comment: The proof of Theorem 3 has been substantially revised

Optimization and Control.title: Universal Extra-Gradient Method for Stochastic Variational Inequalities
Optimization and Control.summary: We study the stochastic Extra-Gradient Method (EGM) for solving a stochastic variational inequality (VI) over a compact convex set. The main assumption is $(δ, L)$-continuity of the VI mapping, which includes Hölder mappings and their linear combinations. We develop new adaptive, line-search-free step-size rules for stochastic EGM. These rules can be interpreted as enhanced AdaGrad-type updates and require no prior knowledge of either the continuity modulus of the VI mapping or the variance of the stochastic oracle. The resulting methods are universal and attain the best complexity bound among the admissible continuity regimes. We prove convergence guarantees in terms of an expected residual function that upper bounds the relevant accuracy measures for several important problem classes, including the dual gap for monotone VIs, and the primal-dual gap for saddle-point and optimization problems. For Hölder-continuous mappings, our bounds recover the optimal dimension-independent complexity of first-order methods.

Optimization and Control.title: Nonminimizing Attration of Stochastic Subgradient Methods on Semialgebraic Functions
Optimization and Control.summary: We construct a globally Lipschitz, coercive, semialgebraic function in two dimensions for which stochastic subgradient iterates converge to the origin, a Clarke critical point that is neither limiting critical nor a local minimizer. For power-law stepsizes, this attraction holds on open sets of initial points and linear tilts, uniformly over all noise sequences within a prescribed bound. The example shows that subdifferential regularity cannot be removed from the generic guarantee of convergence to local minimizers established by Davis, Drusvyatskiy, and Jiang (2026). For the same tilted objectives and initial points, the unique Clarke subgradient flow converges to a strict local minimizer. Thus, convergence of continuous-time flows to local minimizers cannot by itself justify the corresponding guarantee for discrete subgradient methods, even with diminishing stepsizes.
Optimization and Control.comment: 16 pages, 2 figures. This revision adds a proof that the Clarke subgradient flow converges to a strict local minimizer from the same open set of initial points for which the discrete iterates converge to the nonminimizing origin

Optimization and Control.title: Fully First-Order Optimization for Implicit Multilevel Compositions via Recursive Perturbations
Optimization and Control.summary: We study multilevel optimization problems in which the outer objective depends on a finite composition of implicit response maps defined by smooth inner functions. This model covers chains of strongly convex minimization responses, strongly convex--strongly concave saddle responses, or a mixture of the two. We propose a fully first-order method that estimates the outer gradient through recursive response perturbations. The main difficulty with approximate responses is that an adjoint error at one level changes the perturbation vector at the preceding level. To control this propagation, we pair the unperturbed and perturbed updates at each level and track their scaled differences jointly with the forward response errors. The resulting tracking bounds are uniform in the perturbation radius $δ$. For the exact composite objective, we establish an $O(K^{-1}+δ^2)$ bound on the average squared gradient norm after $K$ outer iterations. For fixed problem data and finite depth, a suitable choice of $δ$ yields $ε$-stationarity in $O(ε^{-2})$ outer iterations with inner budgets independent of the target accuracy. For strongly convex minimization chains, we also derive condition-number-dependent first-order oracle complexity bounds.

Optimization and Control.title: Sharp Volume Contraction of a Centrally Cut John Ellipsoid
Optimization and Control.summary:
For a convex body $K\subset\mathbb R^n$ in positive dimension, let $w(K)$ be the volume of its maximum-volume inscribed ellipsoid. For a closed halfspace $H$ whose boundary passes through the center of that ellipsoid, we prove \[ w(K\cap H)\le R_nw(K),\qquad R_1=\frac12,\qquad R_n=\frac12\left(\frac n{n-1}\right)^{(n-1)/2}\quad(n\ge2), \] with equality attained in every fixed dimension. This refines the optimal dimension-independent bound from the author's earlier work on [Khachiyan's ellipsoid conjecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.28447).
  We characterize the full equality family, including nonsimplex extremizers, and establish an exact volume-deficit identity that yields dimension-independent stability of the new ellipsoid and its weighted contact geometry in John coordinates. The proof reduces the problem to finite John contacts and constructs an explicit conic certificate by a transformation of contact directions and a common polar rotation. Its determinant is controlled by a nonnegative contact defect. The sharp contraction theorem, equality classification, stability estimates, and supporting results have been formally verified in Lean 4 using mathlib.

Optimization and Control.title: Exponential memory/query-complexity tradeoffs in high-accuracy feasibility problems
Optimization and Control.summary: We prove memory/query-complexity tradeoff lower bounds for the feasibility problem, where the goal is to find a point within an $ε$-ball hidden in the unit $d$-dimensional ball, with access to a separation oracle. This problem admits three regimes: the low-accuracy regime $ε\geq 1/\sqrt d$ where memory does not play a role, the medium-accuracy regime $1/\sqrt d\geq ε\geq e^{-Ω(d\ln d)}$ where prior works identified strong memory/query-complexity separations, and the high-accuracy regime $ε\leq e^{-Ω(d\ln d)}$ for which much less is known. In this regime, low-memory algorithms with significantly faster convergence rates than gradient descent have been developed in [BZJ24]: for accuracy $ε$ and any $δ\in[0,1]$, these require $d^{1+δ}\ln \frac1ε$ memory bits and use $\left(d\ln\frac1ε\right)^{O(d^{1-δ})}$ oracle queries. In comparison, gradient descent uses the same memory for $δ=0$ but requires $1/ε^2$ oracle queries. On the lower-bound side, no non-trivial memory/query-complexity tradeoff was known: the best lower bound remained the historical memory-independent bound $Ω(d\ln \frac1ε)$ from [NYD83]. We make progress towards characterizing the memory landscape in this high-accuracy regime by showing that for any $δ\in[0,1]$, any algorithm with $d^{1+δ}\ln\frac1ε$ bits of memory uses at least $\left(d\ln\frac1ε\right)^{\widetildeΩ(d^{(1-δ)/8})}$ oracle calls. This result justifies the seemingly peculiar exponential-in-$d$ dependence of oracle complexity for the aforementioned low-memory algorithms. In particular, our result shows that for high-accuracy feasibility problems, insufficient memory does result in an exponential price in the dimension for the query-complexity.
Optimization and Control.comment: Version note. This version revises the compression reduction and mutual-information accounting in Section 4.3. The revised argument explicitly includes the shared randomness in the Message between encoder and decoder

Optimization and Control.title: Learned spatial opportunity cost admission for ride-hailing with calibrated thresholds
Optimization and Control.summary: Ride-hailing operators must decide whether to accept a request before observing future demand. Serving a ride earns revenue and changes where and when the vehicle can serve again. We develop learned spatial opportunity cost admission for a centrally managed fleet. The policy estimates demand from past requests and solves a rolling mean-demand plan. Dual prices account for using a vehicle at its origin and returning it to service at its destination. With positive regularization, the policy accepts a request when its planned service fraction reaches a common threshold. We fix the regularization parameter and select the threshold using validation revenue. For one vehicle on a single route, we derive the exact range of thresholds that attain optimal expected revenue. When several origins share return demand at a hub, the best common threshold can lose revenue in proportion to fleet size. Independent validation bounds the revenue loss relative to the best candidate threshold. At a fixed threshold, under Poisson arrivals and a margin condition, the revenue gap between using estimated and true mean demand has a tight inverse-square-root bound in the number of historical days. We evaluate the policy on 60 synthetic instances across six demand families and on ten New York workdays across 25 taxi zones and three fleet sizes. With two validation days, calibration improves mean paired revenue over the default threshold by 4.93% in the synthetic study and 7.08% in New York. In New York, the policy earns 1.24% to 2.54% less than the best-performing benchmark in mean paired comparisons and takes about one-eleventh as long per decision. Calibration gains are largest for the smallest New York fleet. In the synthetic study, gains over accepting every feasible request are largest under commuting demand.

Optimization and Control.title: Critical Times for Local Controllability and Steady-State Transfer of a Water Tank
Optimization and Control.summary: We determine the critical times for a water tank governed by the one-dimensional Saint-Venant equations with horizontal acceleration as the control. Time is measured in units of the linear wave crossing time. For $C^1$ fluid trajectories and continuous controls, local exact controllability holds exactly for $T>T_c=2+d_c\approx 2.43674$, where $d_c$ is determined by two transcendental equations. In the same trajectory class, the system is locally controllable between still-water equilibria if and only if $T>2$. These thresholds confirm Coron's conjecture for steady-state transfer and give a larger value for local exact controllability. The same quadratic endpoint formula and nonlinear correction yield the positive results for both problems. At $T_c$, comparison with a critical plane curve gives the obstruction to local exact controllability. At $T=2$, the nonlinear flux forces small trajectories between still-water equilibria to be stationary.

Optimization and Control.title: Approximate Controllability of the generalized Burgers-Huxley equation in one dimension
Optimization and Control.summary: The generalized Burgers-Huxley (GBH) equation is a prototype model that describes the interplay among reaction, convection, and diffusion. In this article, we explore the controllability of this model by means of an interior control supported in an arbitrary non-empty open subset of the domain. We establish that the GBH equation is not globally approximately controllable in a given time. However, it is possible to steer the system from any steady state to an arbitrarily small neighborhood of another steady state in some suitable time by means of a localized interior control, provided that both steady states lie in the same connected component of the set of steady states.
Optimization and Control.comment: Updated the abstract and literature review in the introduction, and improved the proofs of theorems and propositions. Main results remain unchanged

Optimization and Control.title: Finite-Dimensional Internal Stabilization of Steady States of the Gray-Scott System
Optimization and Control.summary: In this article, we establish the local exponential stabilization of every steady state of the Gray-Scott system with homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions, other than the trivial state $(0,1)^{\top}$, at any prescribed decay rate by finite-dimensional feedback controls supported in an arbitrary nonempty open subset of the domain and acting only on the first equation of the system. Our approach does not require the steady state to be spatially constant and accommodates non-self-adjoint linearizations with variable coefficients. The proof combines unique continuation, a nonvanishing property of the steady-state coupling, the Fattorini-Hautus condition, and Riccati-based feedback.

Optimization and Control.title: Optimal isotropic three-material conducting composites with an ideal conductor, in the plane and in space.Bounds and optimal structures
Optimization and Control.summary:
The paper describes an optimal isotropic three-dimensional, three-material conducting composite. One material is an ideal conductor, the volume fractions are prescribed, and the objective is to minimize the effective conductivity over all admissible layouts.
  We first derive a lower bound for the effective conductivity as a function of the material properties and volume fractions. The composite energy is bounded below by a constrained polyconvex envelope, where quadratic and cubic null Lagrangians are imposed through Lagrange multipliers. We further assume that the fields in optimal structures are positive semidefinite. Together with the use of the cubic null Lagrangian, this assumption makes the bound exact. The resulting bound determines the extremal conductivity and the set of associated support fields in optimal structures. Depending on the parameters, it has five regions with different analytic expressions.
  We then prove the bound attainability by constructing optimal structures that realize the bound in every region. They are spherical atoms: a core of the intermediate-conducting material, surrounded by a mantle of wrapped optimal planar structures. In the two extreme regions, a crust is added from the material whose prescribed volume fraction is excessive.

Optimization and Control.title: Computer-Aided Analysis of Gradient Descent under Generalized Smoothness
Optimization and Control.summary: First-order methods constitute a central algorithmic paradigm in high dimensional applications. Under classical assumptions, their performance has been studied quite comprehensively with the developed theoretical apparatus of modern optimization. The development of the Performance Estimation Problems framework led to even deeper understanding and allowed computer-assisted derivation of exact worst-case guarantees. Due to convex nature of PEP programs, the framework is not applicable for systems that involve non-convex constraints. This includes a wide range of non-standard assumptions, some of them are highly relevant for practice such as generalized smoothness. In this paper proposes an approach of utilizing template solutions to derive guarantees in settings that do not admit convex formulation of exact worst-case performance problem. The approach is showcased by studying the performance of the gradient descent method for convex functions that also satisfy generalized smoothness assumption. Despite the inherent conservatism of the approach, this paper improves an existing convergence guarantee in the semi-automated manner.
Optimization and Control.comment: This is extended version of paper Krivchenko, V. O. (2026). Computer-Aided Analysis of Gradient Descent under Generalized Smoothness. Doklady Mathematics, 530(1), 5-13. The extended version is much more detailed. It contains proper discussion of the approach as well as descriptions of PEP experiments

Optimization and Control.title: A note on approximate projection onto the semidefinite complementarity set
Optimization and Control.summary: The proximal slack update in an augmented Lagrangian method for semidefinite complementarity constraints requires a joint matrix projection. Given real symmetric matrices $A$ and $B$, we seek the nearest pair $(X,Z)$ with $X$ positive semidefinite, $Z$ negative semidefinite, and $XZ=0$. To approximate this projection, we replace the orthogonal projector onto the subspace allowed for $X$ by a symmetric matrix $T$ with eigenvalues in $[0,1]$. From an optimal solution of the resulting semidefinite program, we form candidate subspaces by starting at the zero subspace and adding the eigenspaces of $T$ in decreasing order of eigenvalue. For each candidate, we compress $A$ to that subspace and $B$ to its orthogonal complement. We keep the positive eigenvalues of the first compression and the negative eigenvalues of the second. The best pair has squared loss at most $1.189$ times the minimum for arbitrary inputs and at most $1.15487$ times the minimum when $A$ is positive semidefinite and $B$ is negative semidefinite. For arbitrary inputs the factor improves to $1.18$ if $T$ has at most two distinct eigenvalues in $(0,1)$. The proofs average over a uniform spectral threshold and use computer-assisted bounds for the resulting scalar inequalities.

Optimization and Control.title: Ordering error estimates under mesh-uniform regularity and optimal two-mesh design for the KdV equation with boundary dissipation
Optimization and Control.summary: We study Galerkin error estimates and optimal two-mesh design for the Korteweg-de Vries (KdV) equation on a bounded interval with boundary dissipation. The ordering error is introduced to measure how much the nonlinearity changes the discretization error. A weighted cubic Hermite Galerkin scheme has mesh-uniform regularity: the discrete semigroups of the linearized equation inherit Crandall-Pazy regularity and Kato smoothing, with bounds uniform in the mesh size $h$. On a small ball of the energy space, the discrete solution maps are also analytic in the initial datum, with bounds uniform in $h$. On this ball the ordering error is at most of order $h^{1/6}$ times the squared energy norm of the datum, for all $t\ge0$. For $u_0$ on this ball and in the domain $D(A)$ of the linearized generator, the bound is of order $h^2\|u_0\|_{H^3}^{3/2}\|u_0\|_{L^2}^{1/2}$. A two-mesh computation adds a nonlinear correction on a coarse mesh to a linear simulation on a fine mesh. Its error is the linear error on the fine mesh plus the ordering error on the coarse mesh. Based on these error estimates, we formulate a model of the optimal two-mesh design: minimize the cost subject to an accuracy constraint given by the error bounds. For data in a small ball of $L^2$, the problem is convex in logarithmic mesh sizes. When the relative error bound for the coarsest allowed mesh exceeds the prescribed tolerance $η$, the optimal pair and its KKT multipliers are unique. For smooth data the problem is convex in the mesh sizes, and the optimal mesh ratio is independent of the tolerance until the coarse mesh reaches its upper limit. In both cases we characterize the small-amplitude limit of the relative cost when the relative tolerance is proportional to the amplitude.
Optimization and Control.comment: 35 pages, 1 figure. Combines a shortened version of arXiv:2610.39269 (energy-level estimates only) with new results on the optimal design of two-mesh computations. Lean 4 files and computational records in the ancillary files

Optimization and Control.title: A Study of the PDE Model for the Anisotropic Consensus-Based Optimization
Optimization and Control.summary: We investigate the nonlinear Fokker--Planck equation associated with anisotropic consensus-based optimization. Under suitable assumptions on the objective function, we establish global existence and uniqueness of density valued weak solutions for bounded initial probability densities with finite fourth moment. The main analytical challenge arises from the component-wise degeneracy of the diffusion, which vanishes along moving coordinate hyperplanes determined by the weighted consensus point. To overcome this difficulty, we develop spatial translation estimates based on weighted gradient bounds and uniform density estimates. Combined with temporal translation and moment estimates, these yield strong compactness in $L^2((0,T)\times\mathbb{R}^d)$ through the Fréchet--Kolmogorov compactness criterion, enabling passage to the limit in the regularized equations. Uniqueness is established through the associated McKean--Vlasov stochastic differential equation and Wasserstein stability of the weighted consensus point. Furthermore, we prove the propagation of $H^2$-regularity for sufficiently regular initial data.

Optimization and Control.title: Optimal Patrol Widths in the Infinite-Corridor Barrier-Guarding Game
Optimization and Control.summary: A guard of speed at most one and capture radius $r$ patrols an infinite corridor. An intruder knows the patrol and can follow any path of speed at most $q$ from one end to the other. We determine where the maximum width permitted by straight wall runners can be guarded against all such paths. Write $W_{\mathrm{opt}}(q)$ for the supremum over patrols with bounded longitudinal excursion and $F(q)=2r\sqrt{1+(3q^2+2q-1)^{-1}}$ for the wall ceiling on $1/3 < q < 1$. A four-leg bowtie attains $F(q)$ exactly for $q_a\le q < 1$, where $0.457892036651 < q_a < 0.457892036652$. For every $1/3 < q < q_a$ the supremum is strictly smaller. As $q$ approaches $q_a$ from below, $F(q)-W_{\mathrm{opt}}(q)$ is bounded above and below by positive constant multiples of $r(q_a-q)^2$. The lower estimate controls near-optimal patrols uniformly in their period. A rescaled bowtie gives the matching upper estimate. We also prove that periodic patrols give the same supremum as bounded-excursion patrols. For $q\ge1$ the one-way optimum is $r\sqrt{4+q^{-2}}$, a transverse sweep. This sweep is optimal against transit in both directions for $q\ge1/2$. At low speeds, $qW_{\mathrm{opt}}(q)/r$ tends to two, and an explicit ten-leg patrol guards width greater than $(2/q-1.235353)r$ throughout $0 < q\le1/40$. Rational spacetime and flux certificates give finite-speed bounds, including $6.944691333740r < W_{\mathrm{opt}}(1/4)\le8.10r$.
Optimization and Control.comment: 34 pages, 2 figures. Exact rational Python verifiers and a Lean 4 library for selected lemmas and finite certificates accompany the submission

Optimization and Control.title: Sharp Convergence of Extended Douglas--Rachford Splitting with Variable Relaxation
Optimization and Control.summary: We establish a sharp convergence theory for extended Douglas--Rachford splitting when the first operator is maximally monotone and the second is a convex subdifferential on a real Hilbert space. The resolvent stepsizes may be chosen independently, and the relaxation parameter may depend on the current and past iterates. For fixed stepsizes $α,β>0$, let $\vartheta=\min\{2,2α/β\}$. Assuming the sum of the operators has a zero, we prove weak convergence under $0<θ_k\le\vartheta$ and $\sum_kθ_k(\vartheta-θ_k)=\infty$. Within these pointwise bounds, the divergence condition is also necessary for a universal convergence guarantee when the relaxation sequence is prescribed in advance. Constant relaxation recovers the exact range $0<θ<\vartheta$, resolving a conjecture of Nilsson, Åkerman, and Giselsson. We also establish a sharp bound on growth of the residual, defined as the difference between the two resolvent outputs. We combine this bound with a new Lyapunov function whose definition is independent of the relaxation parameter to obtain a last-iterate residual rate, including $o(N^{-1/2})$ when the relaxation parameters remain uniformly separated from both endpoints.

Optimization and Control.title: Feedback Exact Controllability of the Nonlinear Diffusion Equation with Controller in Coefficients
Optimization and Control.summary: One designs a feedback controller for semilinear parabolic equations with controller in diffusion coefficients which steers the initial data y0 in a given state y1 in a finite time.

Optimization and Control.title: Handover Cost Optimization in LEO Satellite Networks using an RL-based Multiple-Column Selection Strategy via Branch-and-Price
Optimization and Control.summary: Next-generation wireless networks increasingly rely on low Earth orbit (LEO) satellites for broad coverage and low latency, making efficient handover management essential. We formulate satellite handover as a combinatorial optimization problem, assigning each ground user to exactly one capacity-limited, visible satellite while minimizing network handover costs. We propose a reinforcement learning (RL)-based branch-and-price (B&P) framework with learned multiple-column selection (MCS) to accelerate column generation while retaining exact dynamic programming pricing. We also develop two lightweight heuristic policies: handover-aware visibility duration (HAVD) for online decisions and congestion-aware predictive (CAP) for offline planning. Additionally, a local-search repair algorithm adapts precomputed B&P or MCS-B&P solutions to demand perturbations through single-flip and per-user trajectory re-optimization, avoiding complete re-optimization. Simulations using realistic large scale constellations, including Starlink Gen-1, demonstrate that MCS-B&P achieves solution quality comparable to exact B&P with fewer column-generation iterations, fewer branch-and-bound nodes, and reduced computation time. HAVD and CAP offer effective online and offline cost-latency trade-offs, while local-search repair recovers most performance losses due to demand perturbations at a fraction of the computational cost of full re-optimization.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Attractors Is All You Need: Parity Games In Polynomial Time
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: This paper provides a polynomial-time algorithm for solving parity games that runs in $\mathcal{O}(n^{2}\cdot(n + m))$ time-ending a search that has taken decades. Unlike previous attractor-based algorithms, the presented algorithm only removes regions with a determined winner. The paper introduces a new type of attractor that can guarantee finding the minimal dominion of a parity game. The attractor runs in polynomial time and can peel the graph empty.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: I withdraw this preprint because the algorithm is incorrect. Tom van Dijk provided a four-vertex counterexample, Odd owns all four vertices, labelled by priority. The moves $0\to1\to2\to4$ are forced; from 4, Odd chooses 0 or 2. Even wins every play, yet for d=4 the first pruning step discards the entire Even dominion, contradicting Lemma 3. The claimed polynomial-time result does not follow

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Less Rational, More Transparent: Censorship as (Robustly) Optimal Disclosure
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
Online platforms often control the information behind user decisions they want to influence, such as whether a driver accepts a trip or a buyer completes a purchase. A classical result in information disclosure shows that a {\em censorship} policy is optimal for the platform: the platform pools all sufficiently favorable options under a common message, such as a quality badge, and reveals the rest individually. This result, however, presumes fully rational users. We study disclosure to boundedly rational users who follow the logit quantal response model and whose rationality level the platform may not know.
  Our results deliver a unifying message: less rational, more transparent. Neither bounded rationality nor uncertainty about it calls for a more complex policy; each changes only how much the platform should pool, and only toward greater transparency. When the rationality level is known, censorship remains optimal, and less rational users optimally receive at least as much information as more rational ones. When the rationality level is unknown, censorship remains robustly optimal under each of three criteria: the maximin ratio, maximin payoff, and minimax regret, and the robust censorship can be chosen to be at least as transparent as the policy designed for fully rational users. This additional transparency weakly benefits both parties and acts as insurance against behavioral uncertainty: rationality-robust censorship secures at least 89.96\% of the payoff attainable with knowledge of the user's rationality level, whereas the policy designed for fully rational users can secure as little as 50\%. Taken together, these results suggest that platforms can keep their badge-based disclosure but should narrow its coverage when users may be boundedly rational.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: This paper incorporates selected results from "Rationality-Robust Information Design: Bayesian Persuasion under Quantal Response" (SODA 2024, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2207.08253), and adds substantial new results

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Participation Incentives in Online Cooperative Games
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study cooperative games in which the coalition forms online and the value it generates must be distributed irrevocably among the players present at each time step. We study participation incentives through four axioms: no player gains by delaying their arrival, every newly arriving player who adds value is rewarded immediately, every earlier player whose presence is essential receives a strictly positive share of the new increment, and a player who is a dummy in the current coalition has received nothing. We show that an equal-sharing rule can satisfy all four axioms but requires exponentially many value queries. This barrier is unavoidable as we prove that no equal-sharing rule satisfying the four axioms can be computed exactly with polynomially many value queries. In contrast, weighted sharing rules resolve the issue. For a family of rules that share each increment among a sharing set selected by a greedy deletion scan in reverse arrival order, we characterize exactly the weights under which the four axioms hold. Every rule in this family needs only $O(n^2)$ value queries, and among the desired rules, a unique one has weights that Lorenz-dominate those of all others. We finally characterize a more general class of weighted sharing rules, termed ordinal weighted sharing rules, whose weights depend only on the arrival order and on comparisons between coalition values, that satisfy the four axioms.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: Extended version of the AAMAS 2026 conference paper, with new results on weighted sharing rules, query complexity, and characterizations. Compared with v1, this version corrects a notation typo in the definition of S-STAY, an imprecise statement of the theorem on the IR refinement, and a minor error in the definition of IR-eULMES

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Combatting Fraud in Artificial Currency Based Government Benefits Programs
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Benefits programs are policy tools for providing targeted aid, such as food assistance or transit subsidies. However, these programs are often susceptible to misreporting fraud, wherein users misreport private attributes to obtain excess aid. To address this problem, we introduce a two-stage audit game between an administrator and users in which the administrator can audit users at a cost and levy fines on misreporting users, with player payoff structures designed to reflect real-world benefits programs. We show that the administrator's least-favorable Bayesian Stackelberg equilibria can be computed tractably via linear programming and derive prescriptive bounds on the administrator's excess payments and users' misreporting probability as functions of audit costs and fines. We further establish that, with an appropriately chosen budget level, the reduction in excess payments in any least-favorable Bayesian Stackelberg equilibrium offsets the audit budget required to sustain the mechanism, yielding total costs no greater than those of a baseline without an auditing authority, which we corroborate through a case study of Washington D.C.'s federal transit benefits program.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Event-Time Confounding Under Bursty Human Dynamics
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Web studies often measure what happens after a user action, such as a search after a chatbot answer. To credit an AI answer with later commercial activity, a study must separate what the answer caused from what the user would have done anyway. But people act in the middle of activity already underway, so the activity that drives what follows also chooses when the clock starts. We call this endogenous time zero. Using an opt-in panel that links conversational-AI use, browsing, and search, we insert inert timestamps (moments that match recent activity but mark no event) and rerun the standard analysis. In a pre-registered replication, these timestamps, which by construction cannot cause anything, reproduce 76% of the search increase after AI responses that follow recent browsing. Other users matched on 30-day activity, the usual control, give the same answer, and inert timestamps show a similar search excess across 16 kinds of Web events. Comparing with moments of matching recent history removes most of the increase, but no placebo audit we ran could confirm that this comparison is unbiased, and published studies almost never run one. We give a protocol for choosing comparisons and stress-testing estimators.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: v2: shortened and refocused version (inert-timestamp placebo test for user-timed Web events, a sweep across event types, reference-moment comparisons, and a protocol); 12 pages, 8 figures, 7 tables

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Straight to the Product: What Online Retailers Miss When Shoppers Ask AI First
Human-Computer Interaction.summary:
When people ask an AI assistant what to buy, what happens next at the store? We link the same people's assistant conversations to their later browsing at twenty large online retailers. People go to the product the assistant named: among shoppers who had not visited the store in the past week, visits to the named product within a day rise from 0.02 to 2.07 per 100 answers (+2.0 points [1.7, 2.4]), and on days with a product-page visit at the store, 44% show a product from their own answer, against 1.5% for a matched answer given to someone else. The result replicates in a separate five-month period. Few arrive through the assistant's link: after recommending answers, 89% of visits carry no sign of it, and 54% follow a web search, the same share as their usual visits. When a search comes just before the first visit, it names the answer's product 28% of the time (1% in earlier weeks), as if the search box were an address bar. The chat names the product; the store logs a search. Once there, shoppers keep browsing.
  We propose product follow-through, the share of answers followed by a visit to the product they named, as a way to evaluate shopping assistants and agents by what people do next: it needs no referral data or provider logs and can be computed for each assistant.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Managing Uncertainty in Teacher Vibe Coding: A Comparison of Teacher and Expert Workflows
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Vibe coding, or natural language software development, enables teachers to become creators of digital teaching artifacts. However, novice educators oftentimes face different barriers. This qualitative study examined the workflows of pre-service teachers, in-service teachers, and expert developers through think-aloud protocols. Findings reveal vibe coding operates through a loop of problem framing, development, and verification governed by uncertainty management. Teachers reduced uncertainty by grounding designs in authentic needs: pre-service teachers drew on pedagogical principles, whereas in-service teachers relied on everyday teaching challenges. Conversely, Experts reduced ambiguity by constraining requirements, decomposing artifacts into testable modules, and automating tests. These differences reveal complementary forms of pedagogical, contextual, and technical expertise. Future work may be about supporting nontechnical teachers in developing reliable and educational applications.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 12 pages, 4 figures, 1 table. Accepted for presentation at the 2027 American Educational Research Association Annual Meeting

Human-Computer Interaction.title: But Can You Draw It Live? The Emergence of AI Duidus for Adjudicating Suspected Generative AI Use in Digital Art Commission Communities
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Generative AI poses new challenges for digital art commission communities, where a commission's value often depends on human labor and authorship. We examine a novel community-developed dispute resolution mechanism called an AI duidu, or livestreamed drawing bet, used when an artist is suspected of using generative AI. In an AI duidu, an accuser challenges an artist to create a new artwork live, and community members vote on whether the artist created the disputed artwork without AI assistance. Often, both parties stake money with an intermediary, who releases it after the vote. Through interviews with 17 accusers, accused artists, or intermediaries, we examined how the AI duidu emerged and how participants perceived its effectiveness and risks. We found that AI duidus shift authorship verification from the artwork itself to the artist, using livestreamed creative labor, community adjudication, and wagering to establish provenance and negotiate community norms surrounding AI use.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Immersive Video Effects Persist Beyond Exposure: From Psychological Closeness to Self-Initiated Behaviour in a Two-Week Comparison with 2D Video
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Immersive Video (IV), a live-action stereoscopic 180-degree video format, has been shown to elicit a strong sense of Presence and enhance psychological closeness to individuals depicted in the video. However, whether these effects persist beyond exposure and are accompanied by subsequent self-initiated behaviour remains unclear. In this study, 84 participants were assigned to either an IV or a 2D video group, and psychological and behavioural outcomes were tracked over a two-week period. Psychological outcomes were assessed before and immediately after exposure and at approximately 3, 7, and 14 days post-exposure, while self-initiated behaviour was assessed during follow-up. Psychological closeness remained significantly higher in the IV group than in the 2D group for up to 7 days and remained elevated above baseline within the IV group at 14 days. Lasting-impression ratings were also significantly higher in the IV group throughout the follow-up period. Among participants who completed both scheduled follow-up assessments, 45.9% in the IV group met the operational criterion for early self-initiated engagement, compared with 13.2% in the 2D group. Furthermore, a higher proportion of participants in the IV group reported active or socially oriented behaviours. These findings suggest that IV can elicit psychological effects that persist beyond exposure and may encourage subsequent self-initiated engagement.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: LLM Support for Mathematical Problem Posing: What Changes When Revision Formulations Are Supplied or Withheld?
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: In mathematical problem posing, participants construct or modify problems rather than only solve predefined ones, creating opportunities for Large Language Models (LLMs) to support how those problems are formulated and revised. We investigate two forms of LLM support for revising participant-generated problems: Socratic scaffolding, which uses guiding questions while withholding candidate formulations, and Direct scaffolding, which provides concrete alternative formulations. We conducted a counterbalanced within-subjects study with 20 graduate students who posed and revised problems across two mathematical scenarios. Problems showed larger immediate supported artifact-quality gains under Direct than Socratic scaffolding. Exploratory dimension-level analyses identified statistically significant differences in structural clarity and novelty after correction for multiple comparisons. Socratic scaffolding was associated with longer revision time, highlighting a contrast between immediate artifact outcomes and revision processes. These findings identify the amount of candidate revision content supplied by an LLM as an important design variable in mathematical problem posing.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Micro-level AI Feedback Features and Student Responses in Consecutive LLM Tutoring Interactions
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: AI-assisted feedback research has shown that micro-level feedback features, such as concrete elaboration, affective language, and response length, are associated with learning outcomes. Existing studies have primarily examined these features using session- or task-level measures. We examine how feedback provided in one user-AI interaction is associated with student confusion and understanding in the immediately following interaction in a naturalistic tutoring setting. We focus on three micro-level features of AI feedback: concrete elaboration (analogies, comparison-based explanations, or worked examples), affective language (encouragement, empathy, or apology), and response length. We analyzed 16,851 conversational user-AI interactions from the StudyChat dataset, a naturalistic record of student interactions with an LLM tutor in an undergraduate AI course, and identified 1,718 cases in which students expressed confusion and continued to a subsequent interaction. Using chi-square tests and Generalized Estimating Equations (GEE), we found that concrete elaboration was associated with higher understanding and lower re-confusion in the student's next interaction. Empathetic language showed no significant association with either outcome, while longer responses were independently associated with lower understanding. These findings highlight the value of examining feedback across consecutive user-AI interactions and suggest that concrete elaboration may play an important role in supporting immediate student understanding.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: A Unified Choice Model of News Selection: Experimental Evidence on Stance, Rank, and Engagement Cues
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Social media platforms often display visual engagement cues alongside ranked news articles, yet their influence on clicks remains poorly understood when considered jointly with ranking position and users' political preferences. We propose a unified discrete choice framework using a conditional multinomial logit model to jointly estimate and compare the influence of these factors on news selection. We evaluate the model using 1,480 choices from 370 human participants across four news topics in a controlled study with and without visual engagement cues. The framework allows us to assess the incremental contribution of each factor through nested-model likelihood-ratio tests. We find that including visual engagement cues significantly improves model fit across all topics after accounting for rank and stance. Engagement cues alone also predict clicks better than either of these features, although the full model achieves the highest held-out log-likelihood. Finally, we quantify via counterfactual analysis the impact of ranking position and displayed engagement counts on click probabilities. These findings can inform platform owners, researchers, and policymakers evaluating how platform design affects the selection of political news.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Managing Verification Debt: A Framework for Responsible Human-AI Research Partnerships
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Conversation with generative artificial intelligence (AI) can quickly turn a tentative scientific question into the outline of a research programme. Although this capability can accelerate research, it also places two closely related pressures on human intelligence: 1) temporal asymmetry between rapid AI generation and slower expert evaluation, and 2) a cognitive gap between the available effort, expertise, attention and capacity to assess AI outputs. When unexamined AI contributions are carried into subsequent claims or decisions, these pressures produce verification debt: validation work that remains outstanding before a contribution can be relied upon. If left unresolved, this debt can undermine responsible AI in research, understood here as the transparent and traceable use of AI under effective human oversight and accountability. This commentary argues that responsible human--AI research partnerships therefore require a disciplined method for managing verification debt, not better prompting alone. We propose a shared topology of the research programme: a structured representation that connects questions, claims, assumptions, sources, tests and decisions while recording their provenance, dependencies and verification status. The topology makes unresolved debt visible, enables corrections to propagate through dependent claims and requires consequential contributions to be examined at decision gates before research proceeds. We consider its application in two-way partnerships and supervised partnerships that extend from doctoral research to multi-way research teams, and examine its implications for scholarly assessment, peer review and empirical evaluation.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Chameleon: Exploring Risk Interpretation through Scene-Matched Textures in Virtual Reality
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Users in virtual reality need to judge contact risks around physical objects while remaining engaged in the virtual scene. Scene-matched textures give physical objects a place in virtual reality and provide visual cues for interaction. We examine how Chameleon's risk-aware textures are perceived during a reaching task. A study with 42 participants compared scanned appearances with red warnings, uniform environment textures, and risk-aware scene-matched textures. Participants rated the risk-aware condition more favorably on four aspects of perceived cue clarity than both alternatives. Interviews connected visible warnings with initial caution and linked confidence in physical interaction to material expectations and intended actions. Awareness of an object's location did not necessarily imply confidence in interacting with it. These findings motivate risk cues that connect depicted materials to the physical properties relevant to an intended action, and ways to support verification during interaction.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: EMIP: Embodied Multi-Party Interaction Platform
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Experimental platforms that enable multiple participants to engage in spoken dialogue and perform physical actions concurrently in a shared environment are important for studying cooperation between humans and embodied AI agents. In this paper, we propose EMIP (Embodied Multi-Party Interaction Platform), a virtual environment platform built on Minecraft. Through an Internet-based client-server architecture, EMIP connects multiple humans and multiple AI agents to the same virtual environment and supports full-duplex speech communication and simultaneous physical interaction. It provides interfaces based on the Model Context Protocol (MCP) for environmental observation, physical action execution, and audio input and output, enabling researchers to develop their own agent control methods using large language models (LLMs). Additional features include centralized control of an agent group through a single EMIP agent client, collaborative object transportation by multiple agents, and experimental support functions such as recording and retrieving observation histories. By integrating these features into a reusable platform, EMIP aims to support research on human-human, human-agent, and agent-agent cooperation under different participant configurations and agent control methods. Usage examples illustrate concurrent speech and physical action, task coordination, and overlapping speech. The source code for the platform is publicly available on GitHub (https://github.com/AI-Humans-Lab/EMIP-Embodied-Multi-Party-Interaction-Platform).

Human-Computer Interaction.title: ARRANGE: Agentic Skills for Layering Vocals
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Adding a singing voice to an existing piano recording requires decisions about melody, syllable placement, pronunciation, timing, and vocal register. ARRANGE organizes this work as a sequence of agent skills with readable intermediate artifacts and composer approval checkpoints. An LLM translates instructions in plain English, notes played on a keyboard, and vocal references into local edits; deterministic scripts validate and apply those edits before open audio models render the result. The Score Canvas makes note, syllable, and pronunciation decisions inspectable and editable. In a benchmark of 16 revision requests, three draws per request, and five LLMs, typed edits achieved exact-change correctness of 0.83-0.98, compared with 0.33-0.69 for whole-plan rewriting without ARRANGE instructions. A separate score-editing benchmark and a first-person worked example examine the interaction between representations and corrections. Author listening evaluations further explore voice transfer and register selection, including 185 listening presentations across eight copied voices. These evaluations support the value of constrained editing and expose limits of both model execution and listening measures. The contribution is an interaction architecture for retaining musical decisions through inspectable intermediate representations, rather than a new singing model or evidence of general usability.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 9 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables. Under review at the HUMANE-LLM workshop, ACM IUI 2027 (Helsinki). Code: https://github.com/htansetiawan/ARRANGE ; project page: https://htansetiawan.github.io/ARRANGE

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Play and Learn: Gamified Feedback for Ultrasound-Guided Catheter Insertion Training in Virtual Reality
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: VR is widely used in procedural medical training, but many simulators prioritize realism over formative feedback. We developed a gamified VR simulator for ultrasound-guided peripheral IV catheter insertion, using aligned visual and auditory feedback such as progress indicators, guidance, and rewards. In studies with novices (N=24) and clinicians (N=12), gamification reduced task time, improved usability, and lowered workload. Qualitative results showed clearer goals and greater confidence for novices, and improved pacing for experts. Overall, gamification can provide effective formative feedback in VR medical training.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: EVis+: Literature-Grounded Visual Analytics for Hypothesis-Driven Geoscientific Data Exploration
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Scientific researchers often interpret observational data in light of prior findings reported in the scientific literature. However, scientific literature typically remains external to visual analytics environments, requiring researchers to manually connect published findings with the data and hypotheses under investigation. In this paper, we present EVis+, a literature-grounded visual analytics system for condition-event time series analysis in geoscience. EVis+ enhances observational data exploration by retrieving and synthesizing literature-derived insights relevant to the dataset and analytical goals, transforming user-selected insights into testable hypotheses and mapping them to domain-specific visualizations through expert-curated templates, and supporting evidence examination, discrepancy validation, and literature-driven re-exploration to support iterative hypothesis refinement and scientific exploration. Rather than handing scientific analysis to an unconstrained language model, EVis+ uses structured AI-assisted transformations that keep intermediate results visible, allowing researchers to inspect and guide the analysis at each step. We evaluate the system through an evidence-grounding audit, a structured expert assessment of the insights, and case studies with geoscientists and a comparative study with domain experts.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: DataRecycle: Trustworthy Distillation of Structured Data from Scattered Web Evidence
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: The web contains vast amounts of scattered quantitative evidence that is difficult to organize into comparable and verifiable structures. Yet its unstructured, sparse, and sometimes conflicting nature makes a systematic distillation costly and error-prone. Existing approaches force users to make a trade-off: search engines return document lists that require labor-intensive extraction and reconciliation, while generative AI systems produce fluent summaries that obscure data provenance, introduce reporting bias, and hide inconsistencies. We present DataRecycle, an interactive system that helps transform scattered web evidence into structured tables of comparable numerical facts. Given a user's query or statement, DataRecycle decomposes it into entities and attributes, retrieves candidate evidence, and organizes scattered, potentially conflicting records in a table-based evidence view. To address key challenges in automated data distillation (i.e., incomplete retrieval, untraceable generation, sparse data distribution, and multi-source inconsistency), DataRecycle adopts an ontology-guided, top-down data acquisition strategy, visualizes the recorded lineage from retrieved snippets to extracted values, and aligns heterogeneous data across dimensions such as time, definition, and scale. We evaluate DataRecycle through module-level experiments, a usage scenario, and a user study, showing that the system helps users organize numerical web evidence into provenance-linked tables and inspect uncertainty and conflicting sources.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Inclusive Hand Pose Estimation via Topology-Aware Distillation and Progressive Kinematic Reasoning
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Hand pose estimation aims to recover the spatial configuration of hand joints from visual observations and serves as a fundamental perception module for downstream systems that rely on complete and topologically consistent hand representations. Most existing methods are developed under the assumption of fully articulated hand structures and tend to produce unstable or implausible predictions when parts of the kinematic structure are persistently absent, resulting in degraded performance or even system failure despite available partial observations. To study this challenge, we construct IncNYU, a physiologically constrained benchmark that simulates structural incompleteness through morphological modification of complete hand models and retains reference locations for both intact and synthetically removed regions. Based on this benchmark, we propose InsHaPE, an Inclusive Hand Pose Estimation framework designed to remain robust under structural incompleteness while preserving performance on standard, fully articulated hands. Built on hierarchical kinematic modeling, InsHaPE introduces two complementary components. First, a topology-aware distillation strategy transfers joint-level and relational priors from fully articulated hand representations, providing anatomically consistent initialization under missing structures. Second, a progressive kinematic reasoning module performs structured inference along the kinematic chain, enabling complete and anatomically consistent pose estimation under severe structural variations. Extensive experiments on NYU/IncNYU, together with external validation on MSRA, demonstrate that InsHaPE improves robustness under structural incompleteness while maintaining competitive performance on complete hands. System-level evaluations further show that InsHaPE improves robustness for downstream applications that require fixed-topology hand pose representations.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Accepted to IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics (TVCG)

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Thinking Harder Doesn't Lead to Better Choices: Reasoning Effort Increases the Confidence but Not the Correctness of LLM Shopping Agents
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous shopping agents that process multimodal product listings (consisting of visual and text data) and recommend purchases on behalf of consumers. Naturally, one might assume that models with more thinking power would make higher-quality purchasing decisions. To test this belief, we ask two questions about such agents: does asking a model to think harder make it choose better products, and does the confidence it reports tell us the likelihood it may be wrong? We benchmark ten frontier models on three product-choice benchmarks built from WebShop, Amazon's SQID and Wayfair's WANDS platforms to see if LLMs with more thinking power actually make better-quality product purchase decisions. Across all three benchmarks, we found that increasing the thinking effort does not increase decision quality in a statistically meaningful way. The same change in thinking effort raises stated confidence at a statistically significant level, so extra thinking buys confidence rather than correctness. We also measure the calibration of these models (how well their reported confidence percentage matches their true correctness percentage) in these tasks and show that most models are not well-calibrated at every effort level. We also find that errors are strongly shared: when one model errs in a task, several others tend to err on that same task. Furthermore, on tasks where several models all err, a large number of them pick the same wrong product.

Methodology.title: The Coupled Scaled Dirichlet Distribution
Methodology.summary: We introduce a coupled scaled Dirichlet distribution for paired compositions that may have different dimensions. Building on the matched Gamma-sharing construction of Trick, Rothkopf, and Jäkel (2023) for ordinary Dirichlet vectors, we allow scaled Dirichlet margins and extend the construction to include crossed sharing between non-corresponding latent components. We propose a signed coupling parameter whose sign selects matched or crossed sharing and whose magnitude controls the strength of sharing. We then develop a time-varying extension in which observed covariates determine this parameter. The model can therefore switch between matched and crossed sharing over time while preserving both scaled Dirichlet margins. We derive the joint mixed moments and use them to estimate dependence after fitting the margins separately. The moments can be evaluated by Monte Carlo simulation or by two-dimensional numerical quadrature, regardless of the dimensions of the compositions. Simulations show that the estimator generally recovers the sharing pattern, although weak crossed sharing is harder to detect. In an application to four U.S. equity-index futures, the time-varying model modestly improved the held-out energy and variogram scores for the trading-volume and intraday price-range compositions relative to the static-dependence model.

Methodology.title: Event-Time Confounding Under Bursty Human Dynamics
Methodology.summary: Web studies often measure what happens after a user action, such as a search after a chatbot answer. To credit an AI answer with later commercial activity, a study must separate what the answer caused from what the user would have done anyway. But people act in the middle of activity already underway, so the activity that drives what follows also chooses when the clock starts. We call this endogenous time zero. Using an opt-in panel that links conversational-AI use, browsing, and search, we insert inert timestamps (moments that match recent activity but mark no event) and rerun the standard analysis. In a pre-registered replication, these timestamps, which by construction cannot cause anything, reproduce 76% of the search increase after AI responses that follow recent browsing. Other users matched on 30-day activity, the usual control, give the same answer, and inert timestamps show a similar search excess across 16 kinds of Web events. Comparing with moments of matching recent history removes most of the increase, but no placebo audit we ran could confirm that this comparison is unbiased, and published studies almost never run one. We give a protocol for choosing comparisons and stress-testing estimators.
Methodology.comment: v2: shortened and refocused version (inert-timestamp placebo test for user-timed Web events, a sweep across event types, reference-moment comparisons, and a protocol); 12 pages, 8 figures, 7 tables

Methodology.title: Model-Averaged Shrinkage Estimation of the Spectral Density Using Welch's Method
Methodology.summary: We propose a shrinkage estimator of the spectral density based on a three-level hierarchical model. At the first level, we smooth Welch's spectral density estimator and model it as arriving from a Gaussian distribution centered at the true spectral density. In the second level, we place a normal prior on the true spectral density. We center this prior at a spectral density estimated assuming the data from an ARMA($p$,$q$) process. From these two levels, we create a conditionally specified shrinkage estimator. The conditional specification, of course, is the order of the ARMA process, i.e., the values of $p$ and $q$. We avoid selecting a particular order by creating a third level in which priors are placed on $p$ and $q$. Our final estimator is then a weighted average of shrinkage estimators. The average is taken over a set of ARMA($p$, $q$) models, and the weights are governed by the posteriors of $p$ and $q$. The methods introduced in this paper are similar to those presented in Botts and Daniels, but distinct from them in one critical way: the first level of the hierarchy. In the first level of our model, we borrow from recently developed theoretical results of Welch's spectral density estimator. Our estimator is consistent, computationally simple, and has performance comparable (and often superior) to other estimators.

Methodology.title: Sharpe Ratio Inference after Machine Learning
Methodology.summary: The economic value of return signals is often assessed using the Sharpe ratios of portfolios based on those signals. In modern asset pricing, return signals often depend on many features, including state variables and firm-specific characteristics, and machine-learning methods are increasingly used to estimate them. But how much confidence can we place in the estimated Sharpe ratios? We find that signal-estimation error can remain consequential for inference even in large asset panels. Moreover, pooling observations across assets does not necessarily make this uncertainty negligible when predictors contain common features or exhibit substantial cross-sectional dependence. As a remedy, we develop a debiased Sharpe-ratio estimator that accounts for signal-estimation error and provides valid confidence intervals and tests against benchmarks. Our target is the population Sharpe ratio of a specified portfolio rule evaluated at the true conditional expected returns given the features. The framework covers market-timing, long-short, and other signal-based portfolios, allowing the number of assets to grow with and greatly exceed the time-series sample size. The method combines orthogonal portfolio moments with time-series cross-fitting and remains valid under suitable estimation-error bounds for machine-learning forecasts. Empirically, we revisit the setting of Gu et al. (2020) using machine-learning estimators of the return signals. The strongest long-short Sharpe-ratio gains relative to market benchmarks remain significant after debiasing, providing statistical evidence of the economic value of their feature set. Conventional and debiased Sharpe-ratio estimates are generally similar, while the associated confidence intervals and tests can differ substantially. These differences vary across signal estimators and portfolio rules and do not uniformly weaken the evidence of portfolio performance.

Methodology.title: Directed Hypergraphs: Tensor Representation, Embedding Modeling, and Community Detection
Methodology.summary: Directed hypergraphs, in which each hyperedge connects a set of tail nodes to a set of head nodes, are the natural representation for many-to-many interactions in citation networks, metabolic pathways, and group communications. Despite their broad applicability, community detection for directed hypergraphs remains statistically underdeveloped: most existing methods either collapse hyperedges into pairwise edges, treat the two sides as interchangeable, or require the number of communities to be known. We propose a statistical framework for simultaneous embedding and community detection in nonuniform directed hypergraphs. The method allows each node to have distinct roles as a source and as a target, accommodates varying hyperedge sizes, and automatically determines the unknown numbers of communities on both sides, which need not be equal, through a fusion-penalized likelihood. We establish consistency of the estimated numbers of communities, exact recovery of both membership structures, and consistent probability tensor estimation.
