Optimization and Control.summary: We study stochastic convex optimization with heavy-tailed stochastic gradients under $(\varepsilon, δ)$-user-level differential privacy, which protects each user's entire collection of samples. Instead of assuming a uniformly bounded Lipschitz constant, we only assume bounds on the second- and $k$-th moments of the random sample Lipschitz parameters. This allows for unbounded, heavy-tailed stochastic gradient distributions and can lead to sharper excess risk bounds. We characterize the minimax optimal excess population risk up to logarithmic factors. Our algorithm achieves the optimal rate with only $\widetilde{O}(1/\varepsilon)$ users. As a byproduct of our algorithmic developments, we obtain tight bounds for user-level private mean estimation under norm-moment assumptions, improving over the guarantees of Esfandiari et al. (2022) and Zhao et al. (2024). Finally, for mean estimation under the directional-moment assumption of Agarwal et al. (2025), we close their remaining approximate-DP gap by removing the additional $d/\varepsilon$ user requirement and attaining the optimal sample complexity up to logarithmic factors.

Optimization and Control.title: A Generalized Framework for Structured Low-Rank Approximation and Completion
Optimization and Control.summary: We formulate a generalized version of SLRA, consisting of general affine constraints, which subsumes the problems of structured low-rank matrix approximation and completion as special cases. We characterize its critical points and propose an algorithm to approximately solve the general problem. Finally, we demonstrate the performance of the proposed algorithm for stock-price forecasting, computing approximate gcd of polynomials with noisy coefficients, and time-series denoising.

Optimization and Control.title: Sub-Riemannian flow matching
Optimization and Control.summary: We study sub-Riemannian conditional flow matching (SRCFM) for generative transport with prescribed velocity constraints. Training uses paths between sampled source and target points whose velocities lie in the allowed horizontal directions at each state. A neural network takes time and the full state as input and predicts the coefficients of these directions, and the horizontal frame then determines the full velocity used for generation. We describe constructions based on Heisenberg geodesics and joint endpoint equations in free step-two Carnot groups. We propose a scalable piecewise algorithm that computes horizontal paths directly from their endpoints. A straight segment sets the horizontal coordinates, and a loop in those coordinates corrects the remaining vertical displacement. We verify the algorithm's endpoint accuracy to numerical precision in high-dimensional tests. Synthetic experiments illustrate approximate distribution transport along horizontal trajectories. On resized MNIST, we use the same construction to generate images from Gaussian inputs with fewer controls than pixels.

Optimization and Control.title: A Unified Bregman Projection Framework for Solving Multi-Split Multiple-Set Implicit Convex Feasibility Problems
Optimization and Control.summary: We study the multi-split multiple-set implicit convex feasibility problem (MSMS-ICFP), in which the constraint sets are generated by point-to-set operators and the feasibility conditions are imposed both in the original space and in several image spaces connected by bounded linear operators. We analyze the generalized proximity function, built from weighted Bregman distances and Bregman projections, introduced by Censor and Dey. For translation-type point-to-set operators, we establish the continuity and Lipschitz continuity of the corresponding Bregman projections, the continuous differentiability of the proximity function with an explicit formula for its gradient, and global and local Lipschitz estimates for this gradient. We then propose a generalized simultaneous projection gradient algorithm. In the nonconvex case, the gradient norms of the iterates converge to zero and every accumulation point is stationary. When the proximity function is convex and the solution set is nonempty, the iterates converge in norm to a solution, with an $O(1/k)$ rate for the proximity values, an $O(1/\sqrt{k})$ rate for the gradient norms, and a linear rate under a quadratic growth condition. Cyclic and block-iterative variants are also analyzed. Numerical experiments, including a cooperative sensor network localization problem, illustrate the theory and show that, in contrast with frozen-set implicit projection methods, the proposed gradient schemes remain convergent when the translation operators are expansive.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: It Pays to Brag? On Counterfactual Fair Credit
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Intellectual work, such as software, legal documents, and scientific results, typically builds on the work of others, and the same end product can often be obtained in several different ways. When assigning credit for such work, it is not clear whether credit should go according to the way the work was actually produced or also consider counterfactual ways of obtaining it. We study this question by generalizing Shapley values to account for counterfactual ways of obtaining the same result. We show that the fairness axioms of efficiency, nullity, and submodularity (in particular, additivity) are incompatible with incentivizing creators to maximize social welfare. In fact, fair credit can uniquely incentivize arbitrarily small welfare relative to the optimum. We also show that without submodularity, incentive compatibility is achievable, and that the four classical fairness axioms uniquely determine the Shapley value and prohibit dependence on counterfactual outcomes.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Liquidity Commitments and Strategic Settlement in Financial Networks
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Credible liquidity commitments can prevent self-fulfilling settlement freezes without being drawn. But how should they be designed to minimise reserved capacity while preserving banks' ordinary self-insurance? Missing incoming payments increase precautionary retention, allowing a freeze to coexist with feasible full repayment. We characterise a canonical contingent entitlement that uniquely implements full payment whenever any admissible continuous schedule can, even when alternatives induce nonmonotone repayment responses. Functional contract design therefore reduces exactly to capacity allocation. Contract shape matters even after commitments are optimally allocated within the affine benchmark. At zero usage prices, flexible commitments can require strictly less capacity than globally optimised affine reserve attenuation. An exact critical-mode criterion provides a sufficient condition for these global savings. For fixed positive reservation weights, strict savings are generic in a specified dense-network regime and arise in open families of sparse directed cycles. For heterogeneous directed cycles with one potentially amplifying bank, a compact linear programme characterises the reserve-preserving capacity infimum. Under stated reserve conditions, a sharp comparison identifies when eligibility restrictions increase costs and change the allocation of support. Verifiable incremental-risk eligibility provides a foundation for preserving ordinary reserves at zero usage prices. General-network bounds and exact exponential two-bank results establish that contractual flexibility retains value at positive usage prices.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Finding Integral Stable Matchings is PPAD-Complete: Unimodular Hypergraphs, Network $b$-Matchings, and Kernels in Perfect Graphs
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Polyhedral integrality guarantees integral stable solutions in several classical stability problems: stable matchings in normal hypergraphs, stable $b$-matchings in unimodular hypergraphs, and kernels in clique-acyclic orientations of perfect graphs. Whether they can be computed efficiently has been a long-standing open question; for kernels in perfect graphs it has been open since the existence theorem of Boros and Gurvich in 1996. We show that, unless $PPAD\subseteq FP$, they cannot. Finding a stable matching is $PPAD$-complete already in linear unimodular hypergraphs with hyperedges of size at most three and vertex degrees at most three. Consequently, finding a kernel in a clique-acyclic orientation of a perfect graph is $PPAD$-hard even if all cliques have at most three vertices, answering an open question of Pass-Lanneau, Igarashi and Meunier, and stable matchings are $PPAD$-hard to find in balanced and in normal hypergraphs. This contrasts with the polynomial algorithm of Chandrasekaran and Kalathur for network hypergraphs. With capacities, even network hypergraphs are hard: University Dual Admission is $PPAD$-complete with capacities at most nine, so stable $b$-matching is $PPAD$-complete on network hypergraphs with hyperedges of size three. This yields $PPAD$-completeness for a natural class of hospitals/residents markets with couples where stable matchings always exist, and $PPAD$-hardness of computing the near-feasible stable matchings, where capacities are flexible. Both reductions are from PURE CIRCUIT with constant-size gadgets. For unit capacities we use a dual-rail encoding, a symmetry-breaking gadget made of two coupled $2\times2$ stable marriage markets, and a parity criterion on the bipartite incidence graph that certifies total unimodularity. We expect these tools to be useful for further hardness results about problems with guaranteed integral solutions.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Stackelberg Games with Convex Risk Measures
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Stackelberg games have important real-world applications in which reliable commitments require accounting for multiple sources of uncertainty. We study finite Stackelberg games in which environmental uncertainty makes each mixed strategy profile induce a random reward, and each player evaluates that reward with a convex monetary risk criterion. In reward form, it is a concave, monotone, translation-equivariant utility and also represented as penalized expected reward over distributions of environmental outcomes. We provide two conditions under which the follower has a unique continuous mixed response, which leads to inducible optimistic equilibrium. We show that even approximate equilibrium computation is NP Hard. We then derive an exact mathematical program with equilibrium constraints for the problem. We also develop an action entropy smoothed implicit-gradient method and prove an end-to-end additive approximation guarantee under the assumption that the gradient method reaches global optimality. We validate our scalability and other results with experiments on synthetic and real data.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: DeepVoting: Learning and Improving Voting Rules with Fine-Tuning
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Recently, social choice theory has been found broadly useful for AI alignment and evaluation, often based on the axiomatic properties for combining preferences provided by social choice functions. However, for many sets of axioms, functions which never violate the axioms are known to not exist, e.g., Arrow's Impossibility Theorem. Recent work on learning novel rules to minimize axiom violations shows the effectiveness of machine learning but explores a limited class of axioms. In this work we show the effectiveness of standard social choice data structures as features for learning existing voting rules, resulting in networks that have better accuracy than past approaches while using an order of magnitude fewer parameters. Subsequently, we develop a process for adding axiomatic properties to existing voting rules. By building novel axiomatic loss functions we are able to use transfer learning to fine-tune existing voting rules in a way that quantitatively preserves their original behaviour while also exhibiting strong adherence to previously absent axiomatic properties, resulting in novel voting rules that are closer to the impossibility frontier than those in the machine learning or theoretical literature.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: Accepted to 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Last-Iterate Convergence of Payoff-Gradient Learning in Möbius Pricing Games
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We prove global last-iterate convergence of payoff-gradient learning in every typewise Riemannian metric, which for scalar actions is the same as typewise mirror descent, with explicit rates, in a class of Bayesian bidding and pricing games that includes first-price auctions, unit-demand pay-as-bid auctions, rank-based generalized first-price auctions, and homogeneous-good price competition with inelastic demand. The result holds for symmetric self-play: all players use a common strategy and apply the same payoff-gradient update at each type. Convergence is from every continuous weakly increasing feasible initial strategy, including pooling, and does not rely on the monotonicity or Minty conditions that underlie existing guarantees in other games. Instead, the class is characterized by two structural properties: a direct payoff effect that is independent of the action, and a payoff difference at the allocation threshold that is affine in the action. These properties reduce the learning dynamics to a singular transport-damping equation for the common strategy, which, under the stated coefficient and metric assumptions, admits a unique viscosity solution. Comparison barriers make the uniform distance to the unique rest point a strict Lyapunov functional and yield convergence rates with optimal algebraic exponents. In allocation games, the rest point is the unique weakly increasing symmetric equilibrium under the stated tie-breaking conditions, and a positive lower slope bound converts strategy-error bounds into explicit approximate-equilibrium guarantees. A projected grid scheme with a slope floor makes the approximation constructive, with error bounds under deterministic perturbations and almost-sure convergence on a fixed grid under martingale gradient noise.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Beyond Invoice Volumes: Temporal Network Structure, Maturity Concentration, and Systemic Liquidity Exposure in SME Trade-Credit Networks
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Trade-credit invoices encode directed obligations whose temporal synchronization and counterparty concentration are obscured by annual volume totals. We audit 749,952 atomic B2B invoices from 2012-2023 (EUR 99.705B; 75,343 firms) from the pseudonymized Mendeley Data corpus (Esteva de la Rosa, 2026), separating 1,240 terminal 2024 bridge records (EUR 630.12M; 9 bridge-only firms) and 13 extreme-duration contracts (>3,650 days; EUR 297.75k). Using directed weighted graphs, HHI, Shannon entropy, CR1 shares, spectral centralities, and multi-cadence temporal operators, we formulate and benchmark a Maturity-Aware Network Exposure (MANE) indicator. Invoice values are heavily skewed: the top 1% hold 81.41% of value (Gini = 0.9742). Two-way fixed-effects panels with circular block bootstrapping ($B=999$, 12-month blocks) and Holm-Bonferroni control show higher lagged debtor counterparty concentration is associated with lower MANE ($\hatβ=-0.494$, 95% CI $[-0.752,-0.248]$, $p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.004$). Robustness audits (R1-R4) confirm stability under 2021 exclusion ($-0.402$, $p=0.004$), Shannon entropy ($+0.257$), CR1 ($-0.515$), 1%-99% Winsorization ($-0.462$, all $p=0.001$), and multi-invoice debtors (count $\ge 2$, $-0.334$, $p=0.031$). Conversely, within-FE diagnostics expose severe joint-concentration multicollinearity (VIF = 22.22) that vanishes for multi-invoice debtors ($p=0.719$), while regime splits reveal a macro reciprocity sign reversal between 2012-2019 ($-0.706$) and 2020-2023 ($+0.232$, both $p=0.001$). In 12-month purged forecasting, MANE does not reliably improve over maturity seeds ($Δ\mathrm{MSE}=2.668$, 95% CI $[-0.027,7.954]$; trimmed $0.067$, $[-0.035,0.194]$), positioning MANE as a reproducible screening and auditing diagnostic, rather than a default proxy, for supply-chain finance, multilateral clearing, and RWA tokenization.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: 30 pages, 12 figures

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Open problem: Computing Bayes-Nash equilibrium in simple security games
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: This is an open problem originally posed during the program "Economics and Computation" held in the Fall 2015 semester at the Simons Institute for the Theory of Computing. It asks whether a (Bayes-)Nash equilibrium can be computed in polynomial time for Bayesian simple security games.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Mechanism Design under Belief Disagreement: Allocation Flexibility and Rent Capacity
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: A seller jointly chooses allocation and payments when buyers misperceive competition. Under independent private values, statewise participation, and payment restrictions, allocation determines both required rents and their delivery capacity. We separate these effects under a common subjective law. For three values and shared-top beliefs, explicit score and capacity conditions characterize globally optimal lower-value lotteries, including top-rent overflow and welfare differences among revenue optima. A two-buyer construction establishes a strict allocation advantage over every reserve under the same fixed reporting certificate and positive margin. A transport test and exact band-boundary incentive equalities identify separate conditions restoring objective-law revenue ceilings. For three bands and a common affine belief interval, an explicitly certified reserve attains the ceiling under stated score conditions. A case scaled to public collectible-auction records yields a nominal shared-top allocation gain of 24.72 cents per auction. A one-cent report-by-report margin yields matched gains of 1.48 cents under projection and 3.32 cents under shared-top beliefs; the three-band point-belief gain of 2.50 cents disappears with common-interval protection. These comparisons bound the additional recurring costs an allocation redesign can cover at the specified reporting requirement.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Reimbursement as a Revenue Instrument in Costly Clock Auctions
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Bidders in an ascending auction may incur a cost each time they choose to continue, for example when bidding requires a blockchain transaction. We therefore investigate whether a seller can increase net revenue by reimbursing these costs, and how reimbursements should be distributed across auction rounds. We study auctions in which bidders must actively confirm their participation as prices rise and the seller commits to reimbursements before bidding begins. We first show how a linear program can find the cheapest payments that keep bidders' strategies optimal when participation costs are introduced. Maximizing net revenue, however, can require changing those strategies. In a two-bidder example, we identify conditions under which reimbursing only the last scheduled decision earns the most net revenue among the schedules we analyze. This policy outperforms no reimbursement, full reimbursement, and the cheapest policy that maintains the original strategies. Some auctions end earlier than under full reimbursement, but the seller's savings exceed the resulting loss in sale receipts. Experiments with learning bidders reproduce these revenue comparisons. In a four-bidder example, they also identify a policy with partial reimbursements in earlier rounds that earns more than reimbursing only the final decision. These results show how the seller's preferred reimbursement timing can change across auction environments. Finally, we explain how requiring bidders to confirm continued participation limits the prices they can be charged when messages are missing, and discuss the requirements for implementing these auctions on a blockchain.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Incentivizing Information Acquisition
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: I study a principal-agent model in which a principal hires an agent to collect information about an unknown continuous state. The agent acquires a signal whose distribution is centered around the state, controlling the signal's precision at a cost. The principal observes neither the precision nor the signal, but rather, using transfers that can depend on the state, incentivizes the agent to choose high precision and report the signal truthfully. I identify a sufficient and necessary condition on the agent's information structure which ensures that there exists an optimal transfer with a simple cutoff structure: the agent receives a fixed prize when his prediction is close enough to the state and receives nothing otherwise. This condition is mild and applies to all signal distributions commonly used in the literature.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: SenFabric: 3D Printing On-fabric Sensing Mechanisms for Smart Textiles
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: We present SenFabric, a one-step fabrication technique that 3D prints conductive TPU directly onto existing fabric. Rather than compensating for conductive material instability, SenFabric uses geometry-driven resistive structures in which motion changes conductive contact and reconfigures the effective path, producing characteristic signal responses that remain distinguishable despite variation in absolute resistance. We introduce four sensing primitives, slide, press, stretch, and bend, with geometric variables that control activation force, deformation range, and resolution, and a browser-based tool that adapts them to user-supplied outlines and generates routing, pins, and printable models. Four applications demonstrate wearable sensing, human-robot interaction, garment interfaces, and animal wearables, while evaluations show geometry-dominated sensing, cross-motion selectivity, and stable response under repeated use.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: "What Should I Do?" Guidelines for Responsibly Integrating AI in Software Engineering
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Speculations abound about the "right" ways for developers to integrate AI into their software engineering (SE) work, but the evidence that exists is sparse and contradictory. Yet, developers are held responsible for the products they ship with (or without) AI's help, so they need to integrate AI in responsible ways. To address this gap, we conducted a two-phase, large-scale investigation with 1,118 developers at Microsoft, GitHub, and Pfizer. In Phase 1, we surveyed 860 developers at Microsoft on where they sought and resisted AI support in their daily work, and from their accounts, synthesized 35 developer-facing guidelines: 29 across five categories of SE work and 6 cross-cutting ones. A year later, as AI capabilities and developers' experiences co-evolved, we validated them in Phase 2 with 258 developers in technology (Microsoft, GitHub) and biopharmaceutical (Pfizer) domains. Developers in our study found the guidelines clearly worded (92%) and relevant to their work (91%), and most wanted to adopt them in their own work (89%). We also report how developers described operationalizing these guidelines in practice: using AI to refine their craft and delegate verifiable work, while keeping judgment and accountability for themselves. For relationship-centric work, endorsement varied with developers' domain and their SE and AI experience. Overall, we offer concrete advice from in-the-trenches developers to other in-the-trenches developers, and a shared vocabulary that engineering teams can adopt to integrate AI well in their work.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: MB-SSIM: A Multi-Band Variant of SSIM, Tunable to Viewing Conditions
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: SSIM, as practically deployed, contains a hidden two-band model: although it was introduced as a departure from channel-based vision models, it amounts to a product of one similarity functional applied to a low-pass and a high-pass version of the two images. This split, however, is defined in pixels, so the spatial frequencies each band covers, as seen by the viewer, change with the display and the viewing distance. Making the model explicit and expressing it in cycles per degree gives a version of SSIM that takes the viewing conditions into account while preserving its simplicity. The resulting metric, MB-SSIM, keeps SSIM's per-patch product of similarity ratios; the bands are placed where psychophysics places the visual system's channels, and the viewing geometry enters through a single number, the angular sampling density in pixels per degree. On the CID:IQ dataset, which rates the same 690 images at two viewing distances, one set of sub-band weights fitted jointly and evaluated on held-out content reaches a pooled PLCC of 0.834 against 0.787 for SSIM and 0.808 for MS-SSIM; on LIVE Release 2, calibrating the geometry yields 0.956 against 0.946 and 0.950. As a cross-verification, the CID:IQ weights applied unchanged to the Brightcove-Kingston multi-screen video dataset, which rates the same clips on a television, a tablet and a phone, give a pooled PLCC of 0.844 across devices where SSIM and MS-SSIM, which must return one number per clip, fall to 0.62 and 0.59. Accuracy is flat from three channels to six and insensitive to filter shape, window and peak placement; only the channel bandwidths matter, and the psychophysically measured values are a safe choice. The most sensitive parameter is SSIM's own stabilising constant: reducing it to a third raises the pooled PLCC to 0.857. Source code reproducing the results is available.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Earinter: A Closed-Loop System for Eating Pace Regulation with Just-in-Time Intervention Using Commodity Earbuds
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Rapid eating is common yet difficult to regulate in situ, partly because people seldom notice pace changes and sustained self-monitoring is effortful. We present Earinter, a commodity-earbud-based closed-loop system that integrates in-the-wild sensing, real-time reasoning, and theory-grounded just-in-time (JIT) intervention to regulate eating pace during daily meals. Earinter repurposes the earbud's bone-conduction voice sensor to capture chewing-related vibrations and estimate eating pace as chews per swallow (CPS) for on-device inference. With data collected equally across \modify{sessions in quiet and noisy environments}, Earinter achieves reliable chewing detection (F1 = 0.97) and accurate eating pace estimation (MAE: 0.18 $\pm$ 0.13 chews/min, 3.65 $\pm$ 3.86 chews/swallow), enabling robust tracking for closed-loop use. Guided by Dual Systems Theory and refined through two Wizard-of-Oz pilots, Earinter adopts a user-friendly design for JIT intervention content and delivery policy in daily meals. In a 13-day within-subject field study (N=14), the closed-loop system significantly increased CPS and slowed meal-level eating pace, with statistical signs of carryover on retention-probe days and generally favorable comfort and usability. These effects should be interpreted as changes in eating-pace regulation rather than evidence of weight loss. Our findings highlight how single-modality commodity earables can support practical, theory-driven closed-loop JIT interventions for regulating eating pace in the wild.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Health Ikigai: Semantic Conversational Interfaces for Wearable Health Data to Support Behavioral Change for Senior Indian
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: In ubiquitous health contexts, wearable feedback is often encountered in brief, interrupted moments of everyday life. However, many wearable and mobile health systems still present personal health data through numerical dashboards, leaving users and health coaches to interpret trends, thresholds, and deviations on their own. This interpretive burden may be especially relevant for adults aged 50-65 in India, where digital literacy, health literacy, language, and daily routines can shape how health technologies are understood and used. We present Health Ikigai, a design-oriented proof-of-concept framework that reframes wearable activity feedback from dashboard-based numerical interpretation to semantic conversational feedback. The prototype transforms replayed wearable-derived activity data into baseline-aware triggers, plain-language feedback, limited-turn conversational prompts, and coach-facing review summaries. A preliminary formative evaluation with ten adults in India suggests that participants perceived the interaction as understandable, lightweight, supportive, and actionable. We discuss design implications for low-burden wearable health interfaces that preserve coach oversight while reducing users' interpretive work.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 5 pages, 5 figures, 1 table. Poster presented at UbiComp/ISWC 2026, Shanghai, China; to appear in UbiComp Companion '26 (ACM). Md Haseen Akhtar and Hansoo Lee contributed equally

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Postpartum Sense-Making and AI in a Fragmented Care System
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Postpartum women must navigate health information across a fragmented landscape of clinicians, peers, online communities, influencers, and, increasingly, large language models (LLMs). Existing evaluations of LLMs in health contexts primarily ask whether systems provide accurate, safe, and readable information. We argue that these criteria, while essential, are insufficient for understanding how LLMs may affect postpartum care. LLMs enter an information ecology in which women are already required to reconcile competing forms of expertise, determine whether their experiences are normal or concerning, and decide when and where to seek care. At the same time, online representations of motherhood and femininity shape which postpartum experiences are made visible and what forms of self-management are expected of women. Drawing together research on postpartum care gaps, online help-seeking, influencer cultures, gendered responsibility, and AI-supported health information, we position LLMs as emerging intermediaries within this broader care infrastructure. We argue that evaluating postpartum AI requires examining not only information quality, but also how these systems shape epistemic coordination, transitions to formal care, and the distribution of responsibility for making fragmented systems of care work.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Presented at the CSCW 2026 Workshop on Women's Health as Cooperative Work: Participatory AI Across Care, Community, and Policy (arXiv:2611.03776)

Human-Computer Interaction.title: "I feel like AI is just everywhere": A longitudinal qualitative study on parents' perceptions, use, and mediation of GenAI
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: GenAI has developed rapidly over the last few years, yet few longitudinal studies exploring how individuals' experiences with GenAI have changed over time exist. Even fewer studies have focused on families with children, despite the opportunity to explore how parents have balanced their needs, their children's development, and the fast pace in which technology changes. To better understand how parents' perceptions, use, and mediation of GenAI shifted over two years, we interviewed 10 parents who had participated in a prior study about their families' experiences with GenAI. Parents had shifted from thinking GenAI was novel to feeling like it was unavoidable, characterizing GenAI as a limited tool to believing GenAI development needed to be regulated, and focusing on their personal mediation strategies to wanting systemic plans to curb GenAI's long-term consequences. We position our findings within the context of parental mediation of technology and increasing collective mitigation of GenAI-related risks.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: When Being Wrong Is Right: Reverse-Capability Audio CAPTCHAs through Psychoacoustic Design
Human-Computer Interaction.summary:
Large audio-language models (LALMs) have recently been shown to bypass audio CAPTCHAs designed around limitations of automatic speech recognition. To address this threat, we introduce reverse-capability verification, a general CAPTCHA framework that reverses the conventional human-easy, machine-hard relationship with respect to the physical ground truth. It selects challenges in which stable human perceptual limitations cause the human-reference answer to differ from the physical ground truth, while machine analysis tends toward that truth. Because the verifier accepts the human-reference answer, advanced solver capabilities and resulting improved recovery of the physical ground truth may instead strengthen the human-machine separation.
  We instantiate the framework through psychoacoustics and design two audio CAPTCHAs: HIPI, a classification task, and YINGCHEN, a counting task, together with their conjunctive composition. Across seven LALMs and eight attack strategies, the maximum observed machine acceptance rates are 19%, 17%, and 3% for HIPI, YINGCHEN, and their composition, respectively, compared with 45-100% for nine prior schemes. A multidimensional human usability study yields corresponding human acceptance rates of 78%, 90%, and 76%, while maintaining competitive efficiency and satisfaction. Further analysis demonstrates that advanced LALMs tend toward physical ground truth. These results show that reverse-capability verification substantially reduces machine acceptance while retaining high human acceptance through an approach different from conventional CAPTCHAs.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Learning Recommendations under Imperfect Human Compliance with Record-Level Differential Privacy
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: This paper investigates human-in-the-loop recommendation systems, where effectiveness relies on human compliance and privacy concerns restrict the use of historical response data. The pro posed framework models the implemented action as a random response to the recommendation and formulates the recommendation mechanism as a decision-dependent optimisation problem under an unknown compliance distribution. A batched Gaussian process upper confidence bound algorithm is then adapted to learn from locally perturbed historical actions, providing privacy for individual raw records. The analysis establishes record-level differential privacy and derives high-probability simple regret bounds when the compliance distribution is unknown. These bounds characterise how privacy noise, batch size, and behavioural information affect the guaranteed quality of the learned recommendation. In particular, a known upper bound on the non-compliance rate enables the rec ommendation space to be screened before any private data are queried. Simulations of a fixed-state car-following problem with synthetic historical driver responses demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm and verify the theoretical findings.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Speculative Sampling in Interactive Video Generation
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Interactive video generation commonly relies on small bidirectional chunks to reduce response latency. Yet our preliminary experiments show that larger chunks improve video quality and better utilize GPU parallelism, allowing more latents to be sampled with only a modest increase in sampling time. Motivated by these observations, we propose Speculative Sampling, a strategy that combines the modeling power of large bidirectional windows with the low-latency interaction of small ones. It expands the modeling window by appending noise latents as padding and caches the resulting predictions for reuse when the condition remains unchanged. Predictions are delivered incrementally, while the uncommitted suffix remains replaceable. Our latency analysis shows that this removes the waiting-time lower bound imposed by chunk boundaries, shifting the optimization focus from reducing chunk size to accelerating per-chunk generation. Bidirectional window size thus becomes a decision variable for jointly optimizing visual quality and generation time, rather than a necessary constraint on low-latency interaction. This opens a path to serving large bidirectional models in interactive streaming systems without complex streaming post-training.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: SkillLens: An Interactive Human-LLM System for Diagnosing and Refining Agent Skills
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: LLM agents increasingly rely on reusable skills, yet maintaining them requires developers to connect revisions with changes in behavior and task outcomes. Existing workflows fragment evidence across versions, evaluation cases, and execution traces. We present SkillLens, an interactive human-LLM system for diagnosing and refining agent skills. A formative study with five developers and researchers identified challenges in prioritizing failures, reconstructing case-level evidence, and preserving context across revisions. SkillLens links performance changes, case transitions, skill diffs, invocation sequences, traces, and outputs in a recoverable workflow, while keeping model-generated explanations and refinements under human review. Through a between-subjects user study with 20 participants, we show that SkillLens supports developers in diagnosing and refining agent skills through a more usable and less demanding workflow than the baseline. These findings highlight the value of linking version comparisons, case-level evidence, and human-reviewed refinement across skill iterations.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Fitts' List Revisited: An Empirical Study on Function Allocation in a Two-Agent Physical Human-Robot Collaborative Position/Force Task
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: In this letter, we investigate whether classical function allocation-the principle of assigning tasks to either a human or a machine-holds for physical Human-Robot Collaboration, which is important for providing insights for Industry 5.0 to guide how to best augment rather than replace workers. This study empirically tests the applicability of Fitts' List within physical Human-Robot Collaboration, by conducting a user study (N=26, within-subject design) to evaluate four distinct allocations of position/force control between human and robot in an abstract blending task. We hypothesize that the function in which humans control the position achieves better performance and receives higher user ratings. When allocating position control to the human and force control to the robot, compared to the opposite case, we observed a significant improvement in preventing overblending. This was also perceived better in terms of physical demand and overall system acceptance, while participants experienced greater autonomy, more engagement and less frustration. An interesting insight was that the supervisory role (when the robot controls both position and force) was rated second best in terms of subjective acceptance. Another surprising insight was that if position control was delegated to the robot, the participants perceived much lower autonomy than when the force control was delegated to the robot. These findings empirically support applying Fitts' principles to static function allocation for physical collaboration, while also revealing important nuanced user experience trade-offs, particularly regarding perceived autonomy when delegating position control.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 8 pages, 6 figures, published in IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters, col. 11, no. 1, January 2026

Human-Computer Interaction.title: PatchLens: Adapting Mechanistic Interpretability Techniques for Non-Expert Audiences
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: A chat interface presents a reply as finished text, concealing a model that predicts at every position and reruns. Mechanistic interpretability can show how a large language model produces text, but its tools are built for researchers. We present PatchLens, a browser interface that runs logit lens and activation patching on remotely served research-scale models. Each layer's state appears as the tokens it comes closest to, laid out by layer and input position; an intervention is a drag from one cell onto another. The tokens a learner reads are the tokens they manipulate. In a between-subjects study with 61 non-experts, the comparison against Transformer Explainer was inconclusive on post-test knowledge. PatchLens participants wrote their own prompts (21 of 32 against 1 of 29), reported lower mental demand, and located their difficulty in the interface rather than the material. We read the null as evidence about what such an instrument measures.

Neural and Evolutionary Computing.title: Do Larger Fully Connected Neural Networks Generalize Better?
Neural and Evolutionary Computing.summary: Greater neural-network capacity does not necessarily yield better performance on unseen data. This study investigates whether a deeper, fully connected neural-network architecture generalizes better than a shallower architecture on the Fashion-MNIST dataset. We compare two architectures under two learning rates and two L2-regularization settings, producing eight configurations. The architectures contain 95,410 and 561,470 trainable parameters, respectively, an approximately 5.9-fold difference. Checkpoints and the final configuration are selected by validation loss, and all configurations are evaluated on a held-out test set. The selected larger configuration achieves 89.82% validation accuracy and 88.77% test accuracy. Selecting the lowest-validation-loss configuration within each architecture yields test accuracies of 88.77% and 88.52%, respectively, a difference of 0.25 percentage points. Across matched training settings, the larger architecture achieves higher test accuracy in only one of four comparisons. Class-level errors are concentrated among visually similar garment categories, and qualitative pixel-removal analyses suggest sensitivity to shape and boundaries. Overall, the findings suggest that increasing architectural capacity alone does not guarantee better generalization, highlighting the importance of considering optimization and regularization when selecting neural-network architectures.
Neural and Evolutionary Computing.comment: 5 pages, 3 figures

Neural and Evolutionary Computing.title: RIPE-MambaSpike: Resolution-Independent Spiking-State-Space Interfaces for Parameter-Efficient Event-Based Vision
Neural and Evolutionary Computing.summary: Spiking-Mamba hybrids reach strong accuracy on event-based vision, but existing designs often require tens of millions of parameters. In hybrids that flatten the spiking feature map and project it densely into the scan, much of that cost comes from this interface rather than from the hybrid architecture itself. In a representative model, a single resolution-dependent projection accounts for 33.55M of 36.25M parameters. To that end, we introduce RIPE-MambaSpike (Resolution-Independent, Parameter-Efficient), which replaces that projection with a hierarchical multi-resolution bridge of fixed channel width. Its deployed footprint is 0.870M parameters, constant at fixed time steps and widths across a 43x range of input areas. Reparameterized spiking stages, temporal decoupled modulation, and a dynamic convex-hull-bounded dual-stream membrane-potential attention preserve accuracy under this compact design. Result-wise, RIPE-MambaSpike is pareto-optimal on CIFAR10-DVS, N-Caltech101, and DailyDVS-200. Notably, on the 200-class DailyDVS-200, a scaled 8.04M configuration achieves 45.7% top-1 accuracy, the best reported spiking result on that benchmark, and outperforms prior spiking methods with 3.0-15.1x fewer parameters than dense ANNs. Overall, our findings demonstrate that competitive event-based recognition does not require resolution-dependent parameter growth. Code is available at https://github.com/MuhiminOsim/RIPE-MambaSpike.
Neural and Evolutionary Computing.comment: 34 pages, 10 figures, 24 tables

Neural and Evolutionary Computing.title: Which Model Belongs in the Loop? Evaluating Fitness Functions for Network Topology Optimization with a Quality-Diversity Algorithm
Neural and Evolutionary Computing.summary: Network topology optimization (NTO) can reduce redispatch cost by rerouting power flows in transmission systems. To approach NTO, a complex combinatorial problem, gradient-free optimization algorithms that leverage diversity have shown promising results. These algorithms rely on frequent evaluations of candidate topologies by fitness functions. Recent work has shown that fast DC power flow-based fitness functions can serve this purpose. However, DC power flow fitness functions can misjudge the cost and feasibility of topologies, potentially leading to wrong operational decisions. Understanding the impact of fitness function accuracy on optimization performance is therefore crucial. This study compares the optimization performance of four fitness functions based on DC and AC power flow and on DC and AC optimal power flow. Furthermore, we propose a ranking-based metric to estimate the optimization performance of a fitness function on a curated dataset. Case studies cover the IEEE 118-bus case with 50 congested operating points and a 793-bus case for validation. Results show that optimal power flow-based fitness functions perform better in the optimization loop than power flow-based ones. Additionally, the results indicate that the metric can predict the optimization performance order of the fitness functions, but only if the distribution shift between the curated dataset and the search path of the optimization is small.
Neural and Evolutionary Computing.comment: This preprint is currently under peer review

Neural and Evolutionary Computing.title: Transformer Semantic Genetic Programming for d-dimensional Symbolic Regression Problems
Neural and Evolutionary Computing.summary: Transformer Semantic Genetic Programming (TSGP) is a semantic search approach that uses a pre-trained transformer model as a variation operator to generate offspring programs with high semantic similarity to a given parent. Unlike other semantic GP approaches that rely on fixed syntactic transformations, TSGP aims to learn diverse structural variations that lead to solutions with similar semantics. We find that a single transformer model trained on millions of programs is able to generalize across symbolic regression problems of varying dimensions. Evaluated on 24 real-world and synthetic datasets, TSGP significantly outperforms standard GP, SLIM_GSGP, Deep Symbolic Regression, and Denoising Autoencoder GP, achieving an average rank of 1.58 across all benchmarks. Moreover, TSGP produces more compact solutions than SLIM_GSGP, despite its higher accuracy. In addition, the target semantic distance is able to effectively adjust the step size in the semantic space: small values enable consistent improvement in fitness but often lead to larger programs, while larger values promote faster convergence and compactness. Thus, the target semantic distance provides an effective mechanism for balancing exploration and exploitation.
Neural and Evolutionary Computing.comment: Accepted at ACM Transactions on Evolutionary Learning and Optimization (TELO)

Neural and Evolutionary Computing.title: Neural-Network Approximators for Low-Thrust Multi-Asteroid Rendezvous Optimization
Neural and Evolutionary Computing.summary: Designing low-thrust multi-asteroid rendezvous missions requires the coupled selection of asteroid sequences, encounter epochs, and low-thrust trajectories. Lambert transfers support rapid beam search but do not directly describe thrust-limited transfer capacity or propellant consumption. This paper develops two complementary low-thrust neural approximators. The first directly predicts the continuous maximum admissible initial mass from numerically optimized low-thrust transfers, providing a transfer-capacity estimate for comparison with the current spacecraft mass. The second predicts mass-dependent propellant consumption and propagates spacecraft mass to subsequent legs. With the carefully-designed input features and network structure, the approximators reduce mean absolute errors by 72.2% and 75.5%, respectively, relative to conventional deep neural network baselines. These predictions are incorporated into a Lambert-ranked beam search through resource filtering and recursive mass propagation before final beam selection. The method is evaluated on fixed-visit, maximum-visit, and deployment-collection missions. Across the tested cases, the proposed resource filtering increases the fraction of candidate sequences that yield accepted low-thrust solutions, raises the maximum validated asteroid-visit count by up to 15.4%, and improves the best mission objective by up to 17.8%. These results demonstrate that continuous transfer-capacity and propellant predictions can improve finite-width sequence search.

Neural and Evolutionary Computing.title: On Monotonic Hamming Sphere Landscapes
Neural and Evolutionary Computing.summary: Monotonic Hamming Sphere Landscapes (MHSL) are introduced: binary landscapes whose fitness is nonincreasing with Hamming distance from a unique global optimum, while points on the same Hamming sphere may be ordered arbitrarily. The class includes OneMax, every nondecreasing unitation function with a unique optimum, and positive linear functions with sufficiently balanced weights. The one-to-one MHSL, called Hamming sphere encodings (HSE), are counted in total and up to hypercube symmetry and shown to be a vanishing fraction of all landscapes. For the elitist (1+1) EA, every MHSL in which no two spheres share a fitness value has the optimization-time distribution of OneMax, which with known results makes these landscapes the easiest for mutation rates below one half. The same equivalence and optimality are proved for a two-member genetic algorithm with tournament selection and no crossover, whose hitting time on these landscapes reduces to a chain with quadratically many states. All 40,320 one-to-one three-bit landscapes are then evaluated for the (1+1) EA and the two-member genetic algorithm under eight mutation rates, three crossover operators and two selection schemes. Below one half, the easiest symmetry classes are all and only the HSE; above one half they are the hardest. Differences among HSE are small and stem from selection and from the hypercube symmetries respected by mutation and crossover. Targeted five-bit experiments likewise find their fastest landscapes within the HSE class.

Methodology.title: Fold Weighting for Cross-Validation Under Continuous Distributional Drift
Methodology.summary: Cross-validation weights all folds equally, so under drift the oldest folds count as much as the newest. We model drift by a Hölder condition in total variation distance and give finite-sample bounds on the excess deployment risk of the configuration that sliding-window cross-validation selects. Each bound splits into drift, estimation, and validation-noise terms. With equal weights the drift terms saturate as the record grows. With fold weights fixed in advance, the drift terms become weighted averages, which shrink as weight moves toward deployment. The noise term grows as the weights concentrate and shrinks with the batch size. The drift terms are linear in the weights and the noise term is convex, so minimizing the bound over the weights is a convex problem. Applications to U.S. earnings and flight delays show both sides of this trade-off. Weight on recent folds pays off when a change in the best predictor persists and each period has many observations, and equal weights do best when changes are short-lived.
Methodology.comment: 24 pages, 4 figures, v2: sharper validation-noise bound via a martingale argument

Methodology.title: Individualized Prediction Bands in Causal Inference with Continuous Treatments
Methodology.summary: Individualized treatments are crucial for optimal decision-making and treatment allocation, specifically in personalized medicine based on the estimation of an individual's dose-response curve across a continuum of treatment levels, e.g., drug dosage. Current works focus on conditional mean and median estimates, which are useful but do not provide the full picture. We propose viewing causal inference with a continuous treatment as a covariate shift. This allows us to leverage existing weighted conformal prediction methods with both quantile and point estimates to compute individualized uncertainty quantification for dose-response curves. When used with quantile regression, our method, individualized prediction bands (IPB), enjoys a doubly robust coverage property. We demonstrate IPB via simulations and a real data analysis that assesses the additional medical expenditure caused by continued smoking for selected individuals. Our results show that IPB provides an effective solution to a gap in the individual dose-response uncertainty quantification literature.

Methodology.title: Zero-Shot Prognostic Covariate Adjustment and Mechanistic Week-1 Myelosuppression Updating Across 9,500 Oncology Patients Under FDA Guidance
Methodology.summary: The FDA's 2023 guidance on covariate adjustment recommends "that sponsors adjust for covariates that are anticipated to be most strongly associated with the outcome of interest" and notes that "it may be useful to use previous studies (e.g. a Phase 2 trial) to select prognostic covariates or form prognostic indices." Its August 2024 guidance on dosage optimization, part of Project Optimus, states that "the dose- and exposure-response relationships should be evaluated to select a dosage(s) for clinical trial(s)." We analyzed the control arms of 14 randomized trials from Project Data Sphere, with 5,074 patients with overall survival follow-up, in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) and metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC), and in three AACR Project GENIE Biopharma Collaborative cohorts (4,440 patients). In all, about 9,500 patients were studied. We used the regularized baseline prognostic index to compute out-of-fold estimates of the share of covariate-adjusted log-rank variance removed ($ρ^2$), and found these to be 0.177 to 0.186 for the three indications. For the locked held-out trials, the value was 0.183 (second-line NSCLC docetaxel), 0.177 (first-line PDAC gemcitabine) and 0.110 (first-line mCRC FOLFOX plus bevacizumab). Refitting in GENIE BPC resulted in estimates of 0.073 to 0.127 for first-line and 0.122 to 0.219 for later lines. In a simulated 600-patient trial, 5,000 within-stratum re-randomizations gave a type I error rate of 0.051 for the adjusted test. At $ρ^2 = 0.18$, adjustment raises power from 80.0% to 87.2%, cuts required events by 18% or shrinks the control arm by about 30%. A Friberg marrow prior updated with week 1 blood counts raised the AUROC for new cycle 1 grade 3 or worse neutropenia from 0.791 to 0.816 (n = 3,465; calibration slope 0.999; Brier skill 0.190) and raised it in 5 of 8 cross-trial rows (up to +0.116).

Methodology.title: Stochastic non-metric MDS for noisy high-dimensional data
Methodology.summary: Multidimensional scaling (MDS) constructs low-dimensional embeddings that approximate pairwise distances in a high-dimensional dataset. MDS exists in several flavors, with metric MDS approximating distances directly and non-metric MDS additionally optimizing for an arbitrary monotonic transformation of the high-dimensional distances. Empirically, metric MDS is known to suffer from the curse of dimensionality. Here we extend prior theoretical results for metric MDS on fully uninformative data to a more general case of finite, high-dimensional data with concentrated distances. We show that the metric MDS embeddings of such datasets stay distributionally close to the data-independent limit case. We then show that non-metric MDS is more robust to high-dimensional noise and can yield informative embeddings of such data. While existing implementations of non-metric MDS are slow, we develop a fast implementation using stochastic gradient descent in PyTorch. Using our implementation, we conduct an empirical study using multiple simulated and real-world datasets, including population-genomic and scRNA-seq data, and show that non-metric MDS can strongly outperform other methods in terms of global structure preservation.

Methodology.title: Robust Pair--Restricted Lipschitz Regression with Global--Local Transfer
Methodology.summary: We develop a robust pair-restricted Lipschitz regression framework for grouped longitudinal data represented as finite trajectories in a space equipped with a prescribed or learned pseudometric. For a fixed geometry, latent responses and a Lipschitz bound are estimated jointly through a convex optimisation problem with constraints imposed on selected trajectory pairs. We show that the choice of fidelity loss leads to different structural behaviour: Huber regularisation strictly reduces the pair-restricted Lipschitz seminorm whenever the exact interpolant has a finite positive seminorm, whereas $L^1$ fidelity can preserve exact interpolation below a data-dependent threshold. For grouped observations, global and local Lipschitz structures are combined while keeping group identity outside the trajectory geometry. The global component draws on observations from other groups, while the local component uses each group's history to account for group-specific behaviour. We also characterise when group-specific observations can be fitted exactly under a shared Lipschitz bound and establish a regularity bound for the combined predictor. We describe a computational implementation based on constraint generation and illustrate the framework through an application to longitudinal sow-production data.

Methodology.title: Adaptive Two-Sample Testing for Regression Discrepancy and Model Misspecification in High Dimensions
Methodology.summary: In two-sample regression comparisons, testing for equality is often too restrictive because minor discrepancies in functional form are unavoidable in practice. We study whether the functional discrepancy falls within a practically acceptable tolerance. Such tolerance-based comparison can, however, be unreliable when either regression model is misspecified. To address both issues, we propose a unified adaptive-to-model testing framework for high-dimensional regressions that integrates model checking with functional similarity testing for the two populations. For functional similarity, we develop an adaptive boundary-proxy test whose rejection probability converges to the nominal level at every fixed configuration of the composite null hypothesis, overcoming the conservatism of conventional least favorable configuration tests. For model misspecification, we use projection-based tests for sparse high-dimensional regression models. These components are combined through adaptive gating into a joint test. We investigate its asymptotic null distribution and power properties under global and local alternatives. Numerical studies examine its finite-sample performance.

Methodology.title: Correlation-aware sequential sampling for multi-output polynomial chaos expansions
Methodology.summary: The interaction of multiple physical processes in complex engineering systems is often characterized by several quantities of interest (QoIs) with non-negligible cross-correlations. Accurate uncertainty quantification of these responses requires repeated model evaluations, which can be computationally expensive. As an alternative, polynomial chaos expansion (PCE) provides an efficient surrogate modeling framework for reducing this computational cost owing to its natural structure for statistical analysis, while adaptive sequential sampling can further improve sampling efficiency under a limited model evaluation budget. However, adaptive sampling strategies specifically designed for multi-output PCE remain limited, and existing approaches commonly aggregate information from individual outputs without explicitly accounting for their statistical dependence. When strong correlations exist among QoIs, output-wise aggregation can give greater combined influence to response patterns shared by several outputs. To reduce the influence of such repeated representation on sample allocation, this study develops a principal component analysis-based extension of the multi-output criterion for adaptive construction of PCE. The sampling criterion combines component-wise normalization with the retention of selected principal directions, thereby adjusting the relative influence of shared response patterns while preserving distance-based exploration. The method is verified through numerical examples with different levels of output coupling and is compared with the conventional multi-output criterion and reference sampling strategies. The results demonstrate that accounting for output dependence improves the allocation of new samples among multiple response features and enhances the efficiency of multi-output PCE surrogate construction, particularly for strongly correlated QoIs.

Methodology.title: Twisted Block Particle Filters: A Local Particle-System Change of Measure for High-Dimensional State-Space Models
Methodology.summary: Block particle filters mitigate weight degeneracy in high-dimensional state-space models, but their normalizer estimates can remain highly variable. We introduce a twisted block particle filter (TBPF) that incorporates predictive guidance through an exact change of measure at blockwise resampling. The method guide-tilts one uniformly selected offspring per block, leaves the state-transition kernel unchanged, and computes the resampling correction using finite empirical guide averages. We prove that this correction exactly preserves the finite-particle block particle filter normalizer expectation, separating the effect of guided sampling from the approximation introduced by spatial blocking. Our analysis provides exact conditional local moments and a one-step conditional central limit result. We further derive explicit bounds on the correction accumulated across blocks and time, establish fixed-horizon consistency of the block filter and corrected normalizer under suitable regularity and guide-range conditions, and identify conditional criteria for guide perturbations that reduce variance. Experiments on coupled linear Gaussian and stochastic-volatility models with up to 256 latent dimensions show lower measured log-normalizer variance. For stochastic volatility with a five-step guide, the median reduction is $38\%$. An application to a 100-dimensional financial portfolio panel extends the evaluation to real data.

Methodology.title: Quadruply robust methods for causal mediation analysis
Methodology.summary: Estimating natural effects is a core task in causal mediation analysis. Existing triply robust (TR) frameworks (Tchetgen Tchetgen & Shpitser 2012) and their extensions have been developed to estimate the natural effects. In this work, we introduce a new quadruply robust (QR) framework that enlarges the model class for unbiased identification. We study two modeling strategies. The first is a nonparametric modeling approach, under which we propose a general QR estimator that supports the use of machine learning methods for nuisance estimation. We also study high-dimensional settings, where the dimensions of covariates and mediators may both be large. In these settings, we adopt a parametric modeling strategy and develop a model quadruply robust (MQR) estimator to limit the impact of model misspecification. Simulation studies and a real data application demonstrate the finite-sample performance of the proposed methods.

Methodology.title: Censored Regression Models with Endogeneity: A Survey
Methodology.summary: This survey article provides a comprehensive overview of methodologies developed to handle endogeneity in censored regression models. We emphasize their theoretical basis, and estimating methodologies. The paper summarizes the benefits and drawbacks of each technique and addresses expansions to nonlinear, panel, and high-dimensional settings, offering researchers practical assistance and identifying options for future methodological improvement in censored models with endogenous regressors.

Methodology.title: Cure-Fraction Random Survival Forests: Separating Cure from Latency
Methodology.summary: In many cancer and clinical studies, the population under study has a positive fraction of long-term survivors, motivating survival models that distinguish probability of long-term survival (cure fraction) from the latency of the subgroup that is susceptible to the event. Existing survival trees and forests partition data using criteria that emphasize differences in the ranks of survival times and therefore need not identify covariates associated with cure probability. We introduce cure-fraction based survival trees (CBST) that recursively partition the covariate space using contrasts in tail survival probability supported by adequate follow-up. The resulting ensemble forest targets long-term survival heterogeneity directly rather than ranking of the survival times. We establish consistency for the induced tail-survival target and derive conditions under which our procedure consistently recovers cure-rate related partitions and cure probabilities. The analysis clarifies the separate roles of follow-up maturity, localization, and residual-tail bias in identifying cure effects and supporting statistical inference. We further develop variance estimation and asymptotic results and uncertainty quantification for predictions from the ensemble forest. Simulations show that the cure-fraction based splitting criterion can improve recovery of cure heterogeneity relative to a log-rank based forest when cure incidence and latency are driven by different covariates. Analyses of temporally held-out cohorts from the Sao Paulo Hospital Cancer Registry demonstrate that our method produces stable long-term survival risk groups while preserving substantial late follow-up support. The proposed framework provides a nonparametric approach to learning and interpreting cure heterogeneity in settings where long-term survival is the primary scientific objective.

Methodology.title: Conformal prediction for high-dimensional functional time series: Applications to subnational mortality
Methodology.summary: In statistics, forecast uncertainty is often quantified using a specified statistical model, though such approaches may be vulnerable to model misspecification, selection bias, and limited finite-sample validity. While bootstrap procedures may alleviate some of these concerns, their validity is not guaranteed and they are often computationally demanding. Instead, we take a model-agnostic and distribution-free approach, namely conformal prediction, to construct pointwise prediction intervals in high-dimensional functional time series. Among a rich family of conformal prediction methods, we study split, non-conformity score, sequential predictive, and adaptive conformal prediction. In split and non-conformity score conformal prediction, the data are divided into training, validation, and test sets, and the interval width is calibrated on the validation set so that the empirical coverage probability matches the nominal level, by tuning a coefficient of the residual standard deviation and by taking an empirical quantile of the non-conformity scores, respectively. Sequential predictive conformal prediction removes the need for a validation set by updating predictive quantiles sequentially via an autoregressive process, whereas adaptive conformal prediction updates the significance level over time according to the coverage of past intervals. Using subnational age- and sex-specific $\log$ mortality data from Japan and Canada, we compare the finite-sample forecast performance of the conformal prediction methods considered, using empirical coverage probability and the mean interval score.

Methodology.title: Hierarchical Bayesian Estimation of Covariance Matrices
Methodology.summary: We develop a hierarchical Bayesian framework for covariance matrix estimation built on a key observation: while equivariance under the full general linear group GL(p) is well known, it is an extremely restrictive property. Estimators equivariant to GL(p) are limited to scalar multiples of the sample covariance matrix and carry considerably larger risks than shrinkage estimators. By contrast, commonly used shrinkage estimators, including the Haff empirical Bayes estimator and the Ledoit-Wolf estimators, are all equivariant under the smaller orthogonal group O(p). Exploiting this structure, we establish that the Haar measure Bayes rule in an oracle eigenvalue model is the minimum risk estimator within the class of O(p)-equivariant estimators, and derive oracle Bayes rules for the covariance and precision matrices under the squared Frobenius, Stein, and squared Stein loss functions. These oracle rules serve as theoretical benchmarks for all O(p)-equivariant estimators. To approximate them when the true eigenvalues are unknown, we introduce a hierarchical Bayes model that places a finite Pólya tree prior on the eigenvalue distribution and uses Gibbs sampling to generate posterior draws, yielding both shrinkage estimates for the eigenvalues and approximations to the oracle Bayes rules. In simulations, the resulting estimators come close to the risk of the oracle rules and have smaller risk than commonly used estimators, particularly when p/n is large. In an application to monthly returns of 49 US industry portfolios, the proposed estimators had the highest out-of-sample likelihood of all the estimators we compared, and their minimum-variance portfolios had variance comparable to that of estimators designed specifically for portfolio selection.

Methodology.title: Tuning the false discovery rate in the closed eBH procedure
Methodology.summary: The closed eBH procedure controls the false discovery rate under arbitrary dependence between the input e-values. It takes the target false discovery rate $α$ as its input and outputs a rejection set $R$, the usual goal being to maximize its size $\left|R\right|$. This note discusses a modification of the closed eBH procedure that allows choosing the target false discovery rate post hoc: the rejection set and its level $α$ can be chosen after seeing the data, and the expected ratio of the false discovery proportion to $α$ is at most 1. We adapt Vovk and Wang's (2023) algorithm for computing discovery e-matrices to computing, in quadratic time, the frontier of achievable combinations $(\left|R\right|,α)$ of the size of a rejection set $R$ and its level $α$. The frontier allows us to compute an optimal rejection set in view of a given utility function $F$, $F(\left|R\right|,α)\to\max$, striking a balance between the goals of reducing $α$ and increasing $\left|R\right|$.

Methodology.title: Robust Forest-based Estimation of Heterogeneous Treatment Effect Under High-dimensional Confounding
Methodology.summary: Understanding how patients with Alzheimer's disease respond differently to treatment is important for individualized therapeutic assessment. Using observational data from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), we investigate how the association between donepezil dosage and 12-month cognitive performance varies across diagnostic stages and hippocampal volumes. This analysis presents several statistical challenges, including potentially nonlinear treatment effect heterogeneity, high-dimensional confounding, and heavy-tailed outcomes with extreme observations. To address these challenges, we develop an Orthogonal Huber Random Forest (OHRF) framework that combines Huber-based robust estimation, Neyman orthogonality, and forest-based adaptive weighting. The proposed method accommodates complex treatment effect heterogeneity while reducing sensitivity to nuisance estimation errors and extreme outcomes. We establish its consistency, asymptotic normality, and finite-sample error bounds. Simulation studies demonstrate favorable estimation accuracy and robustness across a range of error distributions, particularly under heavy-tailed noise and outlier contamination. In the ADNI application, OHRF produces generally narrower pointwise confidence intervals than the conventional Orthogonal Random Forest (ORF) while revealing distinct patterns of treatment effect heterogeneity across diagnostic groups and hippocampal volumes. These findings illustrate the potential of robust, data-adaptive methods for studying heterogeneous treatment responses in complex observational biomedical data.

Methodology.title: Statistical Inference with Ill-Conditioned Random Weight Neural Network Sieves
Methodology.summary: Random weight neural networks (RWNNs) are shallow networks whose hidden-layer parameters are randomly generated and then kept fixed, while only the output coefficients are estimated. Conditional on the sampled parameters, RWNN regression is a linear sieve problem with random approximation space. We show that such random sieves cannot remain uniformly well-conditioned as their dimension grows. For parametrized feature families satisfying polynomial covering and Lipschitz conditions, the eigenvalues of the population covariance matrix are proven to have polynomial upper bounds determined by the covering geometry of the parameter space, leading to a vanishing smallest eigenvalue. We develop approximation, estimation, and inference theory that explicitly treats the ill-conditioning. Under a $β$-Hölder source condition, we obtain both faster-than-Monte-Carlo $L^2$ approximation rates and new $L^\infty$ approximation bounds based on stratified sampling. We then derive improved consistency guarantees for ridge-regularized least squares driven by ridge effective dimension, spectral, and leverage-based stability conditions. For inference, we establish asymptotic linearity and Gaussian limits for linear functional directions while allowing the smallest eigenvalue of the population covariance matrix to vanish. Nondegeneracy is directional: we characterize it with a ridge-normalized Rayleigh quotient and extend it to smooth functionals via Riesz representation. Consistency of ridge-adjusted variance estimators is proved, yielding feasible studentized inference. Numerical experiments illustrate the deterioration of random-feature conditioning and the finite-sample behavior of the resulting estimation and inference procedures.

Methodology.title: KernelMix: Bayesian kernel machine regression in Python
Methodology.summary: Exposures measured together can have nonlinear associations with an outcome, and the association with one exposure may depend on another. Bayesian kernel machine regression represents these patterns through a flexible exposure-response function. We implement this approach in KernelMix, a Python package. To handle different outcome types, KernelMix combines the exposure function with continuous, binary, count and survival models, including selected extensions for clustered observations and censored event times. For fitted models, it returns posterior summaries, uncertainty intervals, joint predictions and sampling diagnostics. Fitting and prediction use NumPy and SciPy without requiring R. To assess the implementation, we compare selected Gaussian and probit posterior summaries and conditional calculations with installed R bkmr 0.2.2 and check additional model components against independent mathematical calculations. A daily ozone analysis illustrates how these components form an analysis workflow.

Methodology.title: Econometric vs. Causal structure learning for time-series data: Implications for policy interventions using COVID-19 data
Methodology.summary:
This study compares regression-based and causal structure-learning approaches to recovering temporal dependencies in UK COVID-19 data and assesses their suitability for policy analysis. We evaluate four econometric methods and eleven structure-learning algorithms using a common lag-expanded dataset that permits edges only from past to current variables. The dataset comprises 866 daily observations and 45 variables, represented by 55 numeric series after categorical encoding. Maximum lags of 1, 7, 14, 17 and 21 days are examined; all four econometric methods and ten structure-learning algorithms successfully return structures at every lag specification.
  We compare graph structure, complexity, fit and temporal-edge stability across lag specifications. The resulting graphs vary substantially in density, complexity, fit and stability. Agreement with the knowledge graph is limited, while low structural Hamming distance sometimes reflects sparsity rather than recovery of known relationships. Edge recurrence also varies markedly by method, revealing sensitivity to the allowed history window. Diagnostics for VAR models using all lagged predictors indicate residual dependence, non-normality and instability; estimation becomes infeasible at longer lag orders. Policy evaluation raises further concerns: few mobility-to-infection links emerge, few meet the empirical coverage criterion, and none do so in longer-lag analyses. Common temporal constraints therefore do not resolve methodological disagreement. Learnt dependency structures should not be treated as policy-ready causal models without stronger identification assumptions, robustness checks and sufficient empirical support for the interventions assessed.

Methodology.title: The Curved Exponential Family of Cylindrical Distributions: m-Projection, Curvature and a Test of the von Mises-Fisher Component
Methodology.summary: Cylindrical data pair a vector in R^d with a direction in S^(m-1). We study a family in which the direction is von Mises-Fisher and, given the direction, the vector is Gaussian with mean affine in it; this generalizes the Mardia-Sutton model. The family is a curved exponential family inside a regular family with Fisher-Bingham directions. We state necessary and sufficient conditions for the maximum-likelihood estimator to exist and be unique. The estimator is explicit except for one scalar root and is the m-projection (Kullback-Leibler projection) of the moment-matching member. Every moment it does not match is a function of one residual, the gap between the sample and fitted second moments of the direction. The squared length of this gap in the Fisher metric is the classical score test of von Mises-Fisher against Fisher-Bingham directions, due to Cox on the circle and extended by Mardia, Holmes and Kent. Specific here are this reading and the exact invariance of its law to the regression part. The exponential curvature lies only in the directions of the regression matrix. In closed form, the information lost on this matrix against the expected information is m-1 observations for uniform directions and (m+1)^2/(m-1) in the limit of high concentration; conditioning on the directions recovers it. Finite mixtures are identifiable.
