Optimization and Control.summary: The proximal slack update in an augmented Lagrangian method for semidefinite complementarity constraints requires a joint matrix projection. Given real symmetric matrices $A$ and $B$, we seek the nearest pair $(X,Z)$ with $X$ positive semidefinite, $Z$ negative semidefinite, and $XZ=0$. Hou, Peng and Ding obtain a squared-loss factor of $2$ by fitting the pair in an eigenbasis of $A+B$. To improve this bound, we replace the orthogonal projector onto the subspace allowed for $X$ by a symmetric matrix $T$ with eigenvalues in $[0,1]$. From an optimal solution of the resulting semidefinite program, we form candidate subspaces by starting at the zero subspace and adding the eigenspaces of $T$ in decreasing order of eigenvalue. For each candidate, we compress $A$ to that subspace and $B$ to its orthogonal complement. We keep the positive eigenvalues of the first compression and the negative eigenvalues of the second. The best pair has squared loss at most $1.189$ times the minimum for arbitrary inputs and at most $1.15487$ times the minimum when $A$ is positive semidefinite and $B$ is negative semidefinite. For arbitrary inputs the factor improves to $1.18$ if $T$ has at most two distinct eigenvalues in $(0,1)$. The threshold-rounding proofs average over a uniform spectral threshold and use computer-assisted bounds for the resulting scalar inequalities.

Optimization and Control.title: Optimal control of symmetry-breaking dynamics near criticality
Optimization and Control.summary: We study the problem of optimal control for dynamical systems near a pitchfork bifurcation, motivated by the role of external cues in guiding symmetry-breaking transitions in cell-fate selection and other natural processes. Using an asymptotic expansion of the optimality conditions obtained from the Pontryagin maximum principle, the leading-order optimal control law for a general n-dimensional system is examined across three dynamical regimes distinguished by scaling of control strength with respect to the distance from criticality. While in the strong control limit the results reduce to known approximations from linear-quadratic control, we derive generalized amplitude equations for the co-evolution of state and costate variables describing the optimized trajectory in the weak and intermediate control regimes. These control normal forms are validated against numerical solutions of the full optimal control problem for a canonical model of a bistable biochemical switch. The bifurcation structure of the optimal control problem is analyzed in the weak control regime. Finally, we demonstrate the construction of asymptotic solutions in the long time limit in this regime using boundary-layer methods.

Optimization and Control.title: Multi-UAV Trajectory Optimization for Bearing-Only Localization in GPS Denied Environments
Optimization and Control.summary: Accurate localization of maritime targets by unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) remains challenging in GPS-denied environments. UAVs equipped with gimballed electro-optical sensors are typically used to localize targets; however, reliance on these sensors increases mechanical complexity, cost, and susceptibility to single-point failures, limiting scalability and robustness in multi-UAV operations. This work presents a new trajectory optimization framework that enables cooperative target localization using UAVs with fixed, non-gimballed cameras operating in coordination with a surface vessel. This estimation-aware optimization generates dynamically feasible trajectories that explicitly account for mission constraints, platform dynamics, and out-of-frame events. Estimation-aware trajectories outperform heuristic paths by reducing localization error by more than a factor of two, motivating their use in cooperative operations. Results further demonstrate that coordinated UAVs with fixed, non-gimballed cameras achieve localization accuracy that meets or exceeds that of single gimballed systems, while substantially lowering system complexity and cost, enabling scalability, and enhancing mission resilience.
Optimization and Control.comment: Published open access in the Journal of Guidance, Control, and Dynamics. 41 pages, 8 figure, and 6 tables

Optimization and Control.title: On Grokking and the Dynamics of Generalization
Optimization and Control.summary: We extend the signal-channel theory of grokking introduced by Litman and Guo by relating training dissipation and evaluation transfer to population risk. For preconditioned gradient flows with time-dependent kernels, we distinguish two sources of limited evaluation visibility, namely small cumulative dissipation and weak transfer. We obtain quantitative bounds for task visibility and establish their stability under signal filtering and changes of evaluation distribution. We describe how task directions enter the effective signal channel through spectral activation or transport. We establish necessary and sufficient conditions for the transferred signal to decrease squared population risk and derive classification error bounds under margin assumptions. These results yield sufficient conditions for the same training trajectory to generalize under one evaluation distribution while failing under another. We show that differences in spectral learning rates can produce arbitrarily long delays between low training loss and low population risk. By relating classification accuracy to the distribution of margin crossing times, we construct a family of gradient flows in which the generalization delay tends to infinity, while both the duration of the transition from zero to full accuracy and the corresponding variation of population risk tend to zero. These phenomena occur without feature evolution during training. Finally, we prove that the occurrence and timing of generalization cannot generally be inferred from training dynamics alone, but depend on the geometry of evaluation transfer and its relation to the target.

Optimization and Control.title: Parallel Policy-Gradient Methods for Parameter Optimization of Nonlinear Feedback Controllers
Optimization and Control.summary: Structured feedback controllers provide stability guarantees, but their performance depends on manually tuned parameters. Policy-gradient methods offer a systematic way to tune these parameters, but evaluating the gradient is computationally expensive because it requires a sequential forward rollout of the state dynamics followed by a backward rollout of the costate dynamics. This letter develops a time-parallel policy-gradient framework for discrete-time nonlinear control-affine systems. We evaluate the policy gradient by formulating the forward state and backward costate rollouts as residual-minimization problems and solving them with Gauss-Newton (GN) iterations that use parallel associative scans. We show that global asymptotic stability and local exponential stability of the closed loop guarantee convergence of the parallel state solver without requiring bounds on Jacobian products throughout the state space. Near the exact trajectory, GN iterations converge quadratically in a neighborhood whose size is independent of the horizon T. When initialized at the equilibrium trajectory, a clipped variant converges at a linear rate that is also independent of T. We also quantify how horizon truncation and solver tolerance affect the accuracy of the policy gradient. Experiments on an LQR problem and a lossless Lorenz-96 system with saturated passivity-based control demonstrate improved closed-loop performance and computational benefits.

Optimization and Control.title: BGPNP: A Non-Euclidean Gradient Projection Newton Pursuit Method for Sparsity-Constrained Optimization
Optimization and Control.summary: A non-Euclidean gradient projection Newton pursuit method is proposed for solving sparsity constrained optimization problem via the Bregman distance. The method is also denoted as BGPNP. The method firstly constructs a gradient projection step based on the Bregman distance to ensure that the iterates satisfy the sparsity constraint. Then, when the support set becomes stable or the gradient norm is sufficiently small, a Newton pursuit step is introduced to improve local convergence efficiency. The BGPNP is proved to possess a sufficient descent property and the non-increasing monotonicity of the objective function values. The full convergence and linear convergence rate of the BGPNP are established under appropriate conditions, which do not involve the symmetry coefficient of Bregman distance and the $θ$-uniform condition. Moreover, the locally quadratical convergence rate of the BGPNP is also obtained. This method provides an effective algorithmic framework for sparse optimization in non-Euclidean setting. Numerical experiments on sparsity-constrained compressed sensing problems validate the competitive performance of BGPNP compared with existing leading solvers.

Optimization and Control.title: Variance Reduction Note 6: The Convergence of SAGA
Optimization and Control.summary: SAGA corrects a sampled component gradient with a table of previously computed gradients. Updating one entry at a time gives an unbiased gradient estimate at the cost of one new component gradient per iteration. This sixth note on variance reduction proves a linear convergence guarantee for a smooth finite sum with convex components and a strongly convex average. A two-component quadratic shows how the spread of the stored evaluation points determines the variance, even at the minimizer. We track the iterate and the table jointly to obtain a last-iterate bound, then relate its dependence on the sample size to the rate at which individual entries are replaced. For generalized linear losses the same gradient table can be represented by one scalar per observation and a running mean.

Optimization and Control.title: Universal Stabilization with Six Records
Optimization and Control.summary: This letter shows that a single feedback controller needs only six retained observation records to handle the largest universally stabilizable uncertainty range for the scalar discrete-time benchmark model of Xie and Guo, when uncertainty is measured by the radius of a generalized Lipschitz ball. Existing constructions can require arbitrarily many records along bounded trajectories. Our controller retains at most six genuine state-response pairs and five auxiliary real scalars. Each update requires a uniformly bounded number of elementary operations. No knowledge of the plant, its generalized Lipschitz constants, or the disturbance bound is required.

Optimization and Control.title: A Stackelberg strategy for the semi-linear heat equation with boundary controls
Optimization and Control.summary: This work continues the results presented in \cite{calsavara2022new} where a hierarchical control problem is solved. Our first goal is the case of both controls acting on the boundary. The follower control solves a null controllability problem, and the leader minimizes a $L^2$ cost functional. Additionally, we solve the case where one control acts on the boundary and the other on an open subset of the domain. More precisely, we prove the existence and uniqueness of a leader-follower couple and give some techniques to solve the problem.

Optimization and Control.title: Physics-Informed Learning for Multiplayer Differential Games
Optimization and Control.summary: Computing per-player feedback strategies in $N$-player adversarial differential games is challenging as the associated coupled Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman system is high-dimensional and generally lacks classical solutions. We address this by approximating viscosity solutions using physics-informed neural networks within a policy iteration scheme with a vanishing-viscosity annealing schedule. Theoretically, we establish an explicit $\varepsilon$-Nash guarantee by bounding per-player regret via computable residuals and prove our method reaches this stopping criterion in finite time. For two-player zero-sum games, we further establish a computable bound on the approximation error of the value function. Numerical experiments on pursuit-evasion scenarios illustrate the tightness of these computed bounds and the framework's scalability to high-dimensional environments.
Optimization and Control.comment: Accepted to IEEE Control Systems Letters (L-CSS) with presentation at CDC 2026

Optimization and Control.title: Solving the capacitated vehicle routing problem with polygonal neighborhoods using a metaheuristic enhanced with block coordinate descent
Optimization and Control.summary: We study a capacitated vehicle routing problem (CVRP) in which customers are represented by planar regions, called customer neighborhoods, rather than fixed points. Visiting a customer consists of selecting a point within its neighborhood. Therefore, besides determining the sequence of customers visited by each vehicle, one must also determine the corresponding visit points. To better reflect practical applications, customer neighborhoods are allowed to be simple polygons, either convex or non-convex, and distances are measured using the Euclidean norm. Applications include aerial reconnaissance, wireless sensor data collection and inspection, and two-stage delivery systems. We propose a general variable neighborhood search framework in which each neighbor is represented by a collection of routes. Constructing a route involves two stages, defining a customer sequence and then determining the associated visit points. The latter task is solved by a block coordinate descent (BCD) procedure, the central methodological contribution of this work, which computes high-quality visit points at a cost low enough to be used repeatedly inside the search. In extensive experiments on newly generated and adapted benchmark instances, within the time limits considered, the proposed framework matches all solutions proven optimal by CPLEX and matches or improves the best solutions found by CPLEX in the remaining instances. For the instances adapted from the CVRP literature, it also improves, in every instance, a CVRP-based upper bound given by the solution of the original CVRP instance reported in the literature, which is feasible for the problem with neighborhoods.
Optimization and Control.comment: 30 pages, 6 figures, 6 tables. Supplementary material (22 pages) available as an ancillary file

Optimization and Control.title: Two-timescale variational Q-learning for ergodic risk-sensitive control of Markov chains
Optimization and Control.summary: We propose a variational Q-learning algorithm for the ergodic risk-sensitive control of a discrete-time Markov chain with finite state and action spaces and an unknown transition kernel. The proposed algorithm is a two-timescale stochastic approximation algorithm, where the slow iteration solves for the fixed point of the multiplicative Bellman equation cast in a variational form, while the fast iteration solves the associated optimization problem over the probability simplex that stems from the variational representation. We prove that the iterates converge almost surely to the risk-sensitive Q-function and maximizing transition kernel. The proof adapts the ODE method for two-timescale stochastic approximation, where we analyze the global asymptotic stability of the equilibria of the corresponding fast and slow ODEs as well as bound the trajectory of the fast ODE away from zero. The main challenge lies in proving that, almost surely, the slow iterates are norm-bounded and the fast iterates are bounded below away from zero on the support of the transition kernel. We address this by using a fluid scaling approach for the slow iteration combined with tailored estimates for the fast iteration to control a certain fluid-scaled relative entropy error that arises in the ODE approximation. Numerical experiments illustrate the performance of the proposed algorithm and compare it with the existing risk-sensitive Q-learning algorithms.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Computing Normal-Form Correlated Equilibria in Extensive-Form Games is in PPAD
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study the computational complexity of finding any normal-form correlated equilibria (NFCE for short) in the succinct games of extensive-form with perfect recall, which is considered as a major open problem in algorithmic game theory. Our main results place this problem in PPAD for an arbitrary numbers of players. Our second result establishes PPAD-hardness of computing such an NFCE with support size of at most quadratic in the size of the game, even for two-player games. The posed restriction on the support size in PPAD-hardness construction is motivated by our PPAD algorithm, which constructs an NFCE with support size quadratic in the size of the input extensive-form game.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Distributed Places and Safe Net Reduction
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
Being able to find small Petri nets with the same behaviour as formal specifications of concurrent systems benefits both effective verification and practical implementation of such systems. This paper considers specifications given in the form of compositionally defined safe nets.
  The paper discusses a novel concept of distributed place which implements the behaviour of an individual net place. It is shown that if distributed places cover a safe Petri net, then it is possible to delete some places without changing the behaviour. Crucially, the reduction is both static and local, making it computationally feasible in practice.
  The resulting reduction technique is then applied to an algebra of safe Petri nets (boxes) derived compositionally from process (box) expressions. Though the original derivation can yield exponentially large boxes, prior research demonstrated that if a box expression does not involve cyclic behaviours, the exponential number of places can be reduced down to polynomial (quadratic). In this paper, using distributed places, it is show that similar optimisation can also be achieved in the case of process expressions with iteration.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Last-Iterate Equilibrium Learning in Symmetric Congestion Games under Semi-Bandit Feedback
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study last-iterate learning of mixed Nash equilibria in atomic symmetric congestion games under resource semi-bandit feedback, where players observe both the costs and the loads of their selected resources. For strictly increasing latency functions, the restriction of the potential function to symmetric marginal profiles is strongly convex. However, players' independent stochastic updates need not preserve this symmetry without explicit synchronization. We show that a quadratic consensus penalty makes the potential globally strongly convex while making the symmetric equilibrium the unique minimizer of the transformed potential. We propose a variant of online projected gradient descent that achieves $O(t^{-2/3})$ squared distance to equilibrium and $O(t^{-1/3})$ maximum deviation gain in expectation, for every $t\geq 1$ and for any initialization. The played profile also converges to equilibrium almost surely.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: 14 pages

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Robust implementation in approximate payoff-monotone equilibrium
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We revisit robust implementation through the lens of empirically plausible behavior. In private-value environments, robustness calls for strategy-proof mechanisms, yet experiments show weakly dominated, near-equilibrium behavior persists. Unlike secure implementation (Saijo et al., 2007), which requires that every equilibrium perform, we require it only of approximate payoff-monotone equilibria (APME, Velez and Brown, 2026), equilibria consistent with experimental regularities. Our main results are a necessary and a sufficient condition for full implementation in APME at a state; we further identify cases in which the two coincide. The direct mechanism is robust for all common priors if and only if the social choice function is strategy-proof and non-bossy, and for all interior priors if and only if it is strategy-proof and weakly non-bossy. We characterize the information structures where the second-price auction fails.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: Previously circulated as "Empirical strategy-proofness"

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Kant-Q: A Q-Learning Algorithm for Kantian Equilibrium in Symmetric Markov Games
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: AI agents increasingly interact with one another, and many of these interactions are mixed-motive games, which have posed a persistent challenge for learning algorithms. Most multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) algorithms are designed to reach Nash equilibria, yet in many such games these equilibria are Pareto-inefficient. We instead study Kantian equilibria, an economic solution concept in which each agent plays the action it would want all agents to adopt. In symmetric games, this corresponds to an optimal common policy. We propose Kant-Q, a Q-learning algorithm in which each agent learns action profiles where all agents play the same action. Each update is then a sample from a single-agent MDP, so Kant-Q inherits the convergence guarantees of standard Q-learning. We show that every symmetric Markov game has a pure Kantian equilibrium. We also prove that all agents' Q-tables converge to the same limit, whose greedy policy is such an equilibrium, and that greedy play converges whenever the optimal common action is unique at every state. We further show that in a subclass of symmetric monotone games, the Kantian equilibrium is Pareto-efficient among pure strategy profiles and strictly individually rational. Empirically, on the iterated Prisoner's Dilemma and the GovSim fishery with up to 200 agents, Kant-Q learns the Kantian equilibrium, while the baselines underperform. Since copies of the same AI system naturally face one another in symmetric games, these results suggest universalization as a design principle for cooperative AI-AI interaction.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: 12 pages, 3 figures

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Faster Algorithms for the Least-Core value and the Nucleolus in Convex Games
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: The nucleolus is a central solution concept in cooperative game theory. While its computation is NP-hard in general, it can be computed in polynomial time for convex games; however, the only published polynomial-time algorithm relies on the ellipsoid method. We develop a combinatorial alternative based on reduced games and iterative least-core value computations. Leveraging submodular function minimization and polyhedral structure in a novel way, we obtain a faster combinatorial algorithm for computing the least-core value, improving the oracle complexity by a factor $n^3$ over previous approaches. As a consequence, we obtain a new strongly polynomial-time and combinatorial algorithm for computing the nucleolus in convex games. Preliminary analysis indicates an improved oracle complexity compared to the ellipsoid-based algorithm.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Computing Feasible EF1 Allocations under Generalized Assignment Constraints
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study the fair allocation of indivisible goods under generalized assignment constraints, where each agent's bundle must fit within her budget, the sizes of goods may differ across agents, and unallocated goods go to a charity. A natural fairness notion here is feasible envy-freeness up to one good (FEF1), which requires an agent's envy towards any feasible subset of another bundle to disappear after some good is removed from this subset. While FEF1 allocations always exist, they could previously be computed efficiently only when sizes are common to all agents. We show that FEF1 allocations can be computed in strongly polynomial time, and more generally whenever each agent's value can be almost exactly maximized over her feasible bundles, a requirement that cannot be relaxed substantially. Our analysis relies on an essentially tight quadratic bound on how often each agent's bundle is repaired. Moreover, the allocation can be made approximately envy-free up to any good while retaining nearly half the Nash welfare of any given allocation. In contrast, requiring a single good to eliminate an agent's envy towards all feasible subsets of another bundle at once, which makes no difference without constraints, renders the problem NP-hard and may halve the attainable Nash welfare.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: The Weak Negotiation Function
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
Subgame-perfect equilibria (SPEs) constitute a refinement of Nash equilibria, where the players are not allowed to resort to non-credible threats to discourage deviations. In graph games equipped with a broad class of objectives, SPEs are captured by a tool called the negotiation function.
  After giving a quick overview of what has already been achieved using this tool, we define a variant of it: the weak negotiation function. We show that weak SPEs, a standard relaxation of SPEs, can be captured by the weak negotiation function exactly like SPEs are captured by the negotiation function. This characterisation yields a new computational result: deciding whether a given game contains a weak SPE where each player's payoff lies in a given interval is an NP-complete problem if the game has mean-payoff objectives. We also provide a new proof that the same problem in Büchi games is in P. The proofs reuse many arguments from their SPE counterpart, demonstrating the robustness of the tool.
  We also use the weak negotiation function to present a new proof, significantly shorter than the known one, of the existence of weak SPEs in mean-payoff games. We argue that those new techniques should be reusable in other settings, in particular to prove an open conjecture about the existence of randomised $ε$-SPEs in mean-payoff games.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Mechanism-Based Intelligence: Differentiable Incentives for Rational Coordination and Equilibrium Alignment in Multi-Agent Systems
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
Autonomous multi-agent systems struggle with the Hayekian Information problem (using dispersed private knowledge) and the Hurwiczian Incentive problem (aligning local actions with global objectives). I introduce Mechanism-Based Intelligence (MBI), an architecture that treats intelligence as emergent from the coordination of specialized modules rather than a single monolithic model. At its core, the Differentiable Price Mechanism computes the exact gradient of the system loss as a price; subtracting its own marginal cost, each agent obtains the incentive signal
  $$\mathbf{G}_i = - \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{global}}}{\partial \mathbf{x}_i},$$
  and the transfers take the Groves form. Each agent's best response minimizes the global loss given the actions of others, so the negative global loss is an exact potential for the resulting game, with a unique equilibrium at the global optimum. Gradient-based play converges to it under a step-size condition when effort is costless, and stops near it otherwise: a satisficing rule halts each agent's search when its marginal gain no longer exceeds its marginal computational cost. The equilibrium requires no knowledge of agents' private costs, so asymmetric information causes no welfare loss; simultaneous gradient dynamics require only a public bound on cost curvature. Each iteration scales linearly ($\mathcal{O}(N)$) with the number of agents, though for losses summed over agents the iteration count also grows with $N$. For known, differentiable losses, MBI avoids the combinatorial search of Decentralized Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes. Under convexity and smoothness conditions, MBI aligns agent self-interest with the Planner's objective, offering an auditable approach to multi-agent coordination.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: v2: substantially revised, new title. Groves-form transfers; exact potential game; Planner prices only the system loss; convergence of simultaneous updates with satisficing stop; limitations stated; related work added. Lean 4 proof checks; code: github.com/stevefatz95/mechanism_based_intelligence

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Vote-Left: A Deterministic Coordination Strategy for the Faithful in The Traitors
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: The Traitors is a social deduction game in which an informed minority of Traitors face an uninformed majority of Faithful, and the recurring question facing the Faithful is how to vote. Eliminating a player chosen uniformly at random is optimal for the Faithful when it can be guaranteed, but when votes are cast individually a random vote is indistinguishable from a strategic one, leaving the Faithful exposed to coordinated Traitor collusion. We introduce the Vote-Left protocol, a deterministic rule under which every player votes for the next surviving player in a fixed cyclic ordering. It reproduces the banishment distribution of random voting, yet any deviation from it is immediately identifiable. Combined with a simple punishment rule, Vote-Left punishes every deviation in the main phase of the game that does not end it at once, whether by a single player or by the Traitors acting together. In the final rounds punishment arrives too late, and the Faithful should return to random voting there. Under this switching protocol no player gains by departing from Vote-Left in the main phase, and with a single Traitor it is a Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium of the whole game. Across the televised configurations, it raises the Faithful's winning probability by a factor of approximately four over random voting under collusion with three Traitors, and by a factor of 62 to 84 with four.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Complexity of Autobidding Equilibria in GSP Sponsored Shopping
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
We revisit autobidding equilibria in GSP sponsored shopping auctions, recently proposed and studied in Dütting et al. We establish computational upper bounds for both budget constraints (ABE-B) and return-on-investment constraints (ABE-R): computing an exact equilibrium is in FIXP, while computing a $γ$-approximate equilibrium is in PPAD even for inverse-exponentially small $γ$. At the same time, we establish tight inapproximability for both models: for every fixed $0\leqγ<1$, computing a $γ$-approximate equilibrium is PPAD-hard, even when all items are displayed and all click-through rates are equal.
  A key ingredient in our hardness reductions is a new variant of PureCircuit with bounded forward span, which we prove remains PPAD-hard. This structural restriction makes our reduction parameters independent of circuit size, enabling hardness for every fixed $γ<1$. More broadly, our approach suggests a strategy for strengthening PPAD-hardness results in other settings, by developing structural insights into the target problem and new hardness-preserving restrictions on PureCircuit in tandem, with each informing the other and the design of the reduction.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: First Attack, Final Offensive: The Dark Forest on an Open Roster
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: The Dark Forest argument holds that a civilization that detects another should strike it at once. The choice it addresses is general: an agent that has located another nearby must decide whether to strike it, collaborate with it, or do neither, without knowing who else is there. Of sixteen treatments of this decision that we examined, ten assume a known set of players; the other six add unobserved agents only in games in which strikes and replies arrive instantly, in simulations, or in informal arguments. We show that when the roster is open, so that no agent knows even its list of nearby agents to be complete, the course that maximizes an agent's expected survival time if no unobserved agent acts still maximizes it, whatever else the agent believes, if and only if the agent gives at most a threshold probability to an unobserved agent acting, by attacking or helping the agent or by striking the located agent. Without further assumptions the threshold is below one half whatever the course, because an unobserved agent may reply to one course with help and to another with an attack, as soon as an agent as near as the located one could reply. If the agent knows the located agent completely and assumes that it would receive no help from unobserved agents, the threshold for collaboration can approach one. Even below the threshold the agent cannot know that the course it favors is in fact better: however much it knows of the one it has located, some world consistent with all it has observed makes another course better. These results do not apply to an agent that knows all but one of its courses would destroy it. For every other agent, no case for striking first, or for any other course, that assumes nothing about the unobserved agents withstands an even chance that one of them acts: some belief that gives that chance favors another course.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: Add delay by distance and unobserved agents that may help, and drop the assumption of v2 that an unobserved agent who sees a strike can only be provoked by it. 23 pages, 2 figures, 1 table, including appendices

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Computing EF1 Allocations under Budget Constraints in Polynomial Time
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
We study the allocation of indivisible goods to agents with budgets and additive valuations. Each agent compares its bundle with every budget-feasible subset of another agent's bundle or of the unallocated goods. We give a strongly polynomial algorithm for computing an allocation that is envy-free up to one good (EF1), even when agents have different valuations and budgets. Deciding whether a given allocation satisfies EF1 is coNP-complete. Equivalently, deciding whether it violates EF1 is NP-complete. When all agents have the same valuation, we can compute an EF1 allocation with welfare at least $(1/2-\varepsilon)$ times the maximum feasible welfare in time polynomial in the input length and $1/\varepsilon$, for any $0<\varepsilon<1/2$.
  Finding an allocation that is envy-free up to any good (EFX) is NP-hard even for one agent. We give polynomial-time EFX algorithms when each agent values goods in proportion to their sizes or when the number of distinct positive item values per agent is bounded by a constant.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: Added a proof that finding an EFX allocation is NP-hard

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Rational Adversaries and the Maintenance of Fragility: A Game-Theoretic Theory of Rational Stagnation
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Cooperative systems often remain in persistently suboptimal yet stable states. This paper explains such "rational stagnation" as an equilibrium sustained by a rational adversary whose utility follows the principle of potential loss, $u_{D} = U_{ideal} - U_{actual}$. Starting from the Prisoner's Dilemma, we show that the transformation $u_{i}' = a\,u_{i} + b\,u_{j}$ and the ratio of mutual recognition $w = b/a$ generate a fragile cooperation band $[w_{\min},\,w_{\max}]$ where both (C,C) and (D,D) are equilibria. Extending to a dynamic model with stochastic cooperative payoffs $R_{t}$ and intervention costs $(C_{c},\,C_{m})$, a Bellman-style analysis yields three strategic regimes: immediate destruction, rational stagnation, and intervention abandonment. The appendix further generalizes the utility to a reference-dependent nonlinear form and proves its stability under reference shifts, ensuring robustness of the framework. Applications to social-media algorithms and political trust illustrate how adversarial rationality can deliberately preserve fragility.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Physics-Informed Learning for Multiplayer Differential Games
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Computing per-player feedback strategies in $N$-player adversarial differential games is challenging as the associated coupled Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman system is high-dimensional and generally lacks classical solutions. We address this by approximating viscosity solutions using physics-informed neural networks within a policy iteration scheme with a vanishing-viscosity annealing schedule. Theoretically, we establish an explicit $\varepsilon$-Nash guarantee by bounding per-player regret via computable residuals and prove our method reaches this stopping criterion in finite time. For two-player zero-sum games, we further establish a computable bound on the approximation error of the value function. Numerical experiments on pursuit-evasion scenarios illustrate the tightness of these computed bounds and the framework's scalability to high-dimensional environments.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: Accepted to IEEE Control Systems Letters (L-CSS) with presentation at CDC 2026

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Welfare-Enhancing Mechanism Design for Agent Ecosystems
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: The emerging Agentic Web forms a multi-agent ecosystem: a decentralized service market where the user agent selects which content agents to query from their submitted profiles, before seeing any documents. Profiles therefore become a new target of optimization. Existing Generative Engine Optimization studies how a single supplier rewrites documents the engine can already retrieve, to improve their citation. In the Agentic Web, multiple content agents optimize profiles to compete for limited opportunities to deliver documents. To study this repeated interaction, we build WildRegistry, a simulation framework and benchmark based on a real agentic-search request stream, and model it as a dynamic game under private monitoring. Long-horizon experiments show that this competition lowers website-selection quality and settles at a harmful stable point, which our empirical criterion identifies as an approximate rewriting equilibrium. We therefore design a welfare-enhancing mechanism, DEC (Delivery-Evidence Credit), a platform-side policy that uses recorded delivery outcomes to reallocate later opportunities and reduce information asymmetry. DEC improves this endpoint, raising website-selection quality while preserving most of providers' exposure gains, for a Welfare Gain of +2.01 points and a healthier long-horizon outcome. More broadly, our findings highlight the importance of mechanism design in agent ecosystems: turning recorded delivery outcomes into evidence that endogenously shapes later user-agent selection and content-agent adaptation can steer long-horizon adaptation toward delivered capabilities.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Non-manipulability and Approachability Beyond Two-Player Games
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
We study the problem of guaranteeing non-manipulability and low regret for $n-1$ independent learners in an $n$-player repeated general game with one optimizer. Non-manipulability is a property which guarantees that learning agents can prevent a strategic opponent from exploiting their learning dynamics for its own benefit, while no-regret provides guarantees to a learner with respect to a fixed static benchmark. This problem is well understood in games with a single learner and a single optimizer, where the intersection of non-manipulable and no-regret algorithms is exactly the class of all no-swap regret algorithms. But having multiple independent learners introduces a fundamental constraint: without shared randomness, the learners' joint mixed actions must remain product distributions and individual no-swap regret guarantees need not provide a guarantee of non-manipulability. Our core contributions are as follows.
  We introduce a set of $n-1$ algorithms that $n-1$ learners can play which individually guarantee sublinear swap regret and, when played in conjunction with each other, jointly guarantee non-manipulability against an optimizer. These algorithms require the computation of a Nash equilibrium at every timestep, and we show that this computational cost is inherent in general games. We construct a reduction from computing Nash in $(n-1)$-player games to finding $n-1$ jointly non-manipulable no-external regret algorithms. Therefore, polynomial time algorithms which guarantee multi-learner non-manipulability in conjunction with no-external regret do not exist unless PPAD $\subseteq$ FBPP. In order to construct these algorithms, we develop new techniques for Blackwell approachability beyond $2$-player games. We provide a general characterization for sets which are approachable by $n-1$ players without correlated randomness.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: MidasTUI: Instant Tangible User Interfaces for Wearable Displays using Everyday Objects
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: While wearable displays can bring digital workspaces anywhere, interaction remains limited by mid-air gestures that lack tactile feedback and induce fatigue, or controllers that are cumbersome to carry. We present MidasTUI, a system that instantly transforms arbitrary everyday objects into opportunistic tangible user interfaces through brief interaction demonstrations. For example, a user can slide an earbud case across a table as a mouse, enabling opportunistic interaction without carrying a dedicated input device. MidasTUI detects when a user is holding and moving an object using the wearable display camera and a Transformer-based temporal classifier. It then infers the intended input modality (e.g., slider, mouse, keypad) from hand movement and maps the tracked hand-object interaction to an application function. Our evaluations demonstrate reliable cross-object and cross-user generalization. A comparative user study further shows that grounding interaction in everyday objects reduces physical burden and improves perceived usability and control relative to mid-air interaction.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Supporting Without Taking Over: AI Support in Gratitude Writing
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Gratitude writing can support well-being, but independent practice may lack guidance. Generative AI could help while shaping reflection, agency, and ownership. We investigated how gratitude-writing format and AI-assistance mode influence well-being and writing experiences. In a 2x2 between-subjects study (N=401), participants completed a gratitude reflection or a gratitude letter using two AI-assistance modes: scaffolding, which provided reflective questions after inactivity, or co-writing, which offered inline text suggestions. Participants' well-being improved after using our AI-assisted gratitude-writing system, consistent with the activity's intended benefits. However, participants' experiences revealed a trade-off between the AI-support types: co-writing received higher usability ratings, yet its immediacy could disrupt writing, and greater suggestion acceptance was associated with weaker perceived agency. Scaffolding supported stronger perceived human ownership but was sometimes overlooked. These findings extend human-AI writing research beyond productivity and text quality by showing how AI involvement shapes psychological outcomes and the experience of self-guided, emotionally meaningful writing.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Tap-to-Adapt: Learning User-Aligned Response Timing for Speech Agents
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Aligning speech agents' response initiation with users' expectations remains challenging. We introduce Tap-to-Adapt, a framework for interactive speech systems in which manual activation and interruption provide both immediate response control and online supervision for personalized initiation timing. To learn from sparse corrections and recent feedback, we introduce \emph{Balanced Proximal Replay for History-conditioned Timing} (BPRHT) as its response initiation timing control mechanism, combining frozen speech representations, class-balanced replay with proximal regularization, and recent correction history. We evaluate acoustic backbones for BPRHT on recorded speech and compare update rules and recent-history configurations in simulation. The selected replay and history mechanisms lower simulated correction rates relative to their respective baselines. To reduce new users' cold-start correction burden, we evaluate shared initialization in a two-stage user study. Stage~1 established shared initialization with 20 participants, locking the average of earlier participants' final heads upon parameter and opening-correction plateaus. Stage~2 assigned 48 new participants equally to online adaptation with or without shared initialization, or frozen shared initialization. Online adaptation without shared initialization had more opening corrections per minute than with it (rate ratio 1.69, 95\% confidence interval 1.15--2.49). Final-block correction rates were similar across conditions. Online updates accompanied reported speaking and waiting adjustments. Declining corrections under frozen parameters also suggest user accommodation. Code and 1,000 labeled pilot recordings are available at: https://github.com/ZihongHe/tap_to_adapt

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Procedure Inference as Memory: Learning Recruiter Decision Procedures from OKF-Structured Episodes in Multi-Session Hiring Assistants
Human-Computer Interaction.summary:
Multi-session hiring assistants must infer evolving recruiter preferences and decision patterns across projects and time. We introduce Open Knowledge Format (OKF)-indexed episodic memory to organize interactions and retrieve related events through their lineage. We also introduce Procedure Memory, which learns reusable decision procedures from these episodes through prompted reflection or reinforcement learning. We compare these approaches with no memory, full-history context, and conversation search, and evaluate Jev-class models for index navigation and GPT-5.6 Luna as a lower-cost alternative to GPT-5.4.
  In our evaluation, OKF-indexed retrieval achieves low-priority preference F1 scores of 0.93-0.95 at medium and high preference overlap between hiring projects. It significantly outperforms full-history context and conversation search in both settings, and no memory at high overlap, while using 69% fewer context tokens than full history. Procedure Memory reduces conversational turns by up to 39% relative to no memory. Qualitative and long-horizon evaluations provide evidence of temporal reasoning, with RL-learned procedures achieving 60% on both correct abstention and exact-field identification. Jev-class models improve conversational efficiency but more frequently miss temporally relevant evidence, highlighting the importance of evidence selection.
  On PersonaMem-v2, Procedure Memory with OKF retrieval achieves 50.2% accuracy versus 48.6% for full-history context and 29.0% for no memory, using 90.5% fewer reader input tokens than full history. GPT-5.6 Luna performs comparably to GPT-5.4 at lower cost. These findings highlight the value of structured episodic memory and learned decision procedures for efficient personalization and temporal reasoning.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Includes supplementary appendices with experimental configurations, prompts, evaluation protocols, and learned procedure examples

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Decision-Aligned Value Learning for Selective Adoption of EEG Fusion in Human-Robot Collaboration
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Electroencephalography (EEG) captures neural activity associated with human perception and decision-making. It provides human-robot collaboration (HRC) systems with measurable evidence for event recognition, situation assessment, and action preparation. External sensing cannot easily provide such evidence. However, the quality and complementarity of this evidence vary across samples, and existing EEG fusion methods do not explicitly determine when EEG improves a prediction. We therefore framed selective EEG use as a sample-wise incremental-value estimation problem and proposed Value Estimation and Constraint-Aware Triage for Adoption (VECTA). VECTA separates the generation of an EEG-informed Fusion prediction from the decision about whether it should replace the existing Base prediction. The framework uses system gain to quantify the loss reduction from Base to Fusion and matching gain to assess whether benefits arise from sample-matched EEG. A signed-value learner estimates system gain from decision-time evidence and prioritizes high-value Fusion outputs under budget constraints. Cross-subject evaluations on three HRC datasets showed that matched Fusion outperformed shuffled controls. Estimated gains tracked realized gains, with Spearman correlations of 0.347-0.612 and positive-gain areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROCs) of 0.708-0.842. Under budget constraints, VECTA reduced Brier loss and harmful Fusion adoption and achieved the highest mean normalized AUBC across three datasets among the selective-decision methods evaluated. Validation on three external multi-modal datasets showed that VECTA could be applied directly as a post-hoc decision layer to task-specific predictors without retraining. These results show that selective Fusion adoption can translate the uneven utility of EEG into system-level gains.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Beyond Code and Pixels: Co-Generating Editable and Visually Rich Presentations
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Generating PPTX presentations is a structured task that requires semantic planning, visual composition, precise layout, and editability, motivating collaboration among specialized agents. However, programmatic methods offer editability but often produce rigid designs, while image-based methods provide visual richness but flatten content into difficult-to-edit pixels. A hybrid system can combine these strengths, but must coordinate interdependent decisions across content, layout, and appearance. To address this challenge, we propose SlidesWeaver, a hybrid multi-agent system that coordinates language and vision agents through shared deck- and slide-level states. Specifically, it uses staged multimodal commitment, diffusion-based composition planning, and two generation schedules for different priorities between composition freedom and accurate text preservation, while preserving native text and geometry. Across 1,728 generations spanning 24 system-model configurations, SlidesWeaver achieves consistently superior overall quality across all evaluated dimensions while maintaining structural control, editability, and practical generation efficiency.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: RecField: Embedding Recommendations into Spatial Movie Organization as Affordances for Serendipitous Encounters
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Research on serendipity-oriented recommender systems has focused on algorithms that recommend unexpected yet useful items. However, serendipity is increasingly viewed as a user experience shaped by both algorithmic outputs and system features. This study positions recommendations not as the primary goal users pursue but as an environmental affordance that creates opportunities for discovery during other activities. We propose RecField, a spatial movie organization interface where users freely arrange movies into collection zones. For each collection, RecField provides attribute-based recommendation lists labeled according to their recommendation perspectives. A between-subjects experiment ($N$ = 57) examined the effects of recommendations on discoveries made during a foreground task of creating and organizing personal movie profiles. Although recommendations did not significantly affect environment-level perceived serendipity, ratings of encounter-related aspects tended to be higher, with small effect sizes. At the individual-movie level, favorites in the recommendation condition received significantly higher ratings for stimulating the desire to watch and broadening preferences, but not for novelty or unexpectedness. Notably, only 14\% of evaluated favorites in the recommendation condition were added directly from recommendation lists. Differences in ratings showed similar effect sizes even when the analysis was restricted to favorites added through other routes. These findings suggest that embedded recommendations can contribute to serendipitous experiences both directly through item acceptance and indirectly by prompting users' own exploration and re-evaluation. They also highlight the value of evaluating serendipity at both the environment and item levels and the limitations of relying solely on direct recommendation acceptance rates.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: The Socratic PAUSE: safeguarding scientific judgement at AI speed
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Generative AI can turn a tentative scientific question into hypotheses, methods, code and interpretations within minutes. Yet generating a contribution does not establish that it deserves scientific reliance: researchers must still examine its evidence, assumptions and implications, and remain accountable for the decision to rely on it. Using Einstein's sketch of scientific discovery as a lens, we argue that AI has accelerated discovery far more than justification. In human-AI research partnerships, confidence can therefore outgrow evidence through three mechanisms: recursive reinforcement, loss of provenance and miscalibrated reliance on AI-generated contributions. Verification debt accumulates when such contributions are carried into later claims or decisions without adequate scrutiny. Accordingly, we propose the Socratic Pause as a deliberate checkpoint at consequential decision gates, where an AI contribution remains provisional while a researcher examines its basis. The PAUSE protocol structures this examination through five steps: Pin down the claim, Ask and challenge, Uncover assumptions and alternatives, Scrutinise the evidence and Exercise judgement. It concludes with a recorded decision to accept, revise, reject or defer the contribution. We show how AI research tools can support this practice without displacing human judgement, and outline a framework for evaluating whether it improves verification, decision-making and independent understanding. The aim is to preserve the freedom to explore with AI while ensuring that those responsible for the work can say what was examined, what remains uncertain and why the next step is justified.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Prompt Engineer: Analyzing Hard and Soft Skill Requirements in the AI Job Market
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: The rise of large language models (LLMs) has prompted speculation about a new job role: the prompt engineer. However, empirical evidence on how common such positions are and what skills employers expect of them remains scarce. In this paper, we present a data-driven analysis of a snapshot of LinkedIn job postings for data and AI roles taken in April 2025, after LLMs had entered everyday work but before LLM-based agents became widely adopted. We analyzed 20,662 job postings on LinkedIn for prompt engineers (72 postings) and four established data and AI roles: data scientist, data engineer, data analyst, and machine learning engineer. We find that prompt engineer roles were rare even at this point in time, making up less than 0.5% of the postings across the five roles we sampled. Because our snapshot predates the widespread adoption of LLM-based agents, we argue that the data captures the role of prompt engineer under favorable conditions. Whether its share has since declined is an open question that later snapshots can test. Despite its rarity, prompt engineering has a distinct skill profile. Prompt engineer postings emphasize AI knowledge (22.8%), communication (21.9%), prompt design (18.7%), and creative problem-solving (15.8%). These soft and hard skill requirements differ significantly from those of the four established roles. Taken together, the distinct skill profile and the scarcity of dedicated postings suggest that prompt engineering is best understood not as a profession of its own, but as a distinct skill that is useful across many professions. Our findings inform job seekers, employers, and educators about how to position prompt engineering in the evolving AI workforce.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: On Semiotic-Grounded Interpretive Evaluation of Generative Art
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Interpretation is essential to deciphering the language of art: audiences communicate with artists by recovering meaning from visual artifacts. However, current Generative Art (GenArt) evaluators primarily emphasize surface-level image quality or literal prompt adherence, failing to assess the deeper symbolic or contextual meaning intended by the creator. We formalize this observation using Peircean computational semiotic theory that models Human-GenArt Interaction (HGI) as cascaded semiosis. This framework reveals that artistic meaning is conveyed through iconic, symbolic, and indexical modes, whereas appearance-centered evaluators tend to emphasize the iconic mode. Building on this account, we propose SemJudge, an interpretation-centric evaluation framework that uses a Hierarchical Semiosis Graph (HSG) to reconstruct meaning conveyance from prompt to generated artifact. Experiments on an interpretation-intensive benchmark, SemiosisArt, show that SemJudge aligns more closely with human judgments than existing baselines. User studies further demonstrate that SemJudge produces deeper, more insightful artistic interpretations. We hope these findings pave the way for GenArt to move beyond the generation of "pretty" images toward a medium capable of understanding and expressing complex human experience. Project page: https://github.com/songrise/SemJudge

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Interacting with Alexa: A Longitudinal Case Study of Voice Assistant Use in Down Syndrome
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: As life expectancy for individuals with Down syndrome (DS) continues to increase, supporting cog- nitive engagement, everyday autonomy, and participation throughout adulthood has become an important research priority. Conversational voice assistants have emerged as promising assistive tech- nologies for these purposes, yet evidence regarding their long-term use in naturalistic settings remains limited. This paper presents a longitudinal case study of the everyday use of Amazon Alexa by an adult with Down syndrome over nine months in a real domestic environment. The study combines analyses of interaction logs, audio recordings, and qualitative observations to investigate usage pat- terns, interaction performance, communicative adaptation, and the integration of the voice assistant into everyday life. Results show that Alexa became progressively embedded in daily routines, sup- porting entertainment, information access, and autonomy-related activities. Longitudinal analyses reveal stable interaction patterns, reduced retry behavior, and the emergence of effective communi- cation strategies, while qualitative observations highlight increasing communicative engagement and the value of proactive reminders. The study also identifies important limitations of current commer- cial voice assistants, including reduced robustness to non-normative speech, limited conversational continuity, and poor contextual reasoning. Beyond providing rare ecologically valid evidence of long- term voice assistant use, the findings highlight design considerations that are relevant to the ongoing evolution of LLM-based conversational systems.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 19 pages, 16 figures, submitted to a Journal

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Can You Predict the Next Mind in the Symphony? Toward Multi-Turn Multi-Party Mental World Modeling
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Although multimodal foundation models have achieved remarkable progress in modeling, generation, and embodied reasoning in the physical world, their capacity for modeling the dynamic mental world remains underexplored. Existing benchmarks predominantly focus on static mental state perception or single-turn behavioral reasoning, overlooking the dynamic mental transitions of the observed individuals in multi-party, multi-turn interactions. To bridge this gap, we introduce M$^3$WME-Bench, a benchmark designed to evaluate mental world modeling conditioned on evolving actions of interactants. Specifically, models are tasked with forecasting a target subject's future mental states and behaviors over extended social interactions. In addition to the benchmark suite, we construct M$^3$WME-23K, a dedicated training dataset, and establish a competitive baseline named MindNext-7B. Extensive evaluations across four representative paradigms (general MLLMs, emotion-specialized MLLMs, agentic frameworks, and World Foundation Models) reveal that current systems consistently struggle to anticipate forward-looking mental states. Mechanistic analyses further reveal that existing architectures fundamentally lack forward mental state transition dynamics. Our findings highlight a pivotal challenge in advancing agents from physical to mental world modeling, charting new directions for socially adaptive AI.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Somatic Alignment: Scaffolding Non-Visible Inner Body Sensations in and beyond Vocal Pedagogy
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Inner bodily sensations inform expressive musical performance but can be difficult to interpret and communicate. Through two separate workshops with five singing learners and four senior voice teachers, we investigate breath control in vocal pedagogy. Participants reported difficulty interpreting bodily sensations (Opacity of Inner Sensations) and translating awareness into intended adjustments (Disconnected Regulation of Inner Sensations), alongside strategies involving touch, demonstration, and imagery. Building on these accounts, we propose the Somatic Alignment Model (SAM), connecting an Intrapersonal Self-Sensing Loop with an Intercorporeal Co-Sensing Loop. SAM examines how external guidance relates to learners' bodily calibration and how interpretive and regulatory authority is negotiated. We articulate three generative design dimensions, Modality, Agency, and Temporality, and illustrate their possible applications in interactive learning systems and first-person soma design inquiries. SAM offers a conceptual lens for supporting bodily awareness and regulation through interaction design.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: MERIDIAN: Memory-Encoded Rituals for Intimacy across Distance in an Interactive, Asynchronous Neighbourhood
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: How can shared memories become playable structures for partners who live in different time zones, and what becomes of such a gift once it is in use? We present MERIDIAN, a design case of Yi Town, a bilingual browser game developed by one member of a long-distance couple as a gift for the other. Nine levels translate personally meaningful events, places and cultural references into tasks within a navigable pixel town, framed by a birthday prologue and a fictional wedding. This second version extends the record by four weeks. Drawing on research through design, we reconstruct seven design changes from 152 commits, 36 changelog versions and four design specifications. In those weeks the site gained three products that are not levels: an infirmary for the days after a quarrel, which began with a remark by the recipient; a page for her booked flight, which replaces a symbolic ticket with a real one; and a request box whose messages are answered, while the designer sleeps, by a pipeline of a local language model and a hosted one. The request box ends the first version's claim of no author-operated backend, and we trace where her files now travel. An audit reproduced 263 passing unit tests; the progress model is unchanged and keeps its exhaustive check of 1,024 codes. The answering pipeline was tested in parts, and it began to receive real requests on the night it was built. No recipient evaluation or relationship outcome is reported. The contribution is an inspectable account of design decisions and their trade-offs: between authoring a gift and leaving the recipient free to decline or reshape it, and between being reachable across thirteen hours and answering in person. The site is at https://jingyifan.love and its source is public at https://github.com/rayford295/yi-town.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 27 pages, 25 figures, 11 tables. v2 adds four weeks of record and describes the dashboard, three further products, server, automated answering pipeline, service worker, and pose-analysis program. It corrects the backend claim and updates the audit. See "Changes in Version 2". Design case with no recipient evaluation reported

Human-Computer Interaction.title: GlassGround: GUI Grounding Beyond Native Screenshots with Egocentric Wearable Vision
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Wearable assistants must localize interface elements from camera observations when direct screenshot access is unavailable, yet existing GUI grounding benchmarks primarily evaluate native screenshots. We introduce GlassGround, a new benchmark that pairs native screenshots with wearable camera observations while holding GUI states, instructions, and targets fixed. GlassGround contains 3,250 tasks across Android and iOS, captured using four wearable devices under four viewing conditions. Across ten open-source models, mean grounding accuracy drops from 94.8% on screenshots to 48.5% on camera images. Further analysis reveals that changes in target scale, screen geometry, and background cannot fully explain this performance degradation. We then study two ways to narrow this gap. At inference time, local zooming and screen rectification help but leave most of the gap. For training-time adaptation, we build on GlassGround's paired-view design and introduce PairDistill, a baseline that aligns target representations across views alongside coordinate supervision. Trained on independently collected data and using no screenshots at inference, it improves camera-image accuracy by 9.4 and 12.2 points on two backbones and transfers to unseen devices and operating systems. Combined with local zooming, it reaches 69.6% and 64.4%, but does not close the gap. The GlassGround dataset and code are available at https://github.com/yunnw/GlassGround.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: AI Persona Dialogue Pipeline; From Survey Report to Conversational Personas, Evaluated by LLMs and Experts
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Simulating dialogue of a population with LLM-enacted personas is increasingly common, yet each pipeline is generally built for one task, so a new task usually means reworking how the persona is authored, enacted and evaluated. We present an end-to-end persona dialogue pipeline meant to carry over to other populations as a whole; a background is written by an LLM from a national survey report, an off-the-shelf LLM enacts it without fine-tuning, and both are rated for perceived plausibility. We apply it to thirty personas of Korean older adults living alone; three LLM judges compare eight simulator LLMs, and thirty experts who work with this population evaluate the selected one, GPT-5.5. Experts found the backgrounds and dialogues largely realistic but most often faulted a persona for being more capable than its background said, and agreement between their ratings and the LLM judges could not be established. We release the pipeline, personas and their dialogues.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: RoboJackVR: Turning Robot Tasks into VR Games for Scalable Demonstration Collection
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Scaling robot demonstration datasets requires collection systems that accommodate more participants and diverse tasks, yet teleoperation barriers and task-adaptation effort limit this expansion. We present RoboJackVR, a standalone virtual reality (VR) game in which players manipulate simulated robots to execute combat skills and contribute demonstrations. MuJoCo simulation and demonstration recording run locally on the headset, removing the need for an external PC or simulation server during collection. Tutorials, skill selection, combat consequences, and character progression organize repeated task attempts within a continuing game. Task contracts declare assets, controls, resets, success criteria, and recording semantics; separate game configurations specify guidance, attempt groups, skill effects, and course placement. Shared bindings connect these declarations to task execution, outcome handling, and recording, allowing tasks to reuse the game flow while retaining their control and success semantics. Batch tools package supported resources and generate configurations, with manual adaptation and review for new interfaces and unsupported predicates. We instantiate the approach with SO101-Nexus-derived and LIBERO tasks. On the 66 LIBERO-90 tasks covered by the collected data, ACT policies trained solely on VR demonstrations retain approximately 91% of the full-standard simulation-demonstration baseline's success rate on held-out initial states, averaged over four training seeds. These results support the utility of play-collected VR demonstrations for policy learning in this setting.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Knocking on Minds Door; A Mixed-Methods Field Study of a Voice LLM Companion in Older Adults Daily Lives
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Global aging makes digital technology important for older adults healthy aging, yet graphical user interfaces remain inaccessible to many. Voice agents based on large language models may help, but users needs and reasons for sustained use remain unclear. We developed a phone-call-style companion that initiates conversations proactively and structures calls using a persona, conversation rules, and prior-call memory (facts, insights, relationship background). We conducted a two-week mixed-methods field study with 33 community-dwelling Korean older adults (29 women; aged 67-91), collecting call logs, pre-post questionnaires, and interviews. Participants made 608 calls following a daily-use recommendation; 25 continued afterward despite turn-taking difficulties. Loneliness and depression scores decreased significantly; among loneliness subfactors, only isolation (emotional loneliness) decreased significantly. Participants disclosed concerns withheld from family and linked companionship to being addressed by name, being remembered, and experiencing emotional reciprocity. We propose personalized conversation rules, accessible interaction, and user control over frequency and topics.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: MedGame: Storytelling Gamification Empowered by Large Language Models for Medical Education
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) show promise for medical education, but most existing systems focus on localized interactions such as question answering or single-turn feedback, rather than organizing an entire clinical case into a decision-centered learning trajectory. We introduce \textit{MedGame}, a framework that transforms static clinical cases into structured, executable storytelling games. MedGame uses a dual-engine design: a Medical Narrative Designer synthesizes case-grounded clinical storylines with states and decision nodes, while a Story Director converts them into dependency-aware multimodal orchestration plans rendered by our released interactive platform. We construct MedGame Bench, a 5,000-case benchmark and evaluation protocol for Medical Narrative Generation and Story Direction. Experiments show that task-specific fine-tuning substantially improves open-source LLMs on MedGame Bench and narrows the gap with commercial models. A pilot student study further shows that learners perceive MedGame as more engaging and useful than text-only alternatives.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Work in Progress; an explorational design and study on AI+Education+Game. Updated an author's affiliation. A further revision (v3) is in preparation

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Before They Were Cool: Do Early Fans Abandon Artists Who Suddenly Become Popular? Evidence from Online Music Listening
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Identity-signalling theory, echoed in the hipster's "I liked them before they were cool", expects an artist's first fans to pull away once the artist becomes popular, by leaving or by avoiding what the newcomers play. A rival account expects the event that brings the crowd to renew existing listeners' attention to the artist. We test both in the Last.fm listening histories of 594,415 users (21.1 billion plays, 2005-2013), where every play appears on the user's profile. Study 1 detects 78 crowd arrivals: months in which the number of people discovering an artist tripled without a new album, single or EP, for example after a song appeared in a film. Study 2 compares Grammy and Mercury Prize winners with nominees who won nothing. We compare listeners who had played the artist before the crowd arrived (early fans) with early fans of comparison artists. Early fans did not withdraw. Those still listening stopped less often (25.8% vs. 29.1% over six months), and those who had drifted away returned more often (29.6% vs. 25.0%). Those who kept listening converged on the crowd: the song most newcomers played took a larger share of their plays, with no turn to deep cuts. More lapsed fans returned after larger surges, and neither fans with the most distinctive tastes nor fans facing a more mainstream crowd quit more. Award wins brought few new listeners and no clear change. Where listening is displayed by default, early fans moved towards the crowd after sudden popularity, not away from it.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Evaluating Strategies for Multimodal Bidirectional Interactions between Pedestrians and AVs
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Autonomous Vehicles (AVs) share spaces with Vulnerable Road Users (VRUs) in encounters where driver cues are absent. This can leave people uncertain whether the vehicle has noticed them and understood their request. Existing research has studied how AVs communicate with pedestrians through external human-machine interfaces. This work investigates bidirectional multimodal VRU-AV interactions combining Augmented Reality (AR), speech, and gestures. The study follows four stages: literature synthesis of interactions, a survey with 124 participants, interaction loop implementation, and feasibility evaluation. Participants preferred AR cues that made vehicle motion or warnings explicit, high-level voice commands, and conventional gestures. Prototype measurements revealed a trade-off between faster local processing and more accurate infrastructure-assisted processing. The demonstration shows bidirectional interaction using AR wearables and vehicular communications, while leaving decision-making to the AV. Together, the results support treating AV-VRU interaction as a closed loop of intent expression, recognition, vehicle decision, and feedback.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: EgoCARBS: Egocentric Video Meets Active Acoustics for Kitchen Action Understanding
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Egocentric video records what a person looks at, but often misses what their body does: the hands leave the frame, and arm motion goes unseen. An exocentric camera recovers this context, but it must be installed wherever the activity happens. Active acoustic sensing can recover it from the wearables themselves: a device's speaker emits inaudible chirps, and its microphone senses the motion of the hands, arms, and nearby objects from their echoes. Yet no public dataset pairs it with egocentric video. We present EgoCARBS, with two deliverables. The first is a multimodal dataset and benchmark: 15 participants cook unscripted meals in their own kitchens wearing camera glasses and an off-the-shelf smartwatch that both sense with active acoustics, synchronized with egocentric and exocentric video and the watch's audio and IMU, with 4,019 verb-noun action annotations in 11.4 hours. The second is a study of what the wearables add to egocentric video. On verb recognition, they add at least as much as an exocentric camera for participants seen in training, and even more for new participants, for whom the exocentric camera does not help. Active acoustics alone provides most of this gain, and helps most where the camera does not see the hands. Trimmed action recognition, detection, and anticipation remain open. We will release the data, our data collection and annotation tools, and pre-trained models.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 36 pages (12 main paper and references, 24 supplementary material). Project page: https://saif-mahmud.github.io/projects/ego-carbs

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Designing human and generative AI collaboration: Trade-offs in productivity, satisfaction, and creative diversity
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Rapid advances in generative AI have raised hopes for major productivity gains but recent research has also raised concerns about declining worker satisfaction and reduced creative diversity. While prior research has documented each of these effects individually, it remains unclear how collaboration design shapes the costs that accompany AI-enabled productivity gains. We address this question through a human-subjects experiment on a 1,000-word creative writing task, comparing three human-AI collaboration designs. Completion time was similar across the three designs but quality, satisfaction, and diversity differed across them. The Human Confirmation design, in which AI led ideation, outlining, drafting, and editing while humans primarily confirmed or rejected output, showed the clearest downsides: lower quality and satisfaction, and lower aggregate genre and semantic diversity. By contrast, designs that preserved human involvement in preproduction or throughout the writing process avoided the clearest quality and satisfaction losses without requiring longer overall completion times. Preserving active human involvement in preproduction was also associated with lower aggregate similarity in content than Human Confirmation. These findings show that collaboration design substantially reshapes trade-offs between efficiency, quality, satisfaction, and diversity, suggesting that the central challenge is not whether to adopt AI, but how to allocate creative control between humans and AI. That choice shapes not only the output of creative work but the experience of creative agency.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Published in PNAS Nexus 5(11), pgag353 (2026). Supplementary Information is available with the published article at https://doi.org/10.1093/pnasnexus/pgag353

Machine Learning.title: Tokenisation is not in APX
Machine Learning.summary: In this paper, we prove that, unless P=NP, no polynomial-time algorithm can find a tokeniser whose objective is within any constant factor of the optimum, meaning that tokenisation is not in the APX complexity class.
